title: Preach the Word
subtitle: Why Expository Preaching Still Builds the Church
blurb: The pulpit has become a stage, and the sermon a performance measured by how well it moves a room. This book argues that the preacher's only authority is the text in front of him, that exposition is not a method among methods but the recovery of a church that has stopped expecting God to speak. It is written for the pastor who is tired of being interesting and wants, again, to be faithful.

chapters.title: The Command Beneath the Office
chapters.summary: Paul's charge to Timothy is not advice but an order given under the weight of God and the coming judgment. To preach the word is to obey a command, not to express a gift.
chapters.body:
There is a sentence in the New Testament that should have ended the career of every man who ever stood behind a pulpit to be admired. Paul is in prison. He is going to die, and he knows it, and the next words he writes are not soft. "I charge thee therefore before God, and the Lord Jesus Christ, who shall judge the quick and the dead at his appearing and his kingdom; Preach the word" (2 Timothy 4:1-2). Read it again and notice what it is not. It is not encouragement. It is not a suggestion offered to a younger man with promise. It is a charge laid before the judgment seat, sworn under the name of the God who will sort the living from the dead, and the verb at the center of it is an imperative.

Preach. Herald. Announce what you have been given to announce.

The Greek word is kerusso, and it carries a particular flavor that our soft English "preach" has mostly lost. A herald in the ancient world was not a man with opinions. He was a man with a message that belonged to someone else, usually a king, and his whole job was to deliver that message accurately, publicly, and without alteration. He did not improve the king's words. He did not adjust them to the crowd's mood. He did not water down the parts that would land badly. If he did any of those things he was not a poor herald, he was a traitor, because the authority of his announcement rested entirely on its being the king's announcement and not his own. The moment he started editorializing, he had nothing. His voice carried weight only as long as the words were not his. That is the office Paul is handing to Timothy, and it is the office every preacher inherits, and most of us spend our careers trying to smuggle ourselves back into a job that exists precisely to keep us out of it.

I came to faith out of atheism, and one of the things the church never quite prepared me for was how quickly the sacred can be domesticated by the people who handle it most. I was handed a microphone before I understood what the microphone was for. I assumed, the way most of us assume, that the sermon was the place where I demonstrated that I had something to say. That assumption is the original corruption of the pulpit, and it is so common we have stopped naming it as corruption at all. We call it style. We call it voice. We call it knowing your gifts. Paul calls it nothing. Paul does not ask Timothy whether he has anything to say. Paul tells him what to say, and the thing to say is not his.

I remember the first sermon I ever preached. I had been a Christian for a handful of years and a skeptic for all the years before that, and I stood up in a small room with maybe forty people in it and I had spent the whole week working on me. How would I open. Where would the laugh come. How would I land the thing at the end so they would remember it. I am ashamed to tell you that I barely thought about the text at all until I had already decided what I wanted the night to feel like. I had the order exactly backwards, and nobody corrected me, because the result was that people came up afterward and told me I was good. That word. Good. It is the sweetest poison a young preacher ever drinks, and I drank it down and asked for more.

This is the first wall every preacher hits, and most of us spend a decade pretending it is not there. The word is not yours. You did not write it, you cannot improve it, and on the days you find it dull, the dullness is in you and not in it. The office of preaching is not the platform for a man's insight. It is the conscript service of a herald who carries a message he did not compose and may not edit. John Stott, in Between Two Worlds, called the preacher a bridge between the ancient text and the modern world, and the image is useful as far as it goes, but a bridge does not get to decide where the road leads. It only spans the distance. The traffic is not its own. A bridge that wants to be admired for its own architecture has forgotten that people are trying to get somewhere across it.

Consider the setting of Paul's charge, because the setting is the argument. He invokes God. He invokes Christ as judge. He invokes the appearing and the kingdom. He stacks four eschatological realities on top of one another before he ever reaches the verb, and the effect is to crush every smaller motive a preacher might bring to the task. You cannot stand under that sentence and still be primarily interested in whether the congregation found you compelling. The judgment of the room is swallowed by the judgment of the throne. Spurgeon, who knew more about holding a crowd than any of us, said he trembled lest he should preach himself and not Christ, and that trembling was not false modesty. It was the only sane response to the charge. A man who does not tremble has not understood what he is holding.

Look at the words that follow the command, because Paul does not leave the imperative bare. "Be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine" (2 Timothy 4:2). In season and out. That is, when it is welcome and when it is not, when the room is leaning in and when the room has folded its arms, when the culture applauds the message and when the culture has decided the message is hateful. The preacher does not get to wait for the favorable season. He is on duty in all weather. And the three verbs that follow, reprove and rebuke and exhort, are not the verbs of a man trying to be liked. They are the verbs of a physician, a father, a watchman. They cut, and they correct, and they call, and they do all of it, Paul adds, with longsuffering and doctrine, which is to say with patience and with content. Not patience without content, which is sentimentality. Not content without patience, which is cruelty. Both, held together, under the weight of the charge.

And then Paul tells Timothy why the charge is urgent, and the reason is sobering. "For the time will come when they will not endure sound doctrine; but after their own lusts shall they heap to themselves teachers, having itching ears" (2 Timothy 4:3). Itching ears. There is the whole problem in a phrase. The people will gather teachers who scratch the itch, who tell them what their appetites already want to hear, who turn the pulpit into a service window where the customer orders and the preacher delivers. Paul saw it coming two thousand years ago and named it exactly. The danger to the church has never primarily been the wolf at the door. It has been the appetite in the pew, and the preacher willing to feed it, and the two of them entering into a quiet contract in which the people get comfort and the preacher gets affection and the word gets edited down to whatever both parties can stand.

I have watched the office decay in slow motion across my own ministry, and the decay rarely announces itself. It does not begin with a pastor deciding to abandon Scripture. It begins with a pastor deciding that Scripture needs his help to be heard. He starts with the text and then drifts toward the illustration that lands better than the text did. He notices which sentences earn the nods and which earn the silence, and being human, being a man who wants to be useful, he leans toward the nods. Within a few years the text has become the pretext, a verse read at the top to bless a talk that would have existed without it. The congregation does not notice the substitution because the substitution feels like care. It feels like relevance. It is theft, and it is theft we have learned to praise.

I want to slow down on the phrase "itching ears," because it diagnoses a sickness that has gotten worse, not better, since Paul named it. An itch is not a pain. An itch is a low, persistent demand for a particular sensation, and the relief it craves is not health but scratching, and the scratching makes the itch worse, which is the whole trap. A congregation with itching ears does not want to be healed. It wants to be scratched. It wants the sermon that produces a familiar, pleasant sensation, the sermon that confirms what it already believes and flatters what it already wants and leaves it feeling good about itself on the drive home. And there is always a preacher willing to provide the scratching, because the scratching is rewarded, with attendance and affection and offerings and influence, and the preacher who scratches will always out-draw the preacher who heals, at least in the short run, at least until the catastrophe comes that scratching cannot touch. Paul is warning Timothy that this will be the dominant market condition of ministry, that the demand will run toward the scratch and away from the cure, and that his job is to preach the cure anyway, in season and out, against the appetite, knowing the appetite will not thank him for it.

There is a moment I think about often, late on a Saturday night, when the sermon is more or less done and I am tired and the choices have already been made. By then it is too late to fix anything fundamental. The shape of the thing is set. And in that moment I sometimes feel a quiet panic, the question rising up underneath all the preparation: is this true, or is this just good? Have I built a sermon that obeys the text, or a sermon that will work the room? Because those two questions feel almost identical from the inside, and a man can answer the second while believing he answered the first. The Saturday-night panic, when it is honest, is the conscience asking the herald whether he has delivered the king's message or his own. Most Saturday nights I am too tired to answer it well. But the question is the right question, and the fact that it still rises is, I think, a mercy, a sign that the office has not yet fully decayed into performance in me, that some part of me still knows the difference and still cares which one I have produced.

Martyn Lloyd-Jones, in Preaching and Preachers, refused to let the matter rest on technique. He insisted that preaching is theology coming through a man who is on fire, and that the great need of the church was not better methods but men who had been mastered by the truth before they presumed to deliver it. I think he was right, and I think his diagnosis cuts against the grain of everything our era rewards. We reward the man who has mastered the room. Scripture commissions the man who has been mastered by the word. Those are not the same man, and the distance between them is the distance between a performer and a herald.

I think about young men I have mentored over the years through the Pastors Connection Network, men just starting out, and the thing I most want them to understand at the beginning is the thing I understood last, which is that the call to preach is not first a call to speak but a call to obey. Everything in their formation has pointed them the other way. They have been admired for their gifts, told they have something to say, encouraged to develop their voice, and all of that has trained them to think of preaching as self-expression, the offering of their insight to a waiting world. And then they arrive in an actual pulpit, before actual people with actual sorrows, and the question that the moment poses is not what do you have to say but will you say what you have been given to say, faithfully, whether or not it expresses you, whether or not it shows your gifts, whether or not it lands the way you hoped. The shift from the first question to the second is the whole of a preacher's maturing, and it usually takes years, and some men never make it, spending decades expressing themselves from behind a Bible they never actually submitted to. I tell the young men: the day you realize that the pulpit is not yours to express but yours to obey is the day you actually become a preacher, and until that day you are a gifted person with a platform, which is a more dangerous thing than you currently understand. The gift is real. Thank God for it. But the gift was never the call. The obedience is the call, and the gift is only its servant.

So what does it mean, concretely, to obey the charge rather than fill the office? It means the text sets the agenda before I do. It means that when I open the passage on Monday I am not asking what I want to say this week but what this passage says, and I am binding myself to that answer even when it is inconvenient, even when it preaches against me, even when it will not flatter the people I most want to flatter. It means I preach what is there. Not what I wish were there. Not what the moment seems to demand. What is there. I sit down with the open book and a legal pad and I write at the top of the page, before anything else, the question that governs the whole week: what is this saying, and what does the One who said it want done about it. Everything else is downstream of that question, and the day I stop asking it honestly is the day I become a man with a microphone and no commission.

Augustine understood this fifteen hundred years before any of our anxieties about relevance. In the fourth book of On Christian Doctrine he turned to the question of Christian eloquence and concluded that the preacher's eloquence must serve the truth and never the reverse, that a wise man speaking obscurely is better than a fool speaking beautifully, and that the highest skill is the skill that disappears so the matter can be seen. He did not despise rhetoric. He had taught it for a living, had stood in front of paying students in Carthage and Rome and Milan and made his bread by the beauty of his sentences. But he subordinated it, completely and without apology, to the thing being said. That subordination is the whole ballgame. The moment the saying becomes more important than the said, you have left the office of herald and entered the trade of entertainer, and you will be paid accordingly, in the currency of applause that means nothing on the day Paul described.

Let me put the objection that is surely forming, because I would be forming it if I were reading this. Someone says: but God gave me gifts, a voice, a mind, a way with words, and surely he gave them to be used, surely it dishonors the Giver to bury them. And that is true, as far as it goes. The gifts are real and they are given and they are meant to be used. But notice the difference between a gift used and a gift displayed. A surgeon's hands are a gift, and we want them used, skillfully, to the limit of their ability, on the operating table. But we do not want the surgeon to spend the operation admiring his own hands, or pausing to show the gallery how gracefully he moves, or choosing the more elegant incision over the one the patient actually needs because the elegant one shows off his training. The gift is for the patient, not for the surgeon's reputation, and a surgeon who forgets that is dangerous precisely in proportion to his skill. So with the preacher. Use every gift God gave you, to the hilt, in the service of the message. But the instant the gift becomes the point, the instant you are preaching to display the gift rather than to deliver the word, you have taken a thing God gave for the people and turned it toward yourself, and the more impressive the gift, the more impressive the theft.

I am inside this indictment. I have preached myself. I have stood up with a text I had not loved enough to obey and dressed it in a delivery I had practiced more than I had prayed over. I know the particular guilt of watching a room respond to a sentence I knew was mine and not God's, and feeling, for one ugly second, glad. That second is the sickness. Naming it is the beginning of health. I have five sons, and one of the things being a father has taught me is that children can tell the difference between a man who is performing fatherhood and a man who is actually present in it. They know. They always know. A congregation is no different. They can tell, over time, whether the man up front is showing them himself or handing them God, and the strange mercy is that even when they cannot name what they are receiving, their souls keep the books accurately.

I want to sit with the four realities Paul stacks before the verb, because most of us read past them as a pious flourish and they are not a flourish, they are the whole pressure of the sentence. God. The Lord Jesus Christ. The judging of the living and the dead. The appearing and the kingdom. Paul could have said, Timothy, preach the word, and left it there, and the command would have stood. Instead he buries the command under four mountains, and the burying is deliberate, because he wants the weight of those four realities to crush every smaller motive before Timothy ever reaches the imperative. Think about what each one does. God: the preacher is not finally accountable to his board or his denomination or his audience but to God himself, who is watching, who hears every sermon, before whom the preacher stands whether he remembers it or not. Christ: the One whose word it is, the One the preaching exists to declare, is himself present, not an absent founder but a living Lord who knows whether his herald is faithful. The judgment of the living and the dead: a day is coming when every sermon will be weighed, when the preacher will answer not for how the room responded but for whether he delivered the message, and the dead he preached to will be there, and so will the living, and so will he. The appearing and the kingdom: the whole enterprise is oriented toward a future consummation, a return, a kingdom that makes the applause of the present moment look as small as it actually is. Stack those four together and the room shrinks. The thing you were so worried about, whether they liked you, whether the sermon landed, whether you came across well, evaporates under the weight of who is actually watching and what is actually coming. That is what the four realities are for. They are not decoration. They are the pressure that makes a herald out of a performer, and a preacher who never feels that pressure has never really read the verse he claims to obey.

The charge of 2 Timothy 4 does not lighten as a man grows older in ministry. It grows heavier, because the years add up to a longer list of sermons he will answer for. Paul wrote it from a cell, weeks from execution, with nothing left to gain and nothing left to protect, which is exactly why it is so clean. A man with nothing to protect tells the truth. The truth is that the pulpit is not a stage you have earned. It is a command you have been handed.

Preach the word.

Not because it works. Not because it fills the room. Because you were told to, by a dying man who was told by a risen one, and the judgment seat is real.
chapters.verdict: The pulpit is not yours to fill. It is yours to obey.
reflect: When did you last feel the weight of the charge rather than the pressure of the room?
What are you preaching that you could not defend before God and the living and the dead?
If preaching is obedience before it is art, what would change in how you prepare?

chapters.title: When the People Wept at the Reading
chapters.summary: Nehemiah 8 shows the pattern that founds all expository preaching: the text read clearly, explained faithfully, and the people responding to God rather than to the speaker. The model is older than the church.
chapters.body:
Before there was a sermon there was a reading, and the reading made grown men weep. It is one of the most exact pictures of expository preaching anywhere in Scripture, and it sits in a book most Christians skim, in a chapter about a wall. Nehemiah has rebuilt Jerusalem's defenses. The rubble is cleared. And then, with the work done, the people do something stranger than building: they ask for the book. "And they spake unto Ezra the scribe to bring the book of the law of Moses, which the LORD had commanded to Israel" (Nehemiah 8:1). Notice who initiates. Not the priest. The people. They have been without the word so long that the hunger for it has become a public demand, and they gather as one man in the street before the Water Gate and ask to hear what God said.

Set the scene, because the scene matters. This is around 444 B.C., generations after the exile carried Judah off to Babylon, decades after the first returns under Zerubbabel and Ezra. These are people who have come home to a city that does not feel like home, who have just finished, under Nehemiah's hard-driving leadership, the rebuilding of a wall in fifty-two days against active opposition. They are tired. They have every reason to want a celebration, a rest, a festival of their own accomplishment. And instead, on the first day of the seventh month, they assemble and they ask not for a party but for the law. They want to hear God. After everything, after the labor and the threats and the exhaustion, the deepest hunger that surfaces is the hunger to be addressed by the One they had nearly forgotten how to hear. I find that almost unbearably moving. It tells me what people actually want underneath what they say they want, and it rebukes every assumption I make about what my own tired congregation can bear on a Sunday.

What follows is the founding template, and it is so simple that its simplicity is the scandal. Ezra stood on a wooden platform built for the purpose. He opened the book in the sight of all the people, and when he opened it, the people stood. He read from morning until midday, which is to say for hours, to a standing crowd, and the crowd did not thin out. And then comes the sentence that should be carved over the door of every seminary that has ever existed: "So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading" (Nehemiah 8:8). Read the text. Give the sense. Cause the understanding. That is exposition. That is the whole of it, twenty-five centuries before Haddon Robinson wrote Biblical Preaching and gave us the vocabulary of the big idea. The Levites did not have his vocabulary. They had his practice.

Look at the order, because the order is the doctrine. First the reading, distinctly. The word comes before the explanation, and it comes whole. There is no sermon yet, only Scripture, read with enough care that the words themselves land. We have nearly lost this. In a great many evangelical services the public reading of Scripture has shrunk to a single verse flashed on a screen, a pretext cleared away in eight seconds so the talking can begin. In Nehemiah the reading lasts hours, and the reading itself is treated as the event. The explanation serves the reading. It does not replace it. A church that will not read the Bible aloud, at length, in the assembly, has already decided that its own commentary is more interesting than its text, and that decision is the seed of everything that goes wrong later.

I want to press on this, because it is a small thing that turns out to be a large thing. Paul told Timothy to give attention to the public reading of Scripture (1 Timothy 4:13), and he listed it first, before exhortation and before doctrine, as though the reading were the foundation the other two stood on. When was the last time you sat in a service where the Scripture reading was treated as a holy event and not as a transition? I made a change in our church some years ago that embarrassed me at first by how much it cost me. I started reading longer passages aloud, slowly, without comment, and not rushing to my notes. The first few weeks it felt like dead air. I could feel myself wanting to break in, to do something, to be useful. And then, gradually, something shifted in the room. People began to listen differently. A man told me, months later, that he had heard a passage he had read a hundred times and for the first time it had frightened him, just from the reading, before I said a word. The reading did that. Not me. The word, given room, did its own work, and all I had done was stop interrupting it.

Then, the giving of the sense. The Hebrew suggests a translating, an opening up, a making plain of what the words mean. The people had been in exile; many spoke Aramaic now; the law needed to be carried across a gap of language and time. This is the work of the expositor exactly. He stands between an ancient text and a present people and he does not invent a bridge of his own design. He carries the meaning that is already there across the distance that has opened up. He gives the sense. He does not impose a sense. There is a universe of difference between explaining what the text says and using the text to say what you had already planned to say, and Nehemiah 8 lands hard on the right side of it. The sense given is the text's own. The Levites moved through the crowd, the passage tells us, helping the people understand, so that the meaning was not locked up in one platform but carried out into the whole assembly. That is a picture of a teaching church, not a performing one. The goal was comprehension, distributed, not impression, concentrated.

I want to pause on the help the Levites gave, because it tells us something about the shape of a healthy church that we have largely lost. The text says they helped the people to understand, that they moved among the assembly making the law plain, so that the understanding was not concentrated in one gifted man on a platform but distributed through many teachers out among the people. The whole event was structured for comprehension, not for impression. Compare that to the typical modern arrangement, where one man on a stage does all the teaching and the people are arranged in rows to receive it passively, and where the success of the gathering is measured by how the one man performed. Nehemiah's gathering had a platform and a primary reader, yes, but it also had a whole tier of teachers working to make sure the people actually understood, which tells me that the goal was never the performance of the reader but the comprehension of the people, never the impression made but the understanding produced. A church organized around comprehension looks different from a church organized around impression. It has many who can teach, not just one who performs. It measures itself by whether the people understand and obey, not by whether the preacher dazzled. And it produces, over time, a body of people who know the word, where the impression-centered church produces a body of people who admire the man. The difference goes all the way back to this chapter, to whether you are gathering people to be impressed or to understand, and the structure of your church will quietly answer that question whether you mean it to or not.

And then the result, which is the part no preacher can manufacture. The people wept. They wept at the word, and Nehemiah and Ezra and the Levites had to calm them, telling them the day was holy and they should not mourn but rejoice, for the joy of the LORD was their strength (Nehemiah 8:9-10). I want every young preacher to see and hold this: the weeping was a response to the word, not to the men. Ezra had not told a moving story. He had not built to an emotional crescendo. He had read the law and explained it, and the law itself, understood, broke the people open. Their conviction came from the text. This is the test of whether a sermon has actually been expository. After it is over, are the people responding to God, or to the preacher? Have they met the word, or have they merely admired the man?

And notice what the leaders did with the weeping. They did not exploit it. A lesser shepherd would have seen a room full of weeping people and pressed the advantage, milked the moment, prolonged the emotion for its own sake or for his. Instead they turned the people from mourning to joy, refusing to let even genuine conviction calcify into despair, sending them home to eat and drink and share with those who had nothing. The emotion served a purpose beyond itself. It was not the product. It was the byproduct of an encounter, and a faithful leader handles the byproduct gently and keeps pointing past it to the One who caused it. I have learned to be suspicious of my own ability to produce tears in a room. Tears are easy to manufacture and dangerous to trust. The tears that matter are the ones the word itself drew out, and those I had nothing to do with except to get out of their way.

There is a detail in the chapter that I almost passed over for years until it stopped me cold. After the first day of reading and weeping and rejoicing, the leaders gather again on the second day to study the law more closely, and they discover, in the reading, a command they had forgotten, the command to keep the Feast of Booths, to live in temporary shelters for a week as a remembrance of the wilderness. And they do it. They obey the text the same day they discover it. They go out and gather branches and build the booths and keep the feast, and the passage says there had not been such joy since the days of Joshua (Nehemiah 8:13-17). Think about what that means. The reading of the word did not stop at emotion. It moved into obedience, immediate and costly and public, a whole nation reorganizing its living arrangements because the text said to. That is the full circle of exposition. The word is read, the sense is given, the understanding comes, the heart is broken, and then the life changes, and the changed life produces a deeper joy than the people had known in generations. We tend to stop the circle at the emotion. We measure a sermon by whether it moved people, and we forget that the moving was always meant to produce the obeying, and that the joy Nehemiah's people found was not the joy of having felt something on the first day but the joy of having obeyed something on the second. A sermon that produces tears and no obedience has stopped halfway. The tears were never the point. The booths were the point.

Walter Brueggemann argued in Finally Comes the Poet that the preacher's task is to speak in a way that lets the holy interrupt our settled prose, that the sermon is the moment a community might be addressed by Another and not merely informed by a peer. Nehemiah 8 is that interruption in its purest form. The people came to hear about a wall, perhaps, or to celebrate a finished project. What met them was the voice of God in his own words, and it leveled them. The poet did not generate the holiness. He let it through. That is the most a preacher can do, and it is enough, and it is everything.

There is a question buried in this chapter that every preacher has to answer, and Nehemiah 8 answers it before we even ask: who is the central figure in your service, the preacher or the book? In Nehemiah's assembly the central figure was unmistakably the book. They sent for it, they stood when it was opened, the whole event was organized around its reading, and Ezra, for all his prominence, was its servant and not its rival. Walk into a great many modern services and ask the same question and the answer is different. The central figure is the preacher, or the music, or the experience, and the book has been reduced to a supporting role, a verse or two summoned to lend authority to a service that is really about other things. The architecture tells you, the lighting tells you, the order of service tells you, the proportions tell you, what the gathering is actually centered on, and the centering preaches a sermon louder than anything said from the platform. A church whose every signal says the preacher is the center will produce people who came to see the preacher, and a church whose every signal says the book is the center will produce people who came to hear God, and the difference is set long before the sermon begins, in the thousand small decisions about what the gathering is built around. Build it around the book. Let the reading be central, the word prominent, the preacher visibly subordinate to the text he serves, so that everything in the room, before a word is preached, declares that this is a place where God speaks and we have come to listen, which is exactly what Nehemiah's assembly declared by standing when the book was opened.

I have learned, slowly and against my instincts, to trust the reading. There were years I treated the Scripture reading in our service as throat-clearing, a thing to get past so I could get to my carefully built remarks. I was wrong, and the wrongness was a kind of unbelief. If I believed the word was living and powerful and sharper than any two-edged sword, I would not have rushed it. I rushed it because somewhere underneath I believed my explanation was the sharp thing and the reading was the dull preliminary. That is the heresy of the modern pulpit stated plainly, and most of us are guilty of it without ever having confessed it as heresy.

I want to dwell on the standing, because it is a small physical detail that carries an enormous theology. When Ezra opened the book, all the people stood up (Nehemiah 8:5). They did not stand because Ezra was important. They stood because the book was being opened, because the word of God was about to be read, and standing was their bodies' confession that something holy was happening, that they were in the presence of a King's words and that you do not lounge in the presence of a King. We have lost this almost entirely, and I am not arguing for a liturgical rule about posture. I am pointing at what the posture revealed. Those people believed that when the book was opened, God was about to speak, and the belief was so real it moved their bodies. Ask yourself, honestly, whether your congregation believes that. Ask whether you believe it. When you open the text on a Sunday, is the room braced for an encounter with the living God, or is it settling in for a presentation by a competent man? The difference between those two postures is the difference between a church that expects God to speak and a church that has quietly stopped expecting it, and the second church can have excellent preaching and still be dead, because preaching is not finally a transfer of information but the occasion of an encounter, and where the encounter is no longer expected, the information does its work alone, which is to say it puffs up and does not build.

There is one more thing in this chapter I cannot leave alone, and it is the timing. The reading happened after the wall was finished, not before. Nehemiah had spent himself and driven his people half to death building those defenses, and there was a logic that said the wall was the point, that security was the achievement, that now they could rest in their accomplishment. And instead the achievement turned out to be the prelude. The wall was never the point. The wall was so that the city could exist so that the people could gather so that the book could be read so that God could be heard. All that labor, all that danger, all that fifty-two-day exhaustion, and the purpose of it was to create a place where the word of God could be read to a gathered people. I find that a sharp word to every pastor who has ever mistaken the building of his church for the point of his church. We build walls. We raise buildings, grow attendance, balance budgets, manage staffs, and somewhere in all of it we can forget that every wall we build exists for one reason, to create a space where the book can be opened and the people can hear God. The wall is not the point. The hearing is the point. Nehemiah knew it, which is why a book about a wall ends, at its climax, not with the wall but with the word.

John Calvin, in Geneva, preached through books of the Bible verse by verse, sometimes returning after an exile to take up the very next verse where he had left off years before, as if the interruption had been a weekend. The continuity was the statement. The text, not the calendar and not the crisis, set the order of his preaching. He trusted that if he simply gave the sense of the next passage, week after week, the whole counsel of God would be delivered to his people without his having to decide which parts they needed. That trust is the spine of the expository method, and it rests on the conviction Nehemiah's people demonstrated: that the book itself is sufficient, that the people are starving for it, and that when it is read distinctly and explained faithfully, God himself addresses the assembly.

I want to draw out one more thing from the giving of the sense, because it answers a question pastors ask me constantly, which is how exposition relates to teaching, whether the sermon should explain or exhort, whether the people need information or motivation. Nehemiah 8 refuses the choice. The Levites gave the sense, which is explanation, the careful making-plain of what the words mean, and the explanation itself produced the response, the weeping and then the joy and then the obedience. There was no separate motivational appeal bolted onto the end of the teaching. The understanding was the motivation. When the people grasped what the law actually said, the grasping moved them, because the truth, truly understood, has its own power to move, and does not need the preacher's emotional manipulation added on top. This corrects a deep error in modern preaching, the assumption that explanation is dry and that the preacher must therefore supply the heat himself, must follow his careful exposition with a passionate appeal to make up for the coldness of the teaching. But faithful explanation is not cold. The coldness, when it comes, is usually a sign that the explanation was not deep enough, that the preacher gave the surface sense rather than the real sense, the dictionary meaning rather than the meaning that grips. When Ezra and the Levites gave the real sense, when the people genuinely understood what God had said, the understanding broke them open, and no one had to manufacture the breaking. Aim for that. Aim to make the text so clear and so deep that the clarity itself moves the people, and you will find you need far less of the artificial heat that lesser preaching depends on, because the word, truly understood, carries its own fire.

The platform Ezra stood on was built of wood and would not have lasted. The pattern he enacted on it has outlasted every empire since. Read the word. Give its sense. Let the understanding come. And then step back, because what happens next is not yours to engineer.

The people wept. They wept because they had heard, at last, the voice they had been built to hear. No preacher gets to take credit for that. Every preacher gets to make room for it, or refuse to.
chapters.verdict: Exposition did not begin as a method. It began as obedience to a recovered book.
reflect: Does your congregation respond to the text, or to you?
What would it mean for your sermon to "give the sense" rather than supply your own?
When did the word last reduce your people to silence or tears?

chapters.title: Two Trades That Wear the Same Robe
chapters.summary: Exposition and topical performance can look identical from the pew, but they answer to different masters. One submits to the text; the other recruits the text to a cause already chosen.
chapters.body:
A man can preach a topical sermon that is more faithful to Scripture than another man's verse-by-verse exposition, and pretending otherwise is how the expository cause makes itself ridiculous. So let me say the hard thing first, against my own team. The form is not the virtue. A preacher can march straight through a book of the Bible, paragraph by paragraph, and still be doing the very thing exposition exists to forbid: using the text as a stage from which to deliver his own opinions, dressed in the costume of verse references. The structure is not the safeguard. The submission is.

I have heard verse-by-verse preaching that was a disgrace, and I have heard topical preaching that made me want to fall on my face. I have heard a man walk through Romans a paragraph at a time and never once let Paul's argument actually carry the sermon, treating each verse as a diving board off which to launch into whatever was on his own mind that week. And I have heard a man take up the single subject of suffering, gathering texts from Job and the Psalms and Romans and First Peter, and submit himself so completely to each one that by the end you felt you had been handed the mind of God on the matter rather than the opinion of a clever pastor. So do not hear me defending a method as though the method were holy. I am defending a posture, and the posture can live or die inside either method.

That said, the two trades are real, and they are different, and the difference matters more than almost anything else a preacher decides. Exposition lets the text set the agenda. Topical performance brings an agenda and goes looking for texts. From the pew the two can look identical. Both quote the Bible. Both reach a conclusion. Both may move the room. But they answer to different masters, and over years the master shows.

There is a way the two trades reveal themselves over a long series, and it is worth watching for in your own preaching. Take a man through an entire book of the Bible and ask, at the end, whether the people now know that book or whether they merely heard a series of the preacher's reflections loosely attached to its verses. The expositor who preached through Romans leaves his people knowing Romans, able to trace its argument, to see how chapter builds on chapter, to understand the letter as the unified thing Paul wrote rather than as forty disconnected sermon texts. The topical performer who preached through Romans, treating each passage as a launching pad, leaves his people knowing the preacher's forty reflections and not knowing Romans at all, unable to say what the letter as a whole was doing, because the preacher never let the letter as a whole drive anything; he used its verses as occasions for sermons that could have been preached from anywhere. This is the deepest difference, that the expositor teaches the book and the performer uses the book, and over a long series the difference compounds into two completely different congregations, one that has been given the Scriptures and one that has been given the preacher. I have preached both ways in my life, to my shame, have marched through a book while actually preaching myself, and the test that exposed me was always this: when it was over, did the people know the book, or did they only know me? More often than I want to admit, the honest answer was the second, and the marching through the book had been a costume worn over a ministry that was still, underneath, about the man.

Here is the test, and it is brutally simple. In a genuinely expository sermon, the main point of the sermon is the main point of the passage. Haddon Robinson built his whole approach in Biblical Preaching around this, the discipline of finding what he called the big idea of the text and submitting the entire sermon to it. The preacher does not decide what to talk about. The passage decides, and the preacher's labor is to discover that decision and obey it. In a topical performance the preacher decides first, then assembles texts that support the verdict already reached. The texts are witnesses called by the prosecution. They are not permitted to testify against the case.

Let me give you a worked example, because the abstraction will not bite the way an actual passage will. Take the parable of the prodigal son in Luke 15. A topical performer who has decided this week to preach on the love of God will use that parable to illustrate the love of God, and he will not be wrong to do so, because the love of God is unmistakably in the story. But watch what he leaves out. He will linger on the father running down the road and skip lightly over the elder brother, because the elder brother does not fit the subject he chose. He will arrive at the embrace and stop there. Now watch the expositor. The expositor notices that the parable is the third of three in a chapter that opens with the Pharisees grumbling that Jesus receives sinners and eats with them (Luke 15:1-2). He notices that the elder brother is not a footnote but the point Jesus is driving toward, the figure who refuses to come in to the feast, the religious man who has served faithfully and resents grace extended to the undeserving. He notices that the parable is unfinished on purpose, that we never learn whether the elder brother goes in, because the Pharisees Jesus is addressing have not yet decided, and the open ending is aimed at them and at us. The expositor cannot preach only the love of the father. He must preach the parable, and the parable is about two lost sons, and the more dangerous lostness is the one that looks like obedience. The topical man got a true thing. The expositor got the thing the text was actually saying, which included a knife the topical man left in the drawer.

I want to be careful, because there is an honest topical preaching that the expository tradition has no quarrel with. When a congregation faces a particular crisis, when a doctrine must be taught in its fullness across the whole canon, when a man preaches on marriage or money or suffering and gathers the Scriptures that speak to it, he can do this in submission to the texts he gathers, letting each one say what it says and refusing to make it say more. That is topical method under expository discipline, and the best preachers move between book studies and topical series without ever loosening their grip on the principle. Lloyd-Jones, who is sometimes claimed as a pure verse-by-verse man, in fact preached topically when the occasion called for it, and preached it well, because his submission did not depend on his structure.

I have come to think the most reliable diagnostic for the reversal is to ask a simple question after any sermon, mine or anyone's: could a hearer who paid attention reconstruct the passage from the sermon, or could they only reconstruct the preacher's point? In genuine exposition, the sermon is a window onto the text, and a careful hearer comes away knowing more about what that passage actually says, how it argues, where it goes, what it emphasizes. He could turn to it later and recognize it, because the sermon showed it to him. In topical performance, the sermon is a window onto the preacher's idea, and the hearer comes away knowing the preacher's point but not the passage, having watched the text get used without ever quite seeing it, so that if he turned to the passage later he would not recognize the thing the sermon supposedly came from. Apply this to your own preaching honestly and it is a wounding test, because most of us discover that more of our sermons illuminate our points than illuminate the texts, that we have been teaching people our conclusions while leaving them unable to find those conclusions in the Bible for themselves. The fix is not complicated, though it is humbling. Spend more of the sermon actually opening the text, showing the people how it works, walking them through the argument or the story so that they see it, and less of the sermon on the point you want to make, trusting that a text genuinely opened makes its own point more powerfully than your summary of it ever could. Show them the passage. Do not just tell them your idea about the passage. The window should open onto the word, and when it does, the people learn not only the truth but where the truth came from, which is the thing that lets them find it again alone.

The corruption is not topicality. The corruption is the reversal of authority. The corruption is the sermon in which the preacher's point is the master and the Bible is the servant, summoned to lend its dignity to a conclusion the preacher would have reached without it. You can hear the reversal if you listen for it. The proof-text that does not actually say what the preacher claims it says. The verse lifted clean out of its paragraph and made to stand for something its own context contradicts. The relentless return, in every sermon by a particular man, to the same three or four themes regardless of what the passage in front of him is about. That last one is the tell. When a preacher's text changes every week but his sermon never does, he is not expositing anything. He is broadcasting himself on a Scriptural frequency.

I have done this. I have a handful of ideas I love, convictions I came to hard and hold dear, and there were years when every passage I touched somehow arrived at one of them. I told myself this was integration, the connecting of theology to life that I believe in. It was not integration. It was a leash. I had the text on a leash and I was walking it toward my own backyard, and a member of my church, an older man who had heard more sermons than I had preached, told me so, gently, after about the fortieth sermon that ended where the last thirty-nine had ended. He did not say it unkindly. He said, "Pastor, I've started to be able to guess where you're going to land by Tuesday." That sentence cost me a night's sleep. He was right. The text was not setting my agenda. My agenda was using the text for cover, and a man who loved me enough to say so had heard what I could not hear about myself.

Augustine, in On Christian Doctrine, warned against the man who twists obscure passages to support a meaning he favors, and noted that even when the favored meaning is true, the method that arrives at it through abuse of the text is corrupt and trains the hearer in a corrupt way of reading. This is the long damage of topical performance, the damage that outlives any single sermon. It teaches a congregation that the Bible is a quarry for whatever building you have already decided to build. It teaches them that meaning is something you bring to a text rather than something you receive from it. And a congregation trained that way cannot read its own Bible, because it has only ever seen the Bible used and never seen it obeyed. The expository preacher, week after week, is teaching his people how to read, not only what to think. He is modeling submission to a text they will one day open alone.

Let me give one more worked example, a harder one, because the prodigal son is almost too easy and someone will say the principle only works on the obvious passages. Take a difficult one, the imprecatory psalms, the psalms that pray for God to break the teeth of the wicked, to dash their infants against the rocks, the psalms most preachers skip entirely because they do not know what to do with them. The topical performer, if he touches them at all, uses them to make a point he arrived at elsewhere, perhaps a point about the reality of God's justice, and he lifts a verse or two as proof and moves on, leaving the actual psalm, with its raw and shocking rage, unpreached and unexplained. The expositor cannot do that. He has to deal with the psalm as it stands, has to ask what it is doing in the inspired prayer book of God's people, has to face the strangeness rather than skipping it. And in facing it he discovers things the topical man never reaches: that the psalm hands raw human rage over to God rather than acting on it, that it refuses to take vengeance into its own hands and instead lays even its ugliest impulses before the only Judge who can be trusted with them, that it is, underneath its shocking language, a profound act of restraint and faith, a refusal to be the avenger and a committing of vengeance to God. The expositor preaches a psalm the topical man could not preach at all, and his people come away with something they desperately need, a place to take their own rage that is neither suppression nor revenge but honest prayer. The hard text, submitted to, yields a treasure. The hard text, avoided, leaves the people with no idea what to do with the worst that is in them. That is the difference the submission makes, and it is largest precisely where the text is most difficult.

That last point deserves more weight than it usually gets. Every Sunday you are not only delivering content. You are demonstrating a method, and the people are learning the method whether you intend it or not. They watch you handle a text, and they unconsciously absorb how a text is to be handled. If they watch you lift verses out of context to support points you arrived at independently, then that is how they will read their Bibles at home, and that is how they will be deceived by the next charismatic teacher who does the same thing toward worse ends. But if they watch you submit, week after week, if they watch you say "I would have preferred this passage to mean something easier, but it does not, so here is what it means," then you are training a congregation that can defend itself, that can open a Bible and ask the right questions, that cannot be easily led astray because it has been taught, by example, to follow the text and not the teacher. You are not just feeding sheep. You are teaching them to feed themselves, which is the only kind of feeding that survives your absence.

Let me anticipate a fair objection, because the topical preacher has a real argument and I do not want to win by caricature. He says: people do not live their lives in the book of Leviticus. They live in marriages that are failing and finances that are collapsing and griefs that have no words, and they come to church carrying those things, and a pastor who just marches through whatever book he happens to be in, regardless of what his people are actually facing, is a pastor who has chosen a method over his people, who would rather be systematic than be useful. And there is truth in that. A man can hide behind verse-by-verse preaching the way another man hides behind topical preaching, using the method as an excuse not to know his people, not to address the actual wounds in the room, content to be faithful to his outline while the sheep bleed out in the pews. So I grant the objection its force. The expositor must know his people. He must preach into their actual lives. But the objection misses it: the choice is not between a method that ignores people and a method that serves them. The choice is between letting the text address the people's needs and letting the preacher's diagnosis of the people's needs edit the text. The faithful expositor does both things the objection wants. He knows his people deeply, studies their hearts and their crises, and then he trusts that the God who knew those crises before the preacher did has already spoken to them in the text, and his job is to make the connection visible, not to manufacture it. He does not abandon the text to chase the need. He shows the people that the text was aimed at their need all along, more precisely than the preacher's own diagnosis could have managed.

There is a deeper issue underneath the method, and it is a question about God. The topical performer, at the level of his working assumptions, believes that he knows what his people need and that his job is to deliver it persuasively. The expositor believes that God knows what the people need and has already said it, and that his job is to get out of the way of the saying. One trusts his own diagnosis. The other trusts the Physician. Calvin's confidence in preaching straight through the books of Scripture rested on this exact trust, that the Spirit who inspired the order of the canon would feed the people through it better than the preacher's own sense of the week's most pressing topic ever could. That is not anti-intellectualism. It is a particular intellectual humility, the humility that says my reading of my people's need is fallible, and the word is not.

The two trades wear the same robe. They stand in the same place, hold the same book, use the same vocabulary. But one of them has handed the leash to God, and the other is still holding it, and over a decade in one pulpit the truth comes out. A topical performer's congregation knows the preacher very well. An expositor's congregation knows the Bible. Ask which one a man is by asking what his people have learned to love. If they have learned to love him, examine the trade. If they have learned to love the word, you have your answer, and so does he.

I have served long enough now to watch this play out across whole ministries, my own and others', and the long view changes how the difference looks. In any single sermon you genuinely cannot tell the two trades apart. The topical performer and the expositor stand in the same place, hold the same book, reach conclusions that may even be identical. But run the tape for ten years and the difference becomes impossible to miss. The performer's people, after a decade, can tell you all about their pastor. They can quote his favorite phrases, recount his best illustrations, defend his positions, rally to his side. What they cannot do is open their Bibles and feed themselves, because they have never been taught how; they have only been handed conclusions, never shown the path to them. The expositor's people, after the same decade, may remember their pastor less vividly, but they can open the book and work it, can recognize when a teacher is twisting a text, can be left alone with the Scriptures and not be lost, because they have watched, week after week, how a text is heard and obeyed. The first pastor has produced dependents. The second has produced disciples. And the test of which one you are is not what your people think of you, which is always flattering and always misleading, but what your people can do when you are not there, which is the only measure that survives your departure or your death.

I would rather a congregation forget me entirely and carry the text out the door. The temptation runs the other way, every Sunday. I feel it still. The leash is always in reach.
chapters.verdict: The difference is not the subject. It is who holds the leash.
reflect: Did this week's text choose your subject, or did your subject choose its proof-texts?
Could a hearer reconstruct the passage from your sermon, or only your point?
What does your habitual sermon shape reveal about who you are actually serving?

chapters.title: The Discipline of Letting the Text Win
chapters.summary: Submitting to the text means letting it preach against the preacher's plans, preferences, and prepared conclusions. It is a discipline of surrender practiced in the study before it is seen in the pulpit.
chapters.body:
The first sign that a man is actually doing expository work is that the text starts to ruin his plans. Not occasionally. Routinely. He sits down on Monday with a sense of where the passage is going, where he would like it to go, and somewhere in the labor of study the passage turns and says something he did not want it to say, refuses to make the point he had hoped to make, insists on a meaning that cuts against the very application he had penciled in. And in that moment the whole question of his ministry is decided in private, where no one can see it. Does he let the text win, or does he overrule it?

Most of the corruption of the modern pulpit is not committed in public. It is committed on Tuesday, alone, when a man decides that the text's actual meaning is less useful than the meaning he prefers, and quietly substitutes. The congregation never sees the substitution. They only see a confident man with a Bible. But heaven saw it, and the man's own soul saw it, and over years the habit of overruling the text in the study becomes the inability to hear it at all.

Let me tell you about a Tuesday. I was preaching through the Sermon on the Mount, and I came to the passage on anger, where Jesus says that the man who is angry with his brother is in danger of the judgment, that the man who says "Thou fool" is in danger of hell fire, and that you should leave your gift at the altar and go be reconciled before you presume to worship (Matthew 5:21-24). I had a tidy sermon planned. I was going to talk about anger as a problem out there, in the culture, in the angry age we live in, and I had some good lines about it. And then, somewhere in the study, the text turned on me. Because there was a man in my own life, a man in ministry I had quarreled with, and I had not spoken to him in two years, and I had told myself a hundred reasons why that was acceptable, why he was the problem, why reconciliation was his job and not mine. And Jesus said leave the gift at the altar. He did not say wait for the other man to come to you. He said go. And I sat there at my desk and I knew that I could not preach this sermon, the real sermon, until I had made the phone call I had been avoiding for two years. The text had defeated me. It refused to be a sermon about other people's anger. It insisted on being a sermon about mine. I made the call before I wrote another word, and it was one of the hardest things I have done, and the sermon that came out of that obedience had a weight the clever version never would have had.

Letting the text win is a discipline, which means it is unnatural and must be practiced against the grain. The grain runs toward self. I open a passage and my mind, trained by years of wanting to be useful and admired, immediately begins scanning it for the sermon I can build. I am not reading. I am mining. And mining is not reading. The first labor of exposition is to stop the mining long enough to actually hear what the passage says on its own terms, in its own context, doing its own work in its own book, before I have any business asking what it means for Tuesday afternoon. Robinson's discipline of the big idea is precisely an instrument for this surrender. By forcing myself to state, in one sentence, what this passage is actually about, I am forbidding myself the luxury of preaching what I wish it were about.

I have a friend in the Pastors Connection Network who told me a version of this that I have never forgotten. He had planned a sermon series on grace, and he is a grace man through and through, and somewhere in the study he hit a passage in Hebrews about the impossibility of restoration for those who fall away, one of the hard warning passages that grace men do not enjoy. And he confessed to me that his first instinct was to explain it away, to reach for the interpretation that softened it, to make it mean something less frightening than it appeared to mean, not because the softer reading was clearly right but because the harder reading did not fit the series he had planned and the theology he preferred. He caught himself. He said it was one of the most uncomfortable weeks of his ministry, because he had to sit with a text that would not cooperate with his system, and he had to decide whether he served his system or the text. He preached the hard reading, carefully, honestly, without resolving the tension the text refused to resolve. And he told me his people were better for it, not because he had given them a cleaner answer but because he had modeled, in front of them, a man submitting to a word he did not control. That is letting the text win, and it is harder for the man with a good theology than for the man with a bad one, because the man with a good theology has more to defend, more of a system the troublesome text might dent, more reason to reach for the gloss that keeps everything tidy.

There is a passage I avoided for years. I will not pretend I avoided it by accident. It indicts a thing I do, names a sin I am comfortable with, and every time the preaching calendar drifted toward it I found a reason to take a different text. I told myself I was being strategic. I was being cowardly. The discipline of letting the text win includes the discipline of preaching the texts that win against you, the ones that leave you exposed in your own pulpit, the ones where the honest sermon ends with the preacher inside the indictment rather than above it. Dietrich Bonhoeffer understood this cost. He wrote about cheap grace from a country that was busy buying it, and the writing cost him everything precisely because he refused to soften the text to fit the moment. The text won. It won at the price of his life. Most of us are not asked to pay that. We are asked only to pay the small price of being wrong in front of our people, of saying out loud that the passage corrects the very thing we had been teaching, and most of us will not pay even that.

Calvin, preaching through Scripture in unbroken sequence, built the surrender into his method structurally. By committing to the next passage in the book, he removed from himself the weekly temptation to choose a text that suited his mood or his agenda. He could not skip the hard verse. It was simply next. Lloyd-Jones, too, in Preaching and Preachers, warned against the preacher who is always seeking a striking text, the man hunting for the verse that will let him say the clever thing, and commended instead the man who submits to the discipline of working through Scripture and lets the difficult and the dull and the dangerous passages have their turn. There is wisdom in a method that takes the choosing out of your hands, because the choosing is exactly where self-interest enters.

But the structure alone will not save you, because you can preach in sequence and still overrule the text quietly within each passage. The deeper discipline is interior, and it is this: a settled willingness to be corrected by the word you are preaching. The expositor must come to the text as a hearer before he is a herald. He must be willing to be preached at by the passage before he presumes to preach from it. If a man stands up to deliver a word that has not first done its work on him, he is delivering a corpse, and the people can smell it. They cannot always name what is wrong, but they know. A sermon that has cost the preacher nothing rarely costs the hearer anything either. The text that has not won against the preacher will not win against the pew.

I want to name the specific ways we overrule the text, because they are subtle and they hide. The first is the soft gloss, where the text says something hard and we summarize it in a way that takes the edge off, so that "you cannot serve God and money" becomes "we need to keep money in its proper place," which sounds the same and is not the same at all. The second is the quick pivot, where we read the hard demand and immediately rush to grace, not because the text rushes there but because we cannot bear to let the demand sit, and so we never let the law do its full work of exposing the sin before we apply the balm. The third is the safe target, where a passage that indicts everyone gets aimed only at people who are not in the room, the culture, the other party, the absent sinner, so that the congregation gets to feel righteous about a rebuke that was actually meant for them. Every one of these is a way of letting the preacher win instead of the text, and every one of them feels, in the moment, like good pastoral judgment. I have used all three. I use them less now, not because I am holier, but because I have learned to catch myself doing them, and the catching is most of the battle.

There is a question worth pressing here, because someone will object that this whole chapter assumes the preacher can know the text's real meaning with enough confidence to be defeated by it, and that interpretation is harder than that, that good men disagree, that the text does not always speak as plainly as I am pretending. And that is a fair point, and I do not want to flatten it. Texts are genuinely difficult sometimes, and humility about our interpretations is part of the discipline, not opposed to it. But notice that the difficulty does not let the preacher off the hook; it tightens the hook. Because the man who is genuinely uncertain what a text means has even less business preaching his preferred reading with confidence, even more obligation to do the hard work of weighing the options, even more reason to submit his own preference to the discipline of the evidence. The uncertainty is not a license to preach what you like; it is a summons to work harder before you preach anything. And in my experience, the appeal to difficulty is far more often an excuse than an honest confession. The texts that defeat me are usually not the genuinely obscure ones; they are the perfectly clear ones I wish were obscure, the ones whose meaning is plain and whose demand is unwelcome, and I reach for the language of interpretive humility not because the text is actually unclear but because pretending it is unclear lets me off a hook I do not want to be on. Real humility submits to the clear text and labors at the unclear one. False humility uses the existence of unclear texts as cover for disobeying the clear ones, and the two look similar from the outside but they are opposites, and the preacher knows in his own conscience which one he is practicing.

This is why the study is the real battlefield, not the pulpit. By the time a man stands up on Sunday, the war is over. It was fought on Wednesday, over a commentary and a cold cup of coffee, in the moment he saw clearly what the text meant and felt the pull to make it mean something easier. Stott described the preacher's study as a place of wrestling, where the meaning is fought for and the application is hammered out under the pressure of the text's actual demand. The wrestling is the work. The man who skips the wrestling and goes straight to the outline has not prepared a sermon. He has prepared a speech and attached a verse to it.

I have noticed something over the years about the relationship between this discipline and the preacher's own sanctification, and it is worth naming because it turns a burden into a gift. The texts that win against me, the ones that refuse my plans and indict my sins and force me to abandon the sermon I wanted, are the texts that are actually changing me. The sermons that cost me nothing, that merely confirmed what I already thought and applied comfortably to other people, those sermons left me exactly as they found me, a little more skilled perhaps, no holier. But the sermons born of defeat, the ones where I had to repent before I could preach, where the study became a personal reckoning before it became a public message, those sermons are the milestones of my own growth as a Christian. I can look back over a ministry and see that I grew most in the seasons when the texts were winning, when I was being preached at by the passages I was preparing, when the discipline of letting the text win was not only protecting my people from my preferences but sanctifying me through the very work of preparation. This is one of the hidden mercies of the expository calling, that a man who submits to the text week after week is being slowly conformed to it, sermon by sermon, defeat by defeat, so that the work of feeding the sheep doubles as the work of his own soul's making. The topical performer, who never lets the text win, never gets this. He grows in skill and influence and stays, spiritually, more or less where he started, because nothing he handles is ever allowed to handle him. The expositor who genuinely submits is being changed by his own labor, and the changing is worth more than all the skill, because at the end he will be not only a better preacher but a better man, which is the thing God was after all along.

Let me name the verdict that the discipline serves. The goal is not that the preacher should appear humble. Humility that is performed is just another self-display. The goal is that God should actually be heard, and God cannot be heard through a man who is busy editing him. Every time the preacher overrules the text, he inserts himself between God and the people, and the people go home having heard the preacher's preferences in the costume of God's word, which is worse than hearing nothing, because it inoculates them against the real thing. They think they have heard God. They have heard a man who would not let God win.

There is a deeper theological point under all of this that I want to make explicit, because it is the reason the discipline is not arbitrary self-denial but the only honest response to what Scripture claims to be. If the Bible is what it says it is, the breathed-out word of God, then it has an authority that stands over the preacher, not under him, and the preacher's relationship to it is the relationship of a servant to a master and not a craftsman to his material. A craftsman shapes his material toward his own ends. He bends the wood, cuts the stone, makes it serve his design. And a great deal of preaching treats the text exactly this way, as material the preacher shapes toward his design, and the language we use gives us away when we talk about "using" a text, "working" a passage, finding what we can "do" with a verse. But the text is not material. It is a voice. It is God speaking, and you do not shape the speech of God toward your own design; you submit to it, you obey it, you let it shape you. The discipline of letting the text win is simply the practical, weekly form of believing that the Bible is the word of God and not the raw material of the preacher's art. A man who really believes the first will practice the second. A man who will not practice the second has, whatever he professes, stopped believing the first, because his hands betray a conviction his mouth would deny.

I keep a private measure now, and I offer it to you. When I finish studying a passage, I ask whether it has changed anything I planned to say, or whether it has merely confirmed it. If it has only confirmed me, I am suspicious. Not certain I am wrong, but suspicious, because the living word is sharper than that, and a text that only ever agrees with the preacher is probably not being heard at all. It is being used. The texts that change my sermon are the texts I have actually read.

I want to leave the young preacher with a habit that has guarded me, because the discipline of letting the text win has to be embodied in actual practices or it remains a noble idea that changes nothing. Here is the practice: write down, early in the study, the sermon you want to preach, the thing you are hoping the text will say, the application you are already leaning toward. Write it down explicitly, name your bias, get it out of your head and onto the page where you can see it. And then study the text honestly, and at the end, compare. Did the text confirm what you wanted, or did it resist? If it confirmed you exactly, be suspicious, because the living word rarely confirms us exactly, and a text that perfectly matched your prior hope was probably not heard but used. If it resisted you, if it pushed back, if it sent you somewhere you had not planned to go, then you have evidence that you actually read it rather than projecting onto it. The written-down bias is a check on yourself, a way of catching the quiet substitution before it happens, because the substitution thrives in the dark, in the unexamined assumption that what you wanted the text to say is simply what it says. Drag the wanting into the light at the start, and you make it much harder to mistake your wanting for the word's meaning at the end. I do this still, after all these years, because the temptation to use the text never fully dies, and the only defense I have found is to name my bias before the study so I can recognize it if it tries to disguise itself as the text's conclusion.

A passage you have never let defeat you is a passage you have never preached. You have only borrowed it. And borrowed words, however eloquent, carry no authority, because authority belongs to the One whose word it is, and he does not lend it to men who will not first obey it themselves.

Let the text win. Lose to it on Tuesday, in private, so that on Sunday the people might win something that will outlast you.
chapters.verdict: A text you have never let defeat you is a text you have never actually preached.
reflect: When did a passage last force you to abandon the sermon you wanted to give?
What in Scripture are you quietly avoiding because it preaches against you?
Is your study a search for the text's meaning, or for your sermon's permission?

chapters.title: The Bench Where the Sermon Is Built
chapters.summary: Exposition is not only a conviction but a craft, with a sequence of unglamorous moves from the text's meaning to its structure to its single governing idea. The craft serves the conviction and never replaces it.
chapters.body:
There is a lazy man who hides behind this book's argument, and I had better deal with him before he hides behind this chapter. He says he just preaches the word, that he does not bother with structure or craft or any of that, that he opens the Bible and lets the Spirit lead. And what he means, usually, is that he has not prepared, that he is unwilling to do the slow work of building a sermon, and that he has dressed up his laziness in spiritual language so that no one can call it what it is. Let me say it clearly. Refusing to labor at the craft of preaching is not spirituality. It is contempt for the people, dressed as trust in God. The God who inspired Scripture inspired it in careful Hebrew and careful Greek, with structure and argument and deliberate shape, and a man who will not attend to that shape is not honoring the word's sufficiency. He is presuming on it.

So let me take you to the bench, the actual workbench where a sermon gets built, and walk through the moves, because conviction without craft produces sincere sermons that do not actually feed anyone. I have sat with too many young pastors in the Pastors Connection Network who believe the right things about Scripture and have never been taught how to turn a passage into a sermon, and they are frustrated, and their people are underfed, and the gap is not their theology but their toolbox.

The first move is to read the passage until it is no longer strange and then to keep reading until it is strange again. The first reading you understand too quickly. You think you know what it says because you have heard it preached or because the surface is familiar. The expositor reads past that false familiarity, reads it ten times, twenty, reads it aloud, reads it in more than one translation, until the easy assumptions fall away and the actual questions start to surface. Why does it say it this way and not that way. Why is this here, right after that. What does this word mean, and is it the same word used three verses up. The strangeness is good. The strangeness is the text refusing to be a cliche, and the questions the strangeness raises are the doorway into the real meaning.

The second move is context, and I mean it in widening circles. The immediate context, the paragraph around the passage. The book context, the argument or story the whole book is making, into which this passage fits. The canonical context, where this sits in the unfolding of Scripture, before the cross or after, under the old covenant or the new. And the historical context, what was actually happening, who wrote this, to whom, against what background.
