A verse is a word in a sentence in a paragraph in a book in a covenant in a Bible, and to preach it rightly you have to know where it lives. The man who preaches verses without their neighborhoods will eventually preach nonsense, confidently, and call it faithfulness.

The third move is to find the structure of the passage itself, because the author already organized his material and your job is to discover his organization, not to impose your own. A narrative has a shape, a rising tension and a turn and a resolution. An argument has a flow, a premise and a development and a conclusion, with connecting words, the therefores and the buts and the becauses that are the joints of the reasoning. Hebrew poetry has its parallels, the second line echoing or sharpening or reversing the first. If you can see the author's structure, you can preach with the grain of the text instead of against it, and a sermon preached with the grain has a coherence that the people feel even when they could not diagram it.

The fourth move, and Robinson is the great teacher here, is to compress the whole passage into a single sentence. He called it the big idea, the exegetical idea boiled down to one statement of what this passage is about, the subject and the complement, what the author is talking about and what he is saying about it. This is the hardest move and the most important, because it forces clarity and it forbids cheating. If you cannot say in one sentence what this passage is about, you do not yet understand it well enough to preach it, and you will instead preach three or four things loosely attached to the text, which is what most bad sermons are. The discipline of the one sentence is a discipline of submission, because the sentence has to be the text's sentence and not yours. I write it at the top of my notes, and everything in the sermon either serves that sentence or gets cut. Most of my worst sermons, looking back, were sermons where I never found the one sentence, or found it and would not obey it.

The fifth move is the turn from what it meant to what it means, and this is where many faithful men either get lazy or get reckless. The meaning of the text is fixed; it meant something to the original author and audience, and that meaning does not change. But the significance, the application to these people in this room, has to be freshly discerned every time, and it has to grow out of the meaning rather than being stapled to it. The bad preacher does one of two things here. Either he stops at the meaning and leaves the people with an accurate history lesson that never touches their lives, or he leaps to the application without grounding it in the meaning, so that the application floats free and could have been attached to any verse at all. The expositor does the harder thing. He holds the meaning and the people in the same gaze, and he asks how this fixed truth lands on these particular lives, the marriages and the fears and the besetting sins and the doubts that are actually in the room, and he lets the application come up out of the text like a plant out of its own soil.

Then there is the matter of arrangement, of how you actually lay the thing out so a human being can follow it. The text's structure should govern your structure, but you still have to make decisions about how to open, how to move, how to land. I have learned a few hard rules over the years. Open with the text or with the people, not with yourself. Make the points serve the one idea, not compete with it. Do not let an illustration be more memorable than the truth it illustrates, or the people will remember the story and forget the point, which means the illustration ate the sermon. And land the plane. Have an actual ending, a place the whole thing has been going, a final weight you set down in their hands, rather than circling the runway because you do not know how to stop.

Let me walk one passage through the whole bench, because a list of moves stays abstract until you watch it work on something specific. Take the well-worn opening of Philippians 4, where Paul says be careful for nothing, but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God, and the peace of God which passeth all understanding shall keep your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus (Philippians 4:6-7). The lazy sermon is obvious: do not worry, pray instead, and you will feel peace. Three steps to anxiety relief, and the text becomes a self-help formula with a Bible verse on top. But work the bench. Read it until it is strange again, and the strangeness surfaces immediately, because the command not to be anxious is given by a man in prison, possibly facing execution, who has just told us a few verses earlier to rejoice always. Context: the whole letter is written from chains, and the peace Paul promises is a peace he is himself demonstrating from inside a cell, which means it cannot be a peace that depends on circumstances improving. Structure: notice the military word "keep," which is a garrison word, a word for soldiers guarding a city, so that the peace of God is pictured not as a feeling that washes over you but as a garrison posted around your heart, standing guard against the assault of anxiety. The one idea is not "pray and you will feel better." The one idea is something like: the believer surrounded by reasons to fear can hand those fears to God in prayer and receive in their place a divine peace that stands guard over the heart like a garrison, a peace that does not make sense by any earthly arithmetic. And the turn to application is not a formula but a confrontation: do you actually believe there is a peace available to you that does not depend on your circumstances changing, and if so, why are you trying to manufacture peace by managing your circumstances instead of receiving it by prayer? And where does it land? Not in technique but in Christ, because the peace is "through Christ Jesus," the peace of a God who himself entered the worst circumstances and was not destroyed by them. Same verses. A completely different sermon, and the difference is the bench.

There is a danger here I have to guard, and I will say it against myself. The craft can become its own idol. A man can get so good at building sermons that the building becomes the point, that he starts to admire his own architecture, that he chooses the cleverer structure over the truer one because it is more satisfying to construct. The craft is a servant. The moment it stops serving the text and starts serving the preacher's pleasure in his own skill, it has become the very self-display we are fighting throughout this book, only more dangerous because it is harder to detect. Augustine had taught rhetoric for a living, and when he came to write about Christian eloquence in On Christian Doctrine he insisted that the skill must vanish into the service of the truth, that the best eloquence is the eloquence you do not notice because you are too busy seeing the thing it shows you. That is the standard. Build well enough that the building disappears.

I want to address delivery directly, because it is part of the craft and most expository men neglect it, treating it as beneath them, as though caring how you say a thing were a concession to the performers we have spent this book warning against. It is not. The same care that drives you to handle the text accurately should drive you to deliver it clearly, because a true word mumbled, droned, or buried in a monotone is a true word the people cannot receive, and the failure to deliver well is, like the failure to study well, a failure of love disguised as a virtue. There is a false piety that thinks a dull delivery is more spiritual than a lively one, that the preacher who bores his people is somehow more faithful than the one who holds them, and it is nonsense, a confusion of reverence with dreariness. The text you are preaching is the most interesting thing in the universe, the living word of the living God, and to deliver it in a way that makes it sound tedious is not reverence; it is a kind of slander against the word, an implicit claim that the most thrilling truth there is happens to be boring. Care how you preach. Learn to vary your pace, to pause where a pause lands, to lift your eyes from the page and speak to actual faces, to let your voice carry the weight of what you are saying rather than flattening everything into the same managerial drone. None of this is performance in the bad sense, because the aim is not to display yourself but to deliver the word so that it can be received, and a clear, living, well-delivered sermon serves the text exactly as careful exegesis does, by removing the obstacles between the people and the meaning. The performer cares about delivery so the people will admire him. The faithful preacher cares about delivery so the people will receive the word. Same skill. Opposite aim. Refuse the performer's aim, but do not, in your refusal, embrace the dullness that mistakes itself for depth.

So why labor at the craft at all, if the goal is for the craft to vanish? Because clarity is love and confusion is contempt. When I do the labor, when I have found the one idea and traced the structure and built the thing so it can be followed, I am loving my people with my preparation, spending hours so that they can receive in forty minutes what cost me twenty hours to see clearly. When I skip the work and stand up to wing it, I am asking them to do the labor I refused to do, to sort out for themselves a mess I could have ordered, and that is not trust in the Spirit, it is theft of their time and starvation of their souls. Stott labored. Lloyd-Jones labored. Calvin labored. Spurgeon, who could seem to preach effortlessly, was in fact a man of enormous study, and the apparent effortlessness was the fruit of hidden labor, the way a great athlete makes the impossible look easy because of the thousand unseen hours behind it.

There is the matter of how much to write down, and pastors fight about it, and I have landed somewhere in the middle after trying both ends. Some men preach from a full manuscript, every word written, and some preach from a few notes or nothing at all, and each side is sure the other is doing it wrong. The full-manuscript man fears the looseness of the notes-only man, the rambling, the imprecision, the temptation to fill time with whatever comes to mind. The notes-only man fears the deadness of the manuscript man, the reading, the loss of eye contact and life, the sermon that sounds like an essay being recited because that is exactly what it is. And both fears are justified, because both methods have a characteristic failure. The manuscript can kill the life; the notes can lose the rigor. What I have learned is that the method matters less than the mastery. Whatever you write down, you must own the material so thoroughly that you are not bound to your paper, so that whether you have a full manuscript or a single card, the sermon lives in you and not on the page, and you could preach it if the paper blew away. The danger of the manuscript is not the writing; it is preaching the writing rather than the truth the writing captured. The danger of the notes is not the brevity; it is mistaking unpreparedness for spontaneity. Write down whatever helps you master the material, and then master it so completely that you can look your people in the eye and speak the truth to them as a man who knows it, not as a man reading it. The goal is a prepared freedom, the freedom that only thorough preparation can produce, the freedom of a musician who has practiced so hard that he can finally forget the notes and play.

There is one more move on the bench that the lists usually omit, and it is the discipline of cutting. A sermon is made as much by what you leave out as by what you put in, and the young preacher's besetting error is to include everything he found in the study, every insight, every connection, every interesting thing the text yielded, until the sermon is a bag of good material with no single thrust, a tour of the preacher's research rather than a delivery of the text's one idea. The hard discipline, harder than gathering, is throwing away, deciding that this genuinely good insight does not serve this sermon's one idea and must therefore be cut, however much it cost you to find and however reluctant you are to lose it. I have killed many good paragraphs over the years, paragraphs I loved, because they did not serve the sermon they were in, and the killing always felt like waste and was almost always right, because a sermon that tries to say six true things says none of them with force, while a sermon that says one true thing and ruthlessly cuts everything that does not serve it lands with a weight the cluttered sermon never achieves. Learn to cut. Find the one idea, and then have the discipline to throw away everything, however good, that does not serve it, trusting that the material you cut is not wasted but saved, banked for a future sermon where it will be the center rather than the clutter. The well-built sermon is not the one that contains the most. It is the one that contains only what serves, every part pulling in the same direction, nothing included merely because it was interesting or because it cost you to find.

I want to give the young pastor one practical word, because I wish someone had given it to me. Start the sermon early in the week, not because the Spirit needs more time, but because you do. A sermon needs to sit. It needs days of marinating, of returning to it, of catching in the shower or the car the connection you missed at the desk. The Saturday-night sermon, thrown together in a panic because the week got away from you, is almost always a thinner thing than it needed to be, not because God could not redeem it, but because you did not give the text room to do its slow work on you and through you. I have preached too many Saturday-night sermons. I can usually tell which ones they were, even years later, by the way they sit flat in my memory, all surface and no depth, because they never had the time to grow roots.

I want to say something about illustrations, because they are the place where craft most often goes wrong in otherwise faithful preaching, and young pastors get almost no honest counsel about them. An illustration exists to do one thing: to make a truth visible, to take an abstraction the people cannot picture and give it a window they can see through. That is its whole job. And the test of an illustration is brutally simple: after the sermon, do the people remember the truth, or do they remember the story? If they remember the story and have lost the truth, the illustration failed, no matter how good the story was; in fact the better the story, the more completely it failed, because it ate the very thing it was supposed to serve. I have preached illustrations that were too good, stories so vivid and moving that the room was carried away by them, and afterward people came up talking about the story and could not have told you the point it illustrated. That is craft serving itself. The illustration became a small performance inside the sermon, a moment of the preacher's storytelling skill displayed for its own sake, and it drew the eye to the window instead of through it. The discipline is to choose illustrations that are good enough to illuminate and not so good that they upstage, and to be willing, when you have a story that is simply too dazzling for the truth it serves, to cut it, however much it pains you, because a sermon is not a showcase for your best material. It is a meal, and a garnish that overwhelms the food is a failure of the kitchen, no matter how beautiful it looks on the plate.

Faithfulness is not the enemy of skill. The man who says he is too spiritual to bother with craft is usually just unwilling to work, and the man who is too in love with his craft has made an idol of his tools. Between those two ditches runs the narrow road of the laboring expositor, who works hard at the bench so that the work can disappear, who builds carefully so that what the people see is not the building but the God the building was built to reveal. Pick up the tools. Learn to use them well. And then learn to make them invisible.
chapters.verdict: Faithfulness is not the enemy of skill; sloppiness is the enemy of both.
reflect: Can you state the one idea of this week's text in a single sentence?
Does your sermon's structure follow the text's structure, or fight it?
Are you laboring at the craft, or hiding your laziness behind a claim to be "just preaching the word"?

chapters.title: The Idol Called Relevance
chapters.summary: The pursuit of relevance, pressed too far, hollows out the pulpit by making the preacher's perceived usefulness the measure of the word. The text is most relevant precisely when it refuses to flatter the moment.
chapters.body:
The most dangerous word in the working vocabulary of the modern pastor is relevance, and it is dangerous precisely because it sounds like love. Of course I want the word to connect. Of course I want it to reach the skeptic in the back row, the exhausted father, the woman whose faith is hanging by a thread. I came to Christ out of atheism, and I remember sitting in a service where the preacher was so determined to be relevant to someone like me that he never actually said anything I could not have read in a self-help paperback. He was reaching for me. He missed, because he had emptied his hands of the only thing I had come, without knowing it, to hear.

Let me tell you more about that, because it is the whole reason I care about this. When I was an atheist, I did not need a church that looked like the world I already lived in. I had the world. The world was offering me everything the relevance-driven church was offering me, only the world did it better, with bigger budgets and fewer guilt feelings. If the church was just going to hand me a slightly more wholesome version of the self-improvement I could get from any paperback in the airport, then the church had nothing I needed, and on some level I knew it, and I despised it a little for pretending otherwise. What eventually got through to me was not a church trying to be relevant. It was a man who believed something I did not believe and described it with such seriousness and such conviction that I could not dismiss it as marketing. He was not chasing me. He was standing somewhere, and the somewhere looked solid, and the solidity was the thing that finally made me wonder whether I was the one standing on air.

Relevance becomes an idol the moment it becomes the measure. As long as relevance is a servant of the text, helping the preacher carry an ancient meaning across the distance to a present hearer, it is honorable work, the bridge-building Stott described. But the idol inverts the relationship. The idol makes the present moment the judge of the word, so that whatever in Scripture seems immediately useful is amplified and whatever seems strange, slow, or offensive is quietly set aside. The preacher begins to edit the canon by the standard of the contemporary, and the standard of the contemporary is, by definition, the thing that does not need the church to survive. We end up preaching the parts of the Bible the world already half-agrees with and burying the parts that would actually disrupt it. We call this meeting people where they are. It is closer to abandoning them there.

Brueggemann, in Finally Comes the Poet, made an argument that cuts directly against the relevance idol. He said the dominant consciousness, the settled prose of the culture, is precisely what the prophetic word must interrupt, and that the preacher who only confirms the assumptions his hearers already hold has betrayed the office. The poet, the prophet, the preacher speaks a word from outside the closed system. The relevance idol locks the preacher inside the system and lets the system set the terms. It tells him to speak only in the categories his hearers already accept, about only the problems they already feel, toward only the solutions they already want. But the gospel was never relevant in that sense. The cross was a scandal to the Jew and folly to the Greek (1 Corinthians 1:23), relevant to neither, and Paul refused to file off its edges to make it palatable. He did not preach a Christ adjusted for the audience. He preached Christ crucified, and let the offense stand.

There is a paradox at the center of this that took me years to understand and that I now think is the key to the whole question. The preacher who aims directly at relevance usually misses it, and the preacher who aims at faithfulness usually hits relevance as a byproduct he was not even seeking. It works like happiness, which famously evaporates when pursued directly and arrives when you pursue something worthier. Aim at relevance and you produce a thin, dated, anxious preaching that chases a moving target and is always a step behind the culture it is trying to match, relevant to last year by the time it is delivered. Aim at faithfulness, at the deep true unchanging word pressed into the actual weight of actual lives, and you produce a preaching that turns out to be startlingly relevant, because it addresses the permanent human condition that underlies all the shifting surfaces, the condition the culture's relevant offerings never reach. The most relevant sermons I have ever preached were sermons where I was not thinking about relevance at all, where I was simply trying to be faithful to a deep text and to the actual people in front of me, and the relevance came as a gift I had not chased. And the least relevant sermons, the ones that landed nowhere, were often the ones where I had tried hardest to be relevant, had strained after the contemporary hook and the timely application, and produced something that felt, even to me, like a man working too hard to seem current. Stop chasing relevance. Chase faithfulness, chase the deep word and the actual people, and let relevance arrive as the byproduct it was always meant to be, the natural overflow of a true word meeting a real need, rather than the manufactured product of a man straining to matter.

Here is what the relevance idol cannot see: the word is most relevant precisely when it refuses to flatter the moment. The skeptic in the back row does not need a preacher who agrees with him. He needs a word large enough to be worth disbelieving, a claim with enough weight to be worth the argument. When I was an atheist, the Christians who made me think were not the ones who tried to meet me on my own ground. They were the ones who stood on different ground entirely and described it so clearly that I could see it was solid. Their refusal to chase me was the most respectful thing they did. It told me they believed there was somewhere to stand that was not where I was standing. The chasing preacher tells the skeptic, in effect, that there is nowhere to go, only the same anxious ground rearranged. No one crosses an ocean to reach a country identical to the one they left.

There is a confusion at the root of the relevance idol that I want to expose, because the confusion is what gives the idol its power. We have confused relevance with relativity to the present, when in fact the most relevant thing is usually the most permanent thing. A man whose marriage is dying does not need preaching tuned to this year's anxieties. He needs the oldest truth there is, that he is a sinner married to a sinner and that the covenant he is breaking was made in the image of a God who keeps his covenants at infinite cost. A woman terrified of death does not need a sermon about contemporary wellness. She needs the resurrection, which is not relevant in the sense of being current but is relevant in the sense of being the only thing that actually addresses the thing she is afraid of. The deepest human needs do not change with the decade. They are the same needs the psalmist had, the same needs Augustine had, the same needs I had on my knees the night I stopped being an atheist. A pulpit that chases the surface of the present misses the depth of the present, which is exactly where the ancient word was always aimed.

There is a sleight of hand at the heart of the relevance idol that I want to expose, because once you see it you cannot unsee it. The idol always presents itself as being about the hearer, about meeting their needs, reaching them where they are, serving their interests, and this framing is what makes it so hard to resist, because who could argue against caring for the hearer? But watch closely and you discover that the relevance idol is almost never actually about the hearer. It is about the preacher. The preacher who chases relevance is, far more often than he admits, chasing his own need to be effective, to be liked, to see a response, to feel that his preaching is working. The talk of meeting the hearer's needs is frequently a cover for meeting the preacher's need to feel successful, and you can tell because the relevance idol tends to amplify whatever produces a response in the room and suppress whatever does not, which is to say it is tuned to the preacher's emotional reward and not to the hearer's actual good. The hearer's actual good often requires the slow, the difficult, the unrewarding word that produces no immediate response, and the relevance idol will never preach that word, because that word does not feed the preacher's hunger to feel effective. So the next time you feel the pull to be relevant, ask the uncomfortable question: whose need am I actually serving here, the hearer's, or my own need to see that I am reaching the hearer? The two feel identical from the inside, and they are not the same, and the difference is the difference between a shepherd and a man using the sheep to feel like a shepherd.

The idol exacts a price, and the price is the slow emptying of the pulpit. It happens by degrees. First the hard doctrines go, judgment and wrath and hell and the exclusivity of Christ, because they do not test well. Then the slow texts go, the genealogies and the laws and the long arguments of Romans, because they do not hold attention. Then the strange texts go, the apocalyptic and the imprecatory and the parts that resist a clean application. What remains is a thin band of Scripture, the encouraging and the practical and the inoffensive, preached over and over, and the congregation slowly forgets that the rest of the book exists. They are not being fed the whole counsel of God. They are being fed the relevant fraction, and the relevant fraction cannot sustain a soul through a real catastrophe, because real catastrophes are the moments the relevant fraction never prepared anyone to face.

I have watched this happen in churches I love, and I have felt the pull in my own ministry, the steady gravitational drag toward the useful and away from the true when the two seem to diverge. They do not actually diverge, but they appear to, and the appearance is enough to bend a man over time. The relevance idol whispers that this text, this Sunday, will not land, that the people are tired, that they need something they can use. And the whisper is half true, which is what makes it dangerous. The people are tired. They do need help. But the help they need is not a smaller word. It is the real one, preached into the actual weight of their actual lives, which is a different thing entirely from a word shrunk to fit the size of their attention.

I have watched a particular pattern in churches that chased relevance hard, and the pattern is instructive because it ends in the opposite of what it sought. A church decides it will reach the culture by becoming like the culture, by stripping away everything strange and demanding and old, by making the service feel like a concert and the sermon feel like a talk and the whole experience feel like something a person could get on a Friday night without the inconvenience of God. And for a while it works, by the numbers, because people will come to a good show. But here is what happens over time, and I have seen it more than once. The people who came for the show eventually find a better show, because there is always a better show, and the church cannot win a competition it entered on the world's terms against opponents with bigger budgets. And the people who stayed, who were looking for God, slowly grow malnourished, because a church built to entertain cannot feed, and they drift away hungry, often without being able to say why. What is left is a building optimized for an audience that has moved on, run by people exhausted from chasing a relevance that kept receding. The church that tried hardest to be relevant made itself, in the end, irrelevant, because it had nothing the world could not get elsewhere, and the one thing it had that the world could not supply, the strange ancient word, it had thrown away as a liability. Meanwhile the plain church down the road that just kept opening the book and preaching it, unfashionable, unimpressive, is somehow still there, still feeding people, still drawing the hungry, because it offered the one thing that does not go out of style, which is the truth.

Lloyd-Jones argued that the cure for a powerless church was never a new technique but a recovery of the truth preached with the unction of the Spirit. He was deeply suspicious of every effort to make preaching more effective by making it less theological, because he saw, rightly, that the power was never in the relevance. The power was in the word, applied by the Spirit, and the relevance idol substitutes a human effort for a divine action. It is, at bottom, a failure of faith. It does not believe the word is living and active. It believes the word needs the preacher's cleverness to come alive, and so it pours its energy into the performance and starves the word.

I keep coming back to my own conversion when I think about this, because it is the data I trust most, the thing I cannot argue myself out of. I was an atheist, an intelligent and committed one, and I had heard the relevant, accommodating, culturally fluent version of Christianity, and it did precisely nothing to me, because it offered me a slightly sanctified version of what I already had and asked me to be impressed. What finally cracked me open was the opposite. It was the parts of the Christian claim that were most offensive to me, most resistant to my categories, most impossible to reconcile with the comfortable secular frame I lived inside. The claim that I was a sinner under judgment, which my whole culture told me was a relic of repressive religion, turned out to describe my actual interior life more accurately than anything my culture offered. The claim that a man had risen bodily from the dead, which I had always dismissed as obvious myth, turned out, when I actually examined it, to be a claim with more behind it than I had ever bothered to find out. The hard, strange, offensive parts were the parts that did the work, because they were the parts that were actually different from what I already believed, the parts that gave me somewhere new to stand. A relevant Christianity had nothing to offer a man who already had the culture's relevance. An ancient, strange, demanding Christianity had everything to offer, because it had what the culture did not, which was the truth. I am a pastor today because someone preached the offensive thing to me and did not flinch, and if he had been trying to be relevant I would have remained an atheist, comfortably, with his blessing.

The verdict is hard, so I will say it plainly and stand under it myself. A pulpit that chases the present forfeits the only thing the present cannot supply. The world is already drowning in relevance. Every screen, every feed, every advertisement is relevant, tuned with terrifying precision to the desires of the moment. If the church offers only more of the same, more relevance, better-targeted, it has nothing. The one thing the church has that the world cannot manufacture is a word from outside the moment, eternal, unbought, indifferent to the algorithms, spoken by a God who was here before the present and will be here after it. That word is the church's only treasure. The relevance idol asks the church to bury its treasure and dig up the world's, and then wonders why the world is not impressed.

I want to draw a careful line here, because the chapter could be misread as a license for laziness, as though the cure for the relevance idol were to stop caring whether anyone understands you. That is not it at all. There is a difference between making the word relevant and making the word clear, and the difference is everything. Making the word relevant, in the idol's sense, means adjusting its content to fit the appetites of the hearer, softening what offends, amplifying what flatters, editing the message to suit the market. Making the word clear means laboring so that the unchanged message can actually be understood, removing every needless obstacle that stands between the hearer and the meaning, refusing to hide behind jargon or assume knowledge the people do not have or leave hard things murky because clarity is work. The first is a betrayal. The second is love. The relevance idol confuses them on purpose, so that any call to clarity gets smuggled into a call to compromise, and any refusal to compromise gets defended as a refusal to be understood. But the faithful preacher does the hard double thing: he refuses to change the message and he labors like a dog to make the unchanged message clear, plain, vivid, understandable, landing in the actual lives of actual people, because he loves them too much to bore them and too much to lie to them, and those are not the same temptation and they do not have the same cure.

I am not against connection. I labor for it. But I have learned to suspect myself most at the exact moment I am most determined to be relevant, because that is the moment I am most tempted to make myself the bridge's destination rather than its span. The destination was never me. It was never the moment. It was the word, and the God who speaks it, and the present has no power to judge what does not belong to it.

I want to close this chapter by naming the deepest fear that drives the relevance idol, because naming it is the only way to disarm it. The fear is that the word, left to itself, is not enough, that if I simply preach it faithfully without my cleverness propping it up, nothing will happen, the room will be bored, the skeptic will leave, the church will shrink, and it will all be my fault for failing to make it interesting. That fear is the engine of the whole idol, and it is, at bottom, unbelief, a failure to believe what Scripture says about itself, that the word is living and powerful, that it does not return void, that it accomplishes what God sends it to do (Isaiah 55:11). If I really believed that, I would not feel the desperate need to rescue the word with my relevance, because I would trust that the word can do its own work, that its power does not depend on my packaging, that the God who sends it has staked his own reputation on its sufficiency. The relevance idol is what a preacher reaches for when he has stopped believing the word is enough, and the cure is not a better technique for being relevant but a recovered faith in the word's own power, a settled conviction that the faithful preaching of the unadorned word, trusted and prayed over and delivered with love, will accomplish more than all the cleverness in the world, because the power was never in the cleverness and never in the relevance and never in the preacher, but in the word itself and the God who breathes through it. Believe that, really believe it, and the relevance idol loses its grip, because you no longer need it, because you have remembered that you were handed something that does not need your help to be powerful, only your faithfulness to be delivered.

Preach what does not need the present's permission. It is the only thing the present cannot give them, and the only thing they cannot live without.
chapters.verdict: A pulpit that chases the present forfeits the only thing the present cannot supply.
reflect: Are you making the word relevant, or trusting that it already is?
What have you stopped preaching because it no longer seemed to "connect"?
Whose approval are you actually seeking when you reach for relevance?

chapters.title: The Cost of the Study
chapters.summary: Faithful exposition demands hours of unglamorous labor in the original meaning, the context, and the structure of the text, work no congregation ever sees but every congregation feels the absence of.
chapters.body:
Every faithful sermon is sitting on top of hours that no one will ever see, and the temptation of ministry is to skip them, because they are invisible and unrewarded and the sermon will happen with or without them. This is the secret arithmetic of the pulpit. A man can stand up unprepared and still fill the time, still hold the room, still receive the handshakes at the door. The cost of the skipped study is not paid on Sunday. It is paid slowly, over years, by a congregation that is being fed thinner and thinner gruel by a preacher who has learned he can get away with it.

The study is unglamorous in a way that nothing else in ministry is. Counseling has its visible fruit. Leadership has its visible influence. Even prayer, done in public, has its witnesses. But the hours a preacher spends alone with a text, tracing an argument through a chapter of Romans, comparing the way a word is used across a Gospel, sitting with a commentary until the structure of a passage finally clicks into place, those hours have no audience and no immediate reward. They are the least visible labor in the pastor's week and the most important, and that combination is exactly why they are the first thing sacrificed when the week gets crowded. Something must give, the man tells himself, and the meeting cannot be moved and the visit cannot be canceled, so the study contracts. He will rely on what he already knows. He will lean on his gifts. He has gotten away with it before.

Let me describe the early morning, because that is where I have had to fight this battle in my own life. Six in the morning, the house still dark, five sons asleep, the coffee not yet doing its work, and the open Bible in front of me and a passage I do not yet understand. There is nothing glamorous about that hour. No one is watching. The phone is already lighting up with the day's emergencies. And the temptation, every single morning, is to do the urgent thing instead of the important thing, to answer the email, to return the call, to handle the small fire so that I feel useful, and to tell myself I will get to the text later, knowing that later will be crowded too. The study does not defend itself. It has to be defended, every day, against a hundred legitimate-looking intruders, and the man who does not fight for it will lose it, not in a dramatic collapse but in a slow erosion that he can always justify and never quite notice until the well has run dry.

I have done this, and I want to describe the particular dishonesty of it, because naming the mechanism is the only defense against it. When I shortchange the study, I do not experience myself as lazy. I experience myself as busy, as faithful, as a man so devoted to his people that he is pouring himself out for them in a dozen visible ways. The neglect of the text hides inside the appearance of devotion. I am working hard. I am simply working hard at everything except the one thing the office most requires. And the congregation, on the receiving end, gets a man who is present everywhere except in the word, which is the one place they cannot follow him and so cannot supply for themselves.

The work itself is specific, and it is worth naming, because vagueness about the labor is how the labor gets avoided. The expositor must establish what the text actually says, which means attending to the original where he is able, or to faithful translations and tools where he is not, never preaching a meaning that rests on a translation quirk the original would not support. He must establish the context, the paragraph and the chapter and the book, because a verse torn from its setting can be made to say nearly anything, and the man who preaches verses without contexts is the man who eventually preaches anything he likes. He must trace the structure, the flow of the argument, the way the passage moves from its beginning to its end, because the structure is the author's own emphasis, and to preach against the structure is to preach against the meaning. This is the work Robinson systematized and Stott described and Calvin simply did, week after week, year after year, until the people of Geneva knew their Bibles better than the priests who had kept the book from them for centuries.

I want to say a word here about commentaries and tools, because young preachers often get this wrong in one of two directions. Some refuse to use them, out of a misplaced piety that thinks consulting a scholar is somehow cheating on the Holy Spirit, as though the Spirit who gifted teachers to the church did not intend for those teachers to help the rest of us. That is pride wearing the mask of humility. Use the help. Stand on the shoulders of men who have given their lives to a single book of the Bible. The other error is the opposite, the man who reads the commentaries first and lets them do his seeing for him, so that he never actually wrestles with the text himself but only assembles a sermon out of borrowed insights. The right order is to work the text first, hard, on your own, until you have your own questions and your own tentative answers, and then to bring in the commentaries to correct you, to fill the gaps, to catch what you missed. The scholars are checks on your reading, not substitutes for it. A man who has not first labored alone with the text cannot use a commentary rightly, because he does not yet know what he is looking for.

There is a particular danger in the era of easy answers that I have to name, because it is hollowing out a generation of preachers without their knowing it. A man can now assemble a sermon, in a couple of hours, that sounds learned, that quotes the right scholars, that handles the original languages it never actually studied, because the tools to fake all of that are sitting in his pocket. He can produce, with very little labor, something that has the surface of careful study and none of the substance, and no one in the congregation will be able to tell the difference on any given Sunday. This is a genuinely new temptation, and it is more dangerous than old-fashioned laziness because it does not feel like laziness. The man feels productive. He has a polished sermon and he hardly worked for it. But he has not been changed by the study, because there was no study, only assembly, and the word did not have its way with him because he never sat with it long enough to be found by it. He is, increasingly, a curator of insights he did not earn and was not formed by, and the hollowness will tell over time, in the thinness of the man and the thinness of his people, because you cannot deposit into others a depth you do not possess, however convincingly you can sound deep for forty minutes. The labor was never only for the sermon's sake. It was for the preacher's sake, the slow formation that happens to a man who spends real hours with a real text, and there is no tool that can do that formation for you, because the formation is the friction, and friction is exactly what the tools exist to remove.

There is a theological reason the work cannot be skipped, and it is not merely that good study makes good sermons. It is that the word is God's, and to handle God's word carelessly is to handle God carelessly. Paul charged Timothy to study to show himself approved, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth (2 Timothy 2:15). Rightly dividing. The image is of careful, accurate cutting, the work of a craftsman who respects his material. A man who will not labor at rightly dividing is not merely a poor craftsman. He is a man who does not sufficiently fear the One whose word he is cutting. The carelessness is, underneath, a kind of contempt, however unintended, and the people absorb the contempt even when they cannot name it. They learn from a careless preacher that the Bible is not worth careful handling, and that lesson, taught week after week, is catastrophic.

Augustine, who had been a professional rhetorician before his conversion, understood that the skill of speaking was nothing without the labor of understanding. In On Christian Doctrine he insisted that the would-be teacher must first become a diligent student of the Scriptures, must steep himself in them, must do the slow work of learning before he presumes to teach, and that the man who tries to teach what he has not first labored to understand will only spread his own confusion. The eloquence Augustine prized was the overflow of understanding, not a substitute for it. A man can learn to sound understanding without being it, and the relevance idol of the previous chapter is happy to teach him how, but the sounding without the substance is a fraud, and frauds are eventually found out, usually at the worst possible moment, when a real crisis comes and the congregation reaches for a depth the preacher never built.

I want to describe what good study actually feels like from the inside, because young pastors imagine it as a grim, joyless slog and that misunderstanding is part of why they avoid it. The slog is real, the hours of tracing an argument that will not yield, the mornings that produce nothing. But there is also a particular joy in the study that nothing else in ministry quite matches, and it is the joy of seeing, the moment when a passage that was closed suddenly opens, when the connection you have been hunting for clicks into place and you see what the author was doing all along, and it is so right and so beautiful that you want to laugh or weep or call someone. I have had mornings in the study when the text broke open and I sat there in something close to worship, undone by the sheer craftsmanship of God in a paragraph of Paul, by the way every word turned out to be load-bearing, by a depth I had walked past a hundred times and never seen. Those mornings are the reward, and they only come to the man who has paid the price of the slog, because the seeing is on the far side of the laboring and there is no shortcut to it. The man who skips the study does not only shortchange his people; he robs himself of the deepest pleasure the office offers, the pleasure of seeing the glory of God in the text he was too lazy to mine. I would not trade those mornings for anything. They are why, even after all these years, I still get up in the dark to do this, not only out of duty, though duty would be enough, but because somewhere in the slog there is buried treasure, and I have found enough of it to keep digging.

Here is the cost stated as plainly as I can state it. There is no shortcut to the study that the people will not eventually pay for. The preacher who skips the hours banks them, in a sense, as a debt, and the debt comes due in the spiritual thinness of his people, in their inability to read their own Bibles, in their helplessness when suffering arrives and the easy applications run out. He has been feeding them a diet that cannot sustain a soul through a long night, and the long night always comes. When it comes, they will reach back into everything he taught them, and they will find, or fail to find, the substance he either built or neglected to build in the unseen hours of a hundred ordinary weeks.

I want to confront the specific lie that the neglect of study tells, because it is a clever lie and it fooled me for years. The lie says that the study is in competition with the people, that every hour at the desk is an hour stolen from the sheep, that a pastor who shuts his door to study is choosing books over people, and that the truly devoted pastor is the one who is always available, always present, always with his flock. And there is just enough truth in it to make it stick, because availability is part of the work and a pastor who is never present is failing too. But the lie inverts the actual relationship between the study and the people. The study is not in competition with the people; the study is for the people, the deepest service a preacher renders them, the labor that determines whether the time he does spend with them on Sunday feeds them or starves them. A pastor who is endlessly available all week but unprepared on Sunday has not chosen the people over the study; he has chosen the easy, visible, gratifying part of loving them over the hard, invisible, unrewarding part, and he has called his preference devotion. The most loving thing I do for my people in a given week often happens behind a closed door where none of them can see it, and the discipline of shutting that door, of declining the pleasant interruption, of telling a well-meaning member that I cannot meet this morning because I am in the word, is not a failure of pastoral love but its costliest expression. It took me years to believe this, because the lie is so plausible and the guilt of the closed door is so real. But the people I serve are better fed because I learned to feel that guilt and shut the door anyway, trusting that the invisible labor was the truer love.

I have set my week around the study now, after years of setting it around everything else and squeezing the study into the gaps. The change was a confession. It admitted that I had been treating the most important work as the most expendable, and that the order of my calendar had been quietly preaching a sermon of its own, a sermon about what I actually valued, week after week, more honest than anything I said from the pulpit. A man's calendar does not lie. It shows what he believes the word is worth. I guard the mornings now the way I would guard a meeting with the most important person in town, because in a sense that is exactly what they are. I have told my people that I will not normally be available before midday, and the remarkable thing is that they have respected it, even been glad of it, because they would rather have a pastor who is in the word than a pastor who is always answering the phone and never has anything to say when he finally does.

I want to speak directly to the bivocational pastor here, the man holding down a job and a pulpit at once, because the counsel to set the week around the study can sound cruel to a man who does not have the week to set. Many of my brothers in the Pastors Connection Network are exactly this man. They drive a truck or run a business or teach school all week and then preach on Sunday, and they cannot block out the mornings because the mornings belong to an employer, and a chapter telling them to spend twenty hours in the study lands like a rebuke they have no power to obey. So let me be honest and practical. The principle is not a particular number of hours; the principle is that the study gets the best of what you have, not the leftovers. The bivocational man cannot give the most hours, but he can give the best hours, the freshest part of his limited time, the first energy of his day off rather than the last exhausted scraps of Saturday night. He can carry the text with him through the week, thinking on it on the drive, turning it over on the job, so that the hours at the desk are not starting cold but harvesting what has been quietly growing. He can refuse, above all, to let the smallness of his time become an excuse for carelessness, because a man with four good hours who uses them faithfully will feed his people better than a man with twenty who squanders them. God has never measured the study by the clock. He measures it by the fear of the One whose word is being handled, and that fear is available to the busiest man alive.

The hours are still invisible. No one sees me trace the argument of a paragraph for the third time, looking for the connection I keep missing. No one applauds the morning spent learning that the passage does not mean what I had assumed. But God sees the study, and the people feel its presence or its absence as surely as a body feels nourishment or starvation, even when it cannot name the cause. The study is love made invisible. It is the labor a man performs for people who will never know he performed it, so that on Sunday they might be handed something true.

I think about the difference between a well and a faucet, because it captures what the study builds and the neglect of it destroys. A faucet delivers water as long as it is connected to a source, but it stores nothing; cut the connection and it runs dry instantly, because it never held anything, only passed things through. A well stores water, holds a deep reserve drawn up over time, and can give even when the rain has stopped, because it has depth. A preacher who studies builds a well, accumulates over years a deep reserve of understanding, of Scripture grasped and theology grasped and the text known in its connections and its depths, so that when a crisis comes, when a dying man asks the hard question, when a sermon must be preached on short notice, the preacher draws from the reserve and has something to give. A preacher who neglects the study is a faucet, delivering only what is passing through him at the moment, with no reserve, no depth, nothing stored, so that the day the connection fails, the day the crisis comes and there is no time to assemble a borrowed answer, he runs dry instantly and has nothing, because he never built the well. The years of study are the digging of the well, slow and unglamorous and invisible, and the reserve they build is the thing that makes a preacher useful in the unscheduled emergencies of ministry, the deathbed and the crisis and the moment that gives no warning. Dig the well in the years when there is time. The day will come when there is no time to dig, only time to draw, and on that day you will draw from what you built or discover, too late, that you built nothing.

Pay the cost in private, or your people will pay it in public, in the hour they most need what you never built.
chapters.verdict: There is no shortcut to the study that the people will not eventually pay for.
reflect: How many of your sermon hours are spent in the text itself versus its delivery?
What have you let crowd out the study, and what did you tell yourself to justify it?
Would your preparation survive being seen by the God you claim to be quoting?

chapters.title: The Word and the Wind
chapters.summary: Exposition is not a merely human craft but a supernatural act; the same word can be exegeted flawlessly and remain dead until the Spirit carries it. The preacher labors and then depends on a power he cannot summon.
chapters.body:
There is a moment in every faithful preacher's life when he realizes that everything he can control is not enough, and that the things he cannot control are the things that matter most. He has studied the text. He has found the one idea. He has built the structure and chosen his words and prepared his delivery, and all of it is good, and all of it is necessary, and none of it can make a dead man hear. That last work belongs to Someone else. The preacher can prepare the sermon. He cannot prepare the heart. He can deliver the word. He cannot make it land. The wind blows where it will (John 3:8), and the preacher does not command the wind.

This is the truth that keeps preaching from becoming mere technique, and it is the truth our craft-obsessed, conference-driven, method-saturated era is most prone to forget. We have books on preaching, and I have leaned on the good ones, Stott and Lloyd-Jones and Robinson, and I am grateful for them. But there is a danger in all of it, the danger of coming to believe that if we just get the method right, the results will follow, that preaching is a machine and if we feed it the correct inputs it will produce conversions and growth and changed lives on the other end. It is not a machine. It is a man speaking a word into the dark and pleading with God to make the dead live, and the difference between those two pictures is the difference between a technician and a preacher.

Paul knew it. He told the Corinthians that he had planted and Apollos had watered, but God gave the increase, so that neither he that planteth is anything, neither he that watereth, but God that giveth the increase (1 Corinthians 3:6-7). Read that and feel how it cuts against the whole apparatus of the celebrity pulpit. The man who plants is nothing. The man who waters is nothing. Not nothing in the sense of unnecessary, because the planting and the watering are commanded and must be done well. Nothing in the sense of decisive. The decisive thing, the increase, the actual life, comes from God, and the men are reduced to farmhands, doing the labor, dependent for any fruit at all on a rain they cannot summon. I find this both humbling and freeing. Humbling, because it strips me of the illusion that my eloquence saves anyone. Freeing, because it lifts off my shoulders a weight I was never meant to carry, the weight of having to produce results that were never mine to produce.

I want to ground this in the way Paul talks about his own preaching, because Paul is the last man anyone would accuse of neglecting the human side of the work, and yet his account of his own ministry is saturated with dependence on a power outside himself. He tells the Thessalonians that his gospel came to them not in word only but in power and in the Holy Ghost and in much assurance (1 Thessalonians 1:5). Not in word only. The words were there, the careful argument, the reasoning he was famous for, but the words were not the whole of it; there was a power accompanying the words that the words alone could not account for, and Paul names that power as the Holy Spirit. He tells the Corinthians that his preaching was in demonstration of the Spirit and of power, not in the persuasive words of human wisdom (1 Corinthians 2:4), so that their faith would rest not on the eloquence of a man but on the power of God. Read across his letters and the pattern is unmistakable: Paul labored intensely at the human side of preaching and trusted entirely in the divine side, held the two together without apology, never letting his confidence in his message become confidence in his own ability to deliver it effectively. He knew the difference between a sermon that came in word only and a sermon that came in power, and he knew the difference was not his to manufacture, and he preached every sermon pleading for the power he could not produce. If the apostle who wrote half the New Testament preached in conscious dependence on a power outside himself, the notion that we, with our lesser gifts, can dispense with that dependence and rely on our competence is a self-flattery so absurd it would be funny if it were not killing churches.

Lloyd-Jones gave the best name I know to the thing the preacher cannot manufacture. He called it unction, the anointing of the Spirit, the difference between a sermon that is correct and a sermon that is alive. He insisted, and I have come to believe him, that the two are different in kind and not merely degree, that you can have a sermon that is theologically sound, exegetically careful, well structured and well delivered, and that is still dead, because the wind did not blow on it. And you can have a sermon that is rougher, less polished, even somewhat disorganized, that is nonetheless ablaze, because the Spirit came down on it and on the man preaching it, and the people went home having met God. He prayed for unction. He said a man should never enter the pulpit without seeking it. And he warned that no amount of preparation could secure it, that it was a gift, sovereignly given, to be sought and never presumed.

I have known both kinds of Sunday, and I want to describe the difference, because the contrast taught me more than any book. There have been Sundays when I was prepared to the teeth, when the manuscript was tight and I had rehearsed the turns and I knew it was good work, and I stood up and delivered it cleanly and sat down and nothing had happened. The room was polite. People said the expected things at the door. And I drove home knowing, in a place underneath my pride, that I had given them a fine lecture and that the wind had not blown. And there have been other Sundays, fewer than I would like, when I came in less sure of myself, sometimes after a hard week when the preparation had been a struggle, and I stood up and somewhere in the preaching the thing caught fire, not because of anything I did, but because God came near, and the people knew it and I knew it, and grown men wept and hard hearts broke and I had nothing to do with it except to have shown up with a true word and gotten out of the way. I cannot produce those Sundays. I have tried. The trying is precisely the thing that prevents them, because the trying is me reaching for control over a thing that is not mine to control.

I have learned to recognize the difference between the two kinds of fatigue that follow a sermon, and the difference has taught me something about the wind. There is the fatigue of a performance, the tiredness of a man who has held a room by his own energy, expended himself to keep the people engaged, carried the whole weight of the event on his own back, and that fatigue is a particular kind of empty, a depletion that leaves a man hollow because he has been running on himself and the self has been spent. And there is a different fatigue, the fatigue that follows a sermon the Spirit carried, and it is strange, because a man can be exhausted and full at the same time, spent and yet not hollow, tired in the body and somehow more alive in the soul, because he was not the one carrying it, he was the channel through which something larger moved, and the moving filled him even as it tired him. I cannot fully explain it, but I know the two from the inside, and the contrast taught me where the power was. When I have run a sermon on my own steam, I come home empty and a little anxious, needing the affirmation to refill me. When the wind has blown through a sermon, I come home tired and content, not needing the affirmation because I was not the source and so the result is not mine to be anxious about. The two fatigues are a kind of diagnostic the body gives, telling the honest preacher whether he preached in his own strength or in dependence, and a man who learns to read that diagnostic learns to crave the second kind of Sunday and to be suspicious of the first, even when the first drew more praise.

So what does the preacher do with this? He does two things that look contradictory and are not. He prepares as though everything depended on him, and he preaches as though everything depended on God. The preparation is not made unnecessary by the dependence; if anything the dependence demands the preparation, because a man who truly believed the Spirit must carry the word would never dare to hand the Spirit a careless, lazy, half-built sermon to carry. The dependence dignifies the labor. But when the labor is done, when the study is finished and the structure is set, the faithful preacher does not then trust the labor. He falls to his knees and begs. He asks God to do the thing he cannot do, to take the dead words and make them living, to blow the wind he cannot summon, to do for these particular people what no exegesis however careful and no delivery however polished can accomplish. The prayer is not a formality before the real work. The prayer is the acknowledgment that the real work is God's.

This is why a prayerless preacher, however gifted, is finally a tragic figure. He has mistaken the farmhand's labor for the harvest, and he pours himself into the planting and the watering and never once looks up to the only One who gives increase. He may build a large thing, because human gifts can build large things, but it will be a thing built on sand, dependent on the man's energy and charm and competence, and when those fail, as they fail in every man eventually, the thing will fail with them, because the wind was never in it. Spurgeon, who could fill a hall by the sheer force of his gifts, attributed everything he had to the Spirit and prayed like a man who believed his gifts were worthless without the anointing. He had a room full of people praying beneath the platform while he preached, and he credited those praying saints with more of his power than his own remarkable tongue. He understood the economy. The wind does the work. The man holds the sail.

I think the deepest reason we forget this is that the wind is humiliating, and we do not like to be humiliated. If the power were in the method, then the power would be in our control, and a man who masters the method would master the results, and ministry would be a craft you could get good enough at to guarantee outcomes. That is a flattering picture, and it puts the preacher in charge, and the flesh loves it. But the doctrine of the wind takes all of that away. It says that you can do everything right and see nothing happen, and that you can do everything poorly and see God move anyway, and that the decisive factor is outside your control entirely, resting in the free sovereign choice of a God who blows where he wills and gives no account of himself to the men who hold the sails. That is humiliating. It means the most gifted preacher alive cannot guarantee a single conversion, and the most ordinary preacher alive might see a hundred, and neither of them can take the credit or escape the dependence. We resist this doctrine not because it is unclear but because it dethrones us, and we would rather have a method we control than a God we must depend on, even though the God is infinitely better than the method, because the method makes us masters and the God makes us beggars, and the flesh would rather be a master in a dead church than a beggar in a living one.

There is a balance here that the two ditches keep threatening. On one side is the technician, who believes that method is everything and prays, if he prays at all, as a ritual, trusting really in his preparation. On the other side is the mystic, who despises preparation as a quenching of the Spirit, who refuses to study because he wants to leave room for God, and who mistakes his own laziness for faith. Both are wrong, and they are wrong in mirror-image ways. The technician will not depend; the mystic will not labor. The faithful preacher does both, holding the tension that the whole of the Christian life holds, working out his calling with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in him both to will and to do (Philippians 2:12-13). Both. The working and the God-who-works, held together, neither collapsing into the other.

There is a question this doctrine raises that honest preachers ask, and it deserves a real answer rather than a pious dodge: if the wind is sovereign and I cannot summon it, why labor at all, why study, why pray, why care about craft, if the decisive factor is entirely outside my control? And the answer is that the sovereignty of God over the harvest is precisely what dignifies the labor of the farmhand rather than what undermines it. God has ordained the means along with the ends. He has decided to give the increase through the planting and the watering, not instead of them, so that the farmhand's labor is not made pointless by God's sovereignty but is taken up into it, made the very channel through which the sovereign increase comes. Paul did not conclude from God gives the increase that he should stop planting; he planted his heart out across the known world precisely because he believed God would give increase through faithful planting. The doctrine of the wind does not say your labor does not matter; it says your labor does not control the outcome, which is a different thing entirely. You labor as hard as you can, with everything in you, and then you refuse to take credit for the result or blame for its absence, because the result was always God's to give. That is not a recipe for laziness. It is a recipe for the hardest and freest labor there is, the labor of a man who works with all his might and rests in the knowledge that the harvest was never on his shoulders. The lazy man and the anxious man are both unbelievers here, the lazy man denying that the means matter and the anxious man denying that the ends are God's, and the faithful preacher is the one who labors like the lazy man should and rests like the anxious man cannot.

I want to say a hard word to my own tribe, the people who care about expository preaching, because we are particularly susceptible to one of these ditches. We love the word. We love the careful handling of it. We have made, rightly, a great deal of study and structure and the discipline of the text. And we are therefore in constant danger of trusting the method, of believing that because our exegesis is sound our preaching must be powerful, of becoming the technicians who have everything except the wind. I have met expository preachers whose sermons were unassailable and lifeless, every box checked, every text honored, and nothing happening, because somewhere they had stopped begging and started relying on their own correctness. Correctness is not power. A sound sermon is not the same as a Spirit-borne one. We of all people should know this, and we of all people most easily forget it.

I want to say a word about how this doctrine bears on the way we evaluate preaching, because we have built an entire culture of evaluation on the assumption that results measure faithfulness, and the doctrine of the wind demolishes that assumption. We rank preachers by their crowds, their growth, their visible fruit, and we assume that the man with the larger results is the more faithful man, the better preacher, the one God is more clearly blessing. But if the increase is God's to give, sovereignly, for reasons we cannot see, then the size of a man's results tells us almost nothing about the faithfulness of his preaching, because God may withhold visible fruit from his most faithful servant and grant it to a less faithful one, for purposes entirely his own. Isaiah was faithful and saw little fruit. Some prosperity preachers are unfaithful and see enormous crowds. The results are not the verdict, and a church culture that treats them as the verdict is reading the wrong instrument, crowning men God may not have crowned and overlooking men God may treasure. This should comfort the faithful man in the small place and warn the successful man in the large one, because the small man's barrenness may be God's withholding rather than his failure, and the large man's crowds may be the world's reward rather than God's blessing. We will not know, finally, until the day when the true measure is applied, and the true measure was never the size of the harvest but the faithfulness of the sowing, and on that day many who were last in the rankings of men will be first in the rankings of God, and the wind will have blown where it willed all along, vindicating servants the church never noticed and exposing celebrities the church could not stop admiring.

There is a comfort hidden in this doctrine that I have come to lean on hard in the lean years, and I want to hold it out to the discouraged preacher, the man laboring in a small place where nothing seems to come of anything, who has preached his heart out for years to a room that does not grow and does not change and does not, as far as he can see, respond. If the increase were yours to produce, then your barren years would be your verdict, the proof that you have failed, the evidence that you were never any good at this. But the increase is not yours to produce. The wind is God's. Your job was to plant and water faithfully, to handle the word with care, to preach the truth in season and out, and the fruit was always God's responsibility and never yours. Which means your barren years are not your verdict. They may be God's withholding, for reasons you cannot see, in a timing you cannot judge, for a harvest you may never witness. Isaiah preached for a lifetime to a people God told him in advance would not listen, and Isaiah was not a failure; he was faithful, and the fruitlessness was not his to fix. So preach, faithfully, into the silence, and leave the increase where it has always belonged, in the hands of the only One who can give it, and do not let the absence of visible fruit convict you of a failure that was never within your power to commit or to prevent.

So here is the verdict, and it humbles me as I write it. You can build the sermon. You cannot blow the wind. Everything this book has urged about study and submission and craft and the whole counsel is true and necessary and worth your life, and none of it can do the one thing the sermon exists to do, which is to bring a dead heart to life and a living heart nearer to God. That work is the Spirit's, sovereign and free, given to whom he will and withheld where he will, and the preacher's posture before it is not mastery but supplication. Do all the work. Then get on your knees and admit that the work was never the thing. Ask for the wind. And preach like a man who is asking, not like a man who has already arranged for the rain.
chapters.verdict: You can build the sermon. You cannot blow the wind.
reflect: Do you prepare as if it all depends on you, then preach as if it all depends on God?
When did you last beg for the Spirit's power rather than rehearse your delivery?
Are you trusting your competence to do what only the Spirit can do?

chapters.title: Preaching as an Act of Love
chapters.summary: The deepest motive for expository preaching is not duty or doctrine but love for the people, a love that refuses to feed them anything less than God's own word.
chapters.body:
Underneath all the argument about method there is a question about love, and it is the question that finally divides the faithful preacher from the merely competent one. Why bother with exposition at all? Why pay the cost of the study, refuse the idol of relevance, let the text win against your plans, when easier paths exist that fill the same room and earn the same praise? The answer is not duty, though duty is real. The answer is not doctrine, though doctrine is true. The deepest answer is love, and a particular kind of love, the kind that refuses to feed the people anything less than God's own word because the people are starving for God and nothing else will fill them.

When Jesus restored Peter on the shore after the resurrection, he did not ask Peter about his theology or his rhetorical gifts. He asked, three times, whether Peter loved him, and three times he tied the answer to a command: feed my sheep (John 21:15-17). Feeding. The image is maternal, domestic, unglamorous. It is the work of putting nourishment into mouths that cannot feed themselves, day after day, with no applause, because the ones being fed are too dependent and too hungry to do anything but eat. That is what preaching is, underneath the platform and the microphone. It is feeding. And the love of Christ is the only motive strong enough to keep a man doing it faithfully when the easier paths beckon, because the easier paths feed the preacher's hunger to be admired while leaving the sheep hungry for the only thing that sustains them.

I want to dwell on that scene, because the order of it is the whole thing. Jesus does not say, prove you love me and then I will let you feed my sheep, as though feeding were the reward for love. He says, if you love me, then feed them, as though feeding were the expression of love, the thing love does, the form love takes in a man called to ministry. You cannot separate the two. A man who says he loves Christ but will not feed Christ's sheep the real food of Christ's word is a man whose love is in question, however warm his feelings. And the test is not whether he enjoys the people or whether they enjoy him. The test is whether he feeds them, faithfully, the costly true word, even when the feeding is hard and the food is unwelcome and the sheep would rather have something sweeter. Love feeds. It does not flatter.

Here is the cruelty I have come to fear most in myself. The desire to be liked is not, on its face, a vicious thing. It feels like warmth. It feels like care. But it is the most reliable corrupter of the pulpit, because it bends every decision toward the soft word over the true one, the comforting half over the difficult whole, the application that flatters over the rebuke that heals. And the bending is invisible to the man doing it, because it disguises itself as kindness. He tells himself he is sparing the people, when in fact he is sparing himself the discomfort of their displeasure. He withholds the hard word and calls it gentleness. It is not gentleness. It is the cruelty of a physician who will not name the disease because the diagnosis is unpleasant to deliver, and who therefore lets the patient die comfortable and uninformed.

Bonhoeffer's indictment of cheap grace was, at its root, an indictment of preachers who loved their congregations too little to tell them the truth. Cheap grace is grace preached without the cross, forgiveness offered without repentance, comfort dispensed without cost, and it is, Bonhoeffer saw, the preferred product of a clergy that wants to be loved more than it wants its people to be saved. The costly word, the word that demands and disrupts and calls for death before resurrection, is the loving word, even when it does not feel loving in the moment of its delivery. The cheap word, the soothing word, the word that never asks anything, is the cruel one, however warmly it is received. We have inverted these, in our era, and called the cruelty kindness and the kindness cruelty, and a whole generation of congregations has been comforted to death.

I have to confess where I have fallen on the wrong side of this. There are sermons I softened. There are members I did not want to lose, families that gave generously and served faithfully and whose displeasure would have cost the church and cost me, and the word I preached to them was bent, subtly, toward their comfort and away from their good. I did not experience myself as a coward in those moments. I experienced myself as pastoral, sensitive, wise about timing. Some of that was real. Timing is real, and not every truth must be spoken on every Sunday, and there is such a thing as patience that waits for the right moment. But some of it was fear wearing the robe of love, and I knew the difference even when I would not admit it, and the people I was supposedly loving received less than the word God had for them because I was protecting my standing with them. That is the self-implication I cannot escape and will not pretend away. The kindest preacher I know would rather lose your affection than starve your soul, and I have not always been that preacher.

Let me get specific about how this works, because abstractions let us off the hook.
