A man sits in your church who is cruel to his wife, and everyone knows it, and the texts on how a husband must love his wife as Christ loved the church keep coming up in the preaching calendar, and every time they do you have a choice. You can preach the text in its full demand, knowing he is in the room, knowing it will land on him, knowing he may bristle and his giving may stop and his friends may grumble. Or you can preach it generally, abstractly, in a way that lets everyone nod and no one feels named, and you can tell yourself you are being wise. But you are not being wise. You are letting a man go on destroying the woman he vowed to love because you would rather keep his goodwill than risk it for her sake and his. That is not love. The loving thing, the hard loving thing, is to preach the text so that it finds him, gently but unmistakably, and to trust God with what happens next. I have done both. I am not proud of the times I chose the abstraction.

I grew up without a father, and I have thought a great deal about what that absence did and what it taught me, and one of the things it taught me bears directly on this. A father who is absent does no obvious harm in any given moment. He is not there to wound you; he is simply not there. And for a long time, as a boy, I did not experience the absence as a wound at all, because you cannot feel the lack of a thing you have never had. The damage was invisible and slow and entirely by omission, and it shaped me in ways I could not see and could not name until I was a grown man trying to figure out how to be a father myself with no template to work from. I bring this up because the preacher who withholds the hard word does exactly what the absent father does. He inflicts no visible wound. He is gentle, present, agreeable. And the damage he does is the damage of omission, invisible and slow, a congregation shaped by the absence of words they never knew they were missing, malnourished in ways they cannot name, unequipped for trials they have not yet faced. No one will ever stand up and accuse the agreeable preacher of harm, the way no one accused my absent father of any particular cruelty, because the harm of omission does not look like harm. It looks like peace. And it is the deadliest kind of harm precisely because it never shows up as harm, and the people being harmed will often defend the man harming them, because he was so kind, he never said a hard word, he never made anyone uncomfortable, which is exactly the indictment.

Keller, whose preaching theory has shaped a generation, argued that preaching must always reach the heart, not merely the intellect, and that the way to the heart is not flattery but the gospel applied to the actual idols and fears of the actual hearers. This is love disciplined by truth. It is not the love that tells the people what they want to hear; it is the love that knows them well enough to tell them what their hearts are actually clutching, and then to pry the fingers loose with the only thing strong enough to do it, which is the news of a Savior who loves them more than their idols ever could. That kind of preaching costs the preacher something. It requires him to know his people, to study their hearts as carefully as he studies his text, and to speak into the gap between what they want and what they need with a courage that only love supplies. Fear cannot do it. Only love can say the hard thing and mean it for the hearer's good.

There is a specific failure of love that deserves naming because it is so common it has become invisible, and it is the failure to apply. A preacher can love his people enough to study hard and preach accurately and still fail to love them at the last step, the step where the truth meets their actual lives, because that step is the most uncomfortable and the most personal and the most likely to cost him. It is one thing to explain what a text means; it is another to look at the people you know and name where this truth presses on them, the husband who is harsh, the woman who is bitter, the family that loves money, the man who is drifting toward an affair, the congregation that is comfortable and cold. Application is where preaching gets personal, and personal is where it gets costly, and a preacher who loves his comfort more than his people will preach accurate sermons that never quite land on anyone, that float above the room in the safe air of the general, that explain the disease in textbook terms and never say to the patient in the third row, you have this, and here is what it is doing to you, and here is the only cure. That kind of preaching looks faithful. The exegesis is sound. But it has refused the last and hardest act of love, which is to bring the true word all the way down to the specific life, and a preacher does that only when he loves the people more than he fears their discomfort or his own. I have stopped short of application out of cowardice more times than I have stopped short of accuracy, because accuracy is safe and application is dangerous, and the danger is exactly the measure of the love that application requires.

The expository commitment is, finally, a commitment of love, because it is a commitment to give the people God rather than the preacher. When I submit to the text, when I let it set the agenda and refuse to bend it toward my preferences or theirs, I am insisting that my people deserve the actual word of God and not a substitute, however charming the substitute might be. I am saying that they are worth the cost of the study, worth the risk of the offense, worth the loss of my own popularity, because they are God's sheep and not my fans, and sheep need feeding, not flattering. The topical performer who chases relevance and softens the hard texts is, whatever his intentions, loving himself through his people. The expositor who pays the cost and lets the text win is loving the people through his own discomfort. Same robe. Opposite love.

I want to press the feeding image one step further, because the kind of food matters and we have grown careless about it. A loving parent does not feed a child only what the child enjoys. A child left to choose his own diet will eat candy until he is sick, and a parent who indulges that, who provides only the sweet and the easy because the child smiles when he gets it and cries when he does not, is not a loving parent but a negligent one, however warm his motives. Real love for a child includes the vegetables the child refuses, the bedtimes the child resents, the medicine the child spits out, all the unwelcome goods that the child cannot yet appreciate but desperately needs. And the parent endures the child's displeasure because the parent can see what the child cannot, the long-term good that the short-term resistance is fighting against. Preaching is exactly this. A congregation, left to choose its own diet, will choose the spiritual candy, the comforting and the affirming and the easy, and a preacher who provides only that, who tunes his menu to the congregation's smiles, is the negligent parent who feeds the child sweets until the child is sick. The loving preacher serves the whole diet, including the parts the people would never choose, the hard doctrines and the unwelcome corrections and the demanding calls, and he endures their displeasure because he can see what they cannot, the long-term spiritual health that the short-term resistance is fighting against. Their displeasure is not evidence that he has failed to love them. It is sometimes the clearest evidence that he has, because the candy-only preacher is never resented and never resisted and never angers anyone, and his people grow sick on the diet he serves with a smile.

Eugene Peterson spent his ministry insisting that the pastor's work is the slow, unspectacular cultivation of souls, that it cannot be rushed or scaled or performed, that it is more like farming than like manufacturing. Preaching, in that vision, is not a performance delivered to a crowd but a meal prepared for a family, and the question is never how the meal played but whether it nourished. A man can cook to impress or cook to feed, and the dishes may look identical, but the love is different and the family knows the difference over years. They know whether they have been fed or merely entertained, whether they have grown or merely been amused, whether the one in the kitchen was serving them or serving himself.

I think about my five sons here, because fatherhood has taught me what love costs. There were words my sons needed from me that I did not want to say, corrections that would cost me their momentary affection, truths that a softer father would have skipped to keep the peace. And the soft father, the one who never says the hard thing because he cannot bear his children's displeasure, is not the loving father. He is the cowardly one, sacrificing his children's good on the altar of his own need to be liked by them. A congregation is not a family in every sense, but in this sense it is exactly a family, and the preacher who will not say the hard word because he needs to be liked is the spiritual father who lets his children walk toward the cliff because correcting them would have cost him a hard afternoon.

There is a question I have learned to ask myself that exposes whether love or fear is driving a given sermon, and it is uncomfortable enough that I only ask it when I am ready for the answer. The question is: who am I protecting? When I soften a word, hold back a rebuke, generalize an application that should have been specific, choose the comfortable text over the confronting one, the question is always who I am protecting by the choice, and the honest answer reveals everything. Sometimes, genuinely, I am protecting a fragile soul who has had enough and needs binding rather than breaking, and that is love. But more often, if I am honest, the one I am protecting is me, my standing, my comfort, my relationships, my freedom from the hard conversation the sermon would provoke. The softening I dressed up as pastoral sensitivity turns out, under the question, to be self-protection, the preacher shielding himself behind a fiction of shielding the people. Love protects the people at the preacher's expense. Fear protects the preacher at the people's expense. And the two produce nearly identical sermons, the same softening, the same generality, the same comfortable choice, so that you cannot tell them apart from the outside and often cannot tell them apart from the inside either, unless you ask the question and force the honest answer. Who am I protecting? Ask it of your softened sermons, and brace yourself, because the answer is humbling more often than not, and the humbling is the beginning of preaching that loves the people enough to leave the preacher unprotected, which is the only kind of preaching that actually feeds them.

So I come back to the shore, and to the question that will not leave me. Lovest thou me? Feed my sheep. The whole of expository preaching is contained in those two sentences, the love and the feeding bound together so that neither can exist without the other. To love Christ is to feed his people his word. To feed his people his word is to love them more than I love their approval of me. And to withhold the word for the sake of being liked is the cruelest thing a preacher can do, dressed up as the kindest, fooling everyone, including himself, until the day the unfed sheep go looking for food in the famine and find that their shepherd gave them stones, beautifully arranged, and called it bread.

I have to add one balancing word, because love is not only the courage to wound and a chapter that only celebrated the hard word would be a lie. Love also knows when not to strike, when a soul is already crushed and needs binding rather than breaking, when the text in front of you is hard but the person in front of you has had enough hardness for one season and what they need this Sunday is the comfort the same Bible holds in equal measure. The God who said he would not break a bruised reed nor quench smoking flax (Isaiah 42:3) is the God whose word the preacher carries, and that God knows the difference between the sin that must be confronted and the wound that must be bound, between the hard heart that needs the hammer and the broken heart that needs the balm. A preacher who only ever wields the hard word, who mistakes harshness for faithfulness and thinks every sermon must draw blood, is not loving either; he is just cruel in the opposite direction, and he will crush the very people the gentle coward was failing to challenge. The discipline of love is the discipline of knowing which word this person needs in this season, and that knowing requires the preacher to actually know his people, to be among them, to have sat in their living rooms and at their hospital beds, so that when he stands up to preach he is not aiming a generic word at a generic audience but feeding particular sheep he has come to know, some of whom need the rod and some of whom need the staff, and a shepherd worth the name can tell them apart.

I have one more thing to say before I leave the shore, and it is the hardest, because it turns the question back on the preacher's own motives in a way I cannot escape. The reason we withhold the hard word is almost always that we love something more than we love the people, and usually the thing we love more is ourselves, our comfort, our reputation, our ease, our freedom from conflict. And the cure for cowardly preaching is therefore not, finally, more courage, because courage summoned by willpower runs out. The cure is a deeper love, a love for the people so real that it outweighs the love of self that produces the cowardice. A man does not become a brave preacher by gritting his teeth and resolving to be brave. He becomes a brave preacher by coming to love his people more than he loves his own comfort, so that the bravery flows naturally from the love, the way a mother runs into danger for her child without summoning courage because the love makes the courage automatic. So if you find yourself preaching softly out of fear, the deepest remedy is not to scold yourself for cowardice but to ask God to deepen your love, because the cowardice is a symptom of a love that is still smaller than your self-interest, and when the love grows larger than the self-interest, the cowardice dies of its own accord, no willpower required. Love them more. That is the whole cure. Love them more than you love your own comfort, and the hard words will come, not because you forced them, but because you could no longer bear to withhold from people you love the only thing that could save them.

Feed them. It will cost you their occasional displeasure. Withholding the word will cost them their souls, and you the only thing Christ ever asked you to prove you loved him.
chapters.verdict: To withhold the word for the sake of being liked is the cruelest thing a preacher can do.
reflect: Do you preach to be useful to your people or to be admired by them?
Where has the desire to be liked softened a word your people needed sharp?
If preaching is feeding, what have you actually been setting on the table?

chapters.title: Against the Performance of the Self
chapters.summary: The pulpit's oldest temptation is to display the preacher rather than declare the word. Personality, charisma, and gifting can all become forms of theft from the God who is meant to be heard.
chapters.body:
The most respectable sin in ministry is the one the church most reliably rewards, and that is the display of the self. We have built an entire culture around it. We platform the gifted, we promote the charismatic, we build conferences around the men who can hold ten thousand people and we wonder, quietly, why the churches those men leave behind so often collapse when the personality departs. The answer is uncomfortable. The people had been gathering around a man, and when the man was gone there was nothing underneath, because the man had been the foundation all along, and a man is sand.

Self-display is the oldest temptation of the pulpit because the pulpit is the one place in ordinary life where a person is given sustained, undivided attention by a silent and attentive crowd. There is no other setting like it. The actor shares the stage; the politician faces hecklers; the teacher must manage a room that talks back. The preacher alone is granted thirty or forty minutes of reverent silence from people who have come, in theory, to be changed. That arrangement is an almost irresistible invitation to self-worship, and the tragedy is that the better a man's gifts, the more powerful the invitation, because the more the display actually works. The mediocre preacher is protected from this sin by his mediocrity. The gifted preacher walks toward it every Sunday and must fight it every Sunday, and many do not even know there is a fight.

I want to trace how a man falls into this, because it is never a single decision and naming the slope is the only way to watch your own feet on it. No preacher wakes up one morning and decides to make himself the point. It happens in increments so small that none of them feels like a fall. He preaches a sermon that goes well and tastes the pleasure of it, and there is nothing wrong with the pleasure itself; God made us to enjoy doing well the thing we were made to do. But then he begins, just slightly, to chase the pleasure, to write toward the moments that produced it, to favor the illustration that got the response over the one that served the text better. Still nothing dramatic, still entirely defensible, still invisible to everyone including himself. Then he starts to notice the numbers, the attendance, the shares, the invitations, and he begins, just slightly, to optimize for them, to do more of what grows them and less of what does not. Then the affirmation becomes a need rather than a pleasure, something he requires to feel all right, so that a flat Sunday wounds him in a way that has nothing to do with whether the people were fed and everything to do with whether he was fed by their response. And by the time he arrives, years later, at a ministry organized entirely around his own magnification, he could not tell you when it happened, because it never happened, it accreted, one tiny defensible step at a time, each step too small to notice, the whole descent invisible because no single moment of it was visible. That is how the gifted man falls, not by a decision but by a drift, and the only defense is a vigilance that examines the small steps, because by the time the fall is large enough to see, it is far too late to easily reverse.

Spurgeon, who could hold a crowd of thousands without amplification in the days before microphones, lived in terror of preaching himself. He understood that his gifts were the very thing most likely to destroy him, that the power to move a room is a power that flatters its possessor into thinking the movement is the point. He insisted that the preacher must decrease so that Christ might increase, echoing the Baptist's own confession that he must decrease while Christ increased (John 3:30), and he meant it as a working discipline and not a pious sentiment. The discipline of decrease. The deliberate, repeated choice to remove the self from the center of the sermon so that the word can occupy it. This is brutally hard for a gifted man, because his gifts are constantly volunteering to take the center, and they take it so gracefully that no one objects, least of all the man himself.

I know this temptation from the inside, and I will not pretend to a humility I have not always practiced. There is a particular pleasure in delivering a line that lands, in feeling a room lean in, in sensing that you have them, and that pleasure is a drug, and like every drug it reorganizes the appetites of the one who tastes it. A preacher who has felt that pleasure begins, without deciding to, to write toward it. He builds his sermons around the moments that produce it. He becomes, by slow degrees, a man optimizing for the experience of being powerful in front of people, and he can do this while preaching impeccably orthodox content, which is what makes it so hard to detect. The doctrine is sound. The texts are handled correctly. And underneath, the whole enterprise has quietly become about the man. The word has become his vehicle rather than his master.

I want to tell on myself here in a way that still embarrasses me. Years ago I preached a sermon I knew was good, a sermon with a line in it that I had crafted carefully because I knew it would land, and it did land, and afterward people quoted it back to me for weeks. And I noticed something ugly in myself. I was glad they remembered the line. I was not particularly concerned with whether they remembered the truth the line was supposed to serve. I had wanted the line to be remembered, the line that was mine, the line that showed what I could do. And when I sat with that, honestly, before God, I had to admit that somewhere in the building of that sermon I had stopped serving the text and started serving my reputation, and the people had gone home admiring me, which was, God help me, exactly what I had wanted. That is the sickness, and it can coexist with sound doctrine indefinitely, and most of us never confess it because it never shows up in any way the elders could discipline.

Paul saw this clearly and refused it openly. He told the Corinthians that he came to them not with excellency of speech or of wisdom, that he had determined to know nothing among them save Jesus Christ and him crucified, and that his speech and his preaching were deliberately not with enticing words of man's wisdom, so that their faith would rest on the power of God and not on the wisdom of men (1 Corinthians 2:1-5). Read that as the manifesto it is. Paul, who was capable of dazzling rhetoric when he chose, deliberately disarmed himself before the Corinthians, deliberately refused the tools of self-display, because he understood that a faith built on a preacher's brilliance is a faith built on a man, and men fail, and when the man fails the faith fails with him. He wanted their faith anchored to something that would hold when he was gone, and the only thing that holds is God. So he got himself out of the way on purpose, at the cost of looking less impressive than he could have looked.

This is the deep reason exposition matters, beyond all the arguments about method. Exposition is the discipline that structurally subordinates the preacher to the text. When the main point of the sermon is the main point of the passage, the preacher cannot make himself the point, because the point was decided before he arrived. When the text sets the agenda, the preacher's personality is demoted from author to servant. He may still be vivid, may still be eloquent, may still bear the marks of his particular voice, because God made him a particular man and grace does not erase personality. But the personality is now in service to the word rather than the word in service to the personality, and that inversion is the whole battle. Brueggemann's poet is not displaying his own genius; he is letting a word from outside come through him. The poetry serves the interruption. The moment the poet starts admiring his own poetry, the interruption stops, and the people are left admiring the poet, which is exactly the thing that cannot save them.

I want to name the subtlest form of this sin, because it is the one that catches the men who think they have escaped it. It is the performance of humility. A man can learn that self-display is wrong, can read a chapter like this one, can resolve to decrease, and can then turn his very decreasing into a performance, a calculated self-deprecation, a strategic vulnerability, a public confession of his own smallness that is, underneath, one more bid for the room's admiration. We have all seen it, the preacher who tells a story against himself so charmingly that the room loves him more for it, who confesses a sin in a way that makes him look brave and relatable, who has discovered that the appearance of humility is itself a powerful tool for winning a crowd. This is self-display wearing the mask of self-denial, and it is more dangerous than open arrogance because it is harder to see and impossible to rebuke; you cannot accuse a man of pride who has just publicly called himself the chief of sinners. I catch myself doing this. I will tell a story on myself in a sermon, a real failure, genuinely confessed, and then notice, in the telling, a part of me calculating how it will land, gauging whether the confession is making me look good by making me look bad, and the noticing is horrifying, because it reveals that even my repentance can be conscripted into the service of my reputation. There is no escape from this by technique. The only escape is a real and ongoing death of the self before God, in private, that has nothing to do with how it plays, and the man who has died that death will confess his sins in the pulpit when it serves the people and keep silent when the confession would only serve himself, and the difference between those will be visible only to God and to his own examined conscience.

There is a test I have learned to apply to my own preaching, and I offer it because it has wounded me usefully. After a sermon, I ask what the people went away talking about. If they went away talking about me, about how I said it, about the line that landed, about the way I held the room, then I have to consider that I preached myself, however orthodox my content. If they went away talking about the text, about what God said, about the thing the passage pressed on them, then perhaps, by grace, I got out of the way enough for the word to be heard. The test is not infallible, because people are kind and will praise the man even when the man got out of the way. But it is a useful warning, and the warning I most need, because my flesh will always prefer to be the one remembered.

I want to add a word about our particular moment, because the technology of our age has poured gasoline on this ancient fire. A preacher today does not preach only to the room. He preaches to a camera, to a clip that will be cut and shared, to a platform that rewards the quotable and punishes the slow, to metrics that tell him exactly how many people watched and for how long. Every one of those things tempts him to preach toward the highlight, to build sermons out of shareable moments, to become a producer of content rather than a feeder of sheep. I am not against the camera. The word can go further than it ever could. But I am clear-eyed about what the camera does to the man behind the pulpit, how it whispers to him constantly that he is building a brand, that he is reaching an audience, that his real congregation is out there in the numbers and not here in the pews, and how that whisper, followed, turns a shepherd into a performer with a feed. Guard your heart against the metrics. They are measuring the wrong thing, and they are measuring it precisely so that you will start to care about it.

Lloyd-Jones distinguished between the preacher who has unction, the genuine anointing of the Spirit, and the preacher who has only natural ability dressed up as anointing, and he insisted the two are different in kind and not merely in degree. Natural ability draws attention to itself. Unction draws attention to God. The same words can carry either, which is what makes the distinction so hard to police from the outside, but the fruit differs over time. Where there is unction, people meet God and are changed and the preacher recedes in their memory. Where there is only ability, people meet a remarkable man and are entertained and the man grows in their memory until he eclipses the God he was meant to reveal. The eclipse is the failure. A preacher exists to point past himself, and a finger that draws the eye to the finger has failed at the one thing fingers are for.

I want to give a practical discipline that has helped me fight this, small and concrete, because grand resolutions to be humble accomplish nothing. After I preach, I do not let myself dwell on the compliments. When people tell me at the door that the sermon was good, that I moved them, that the line landed, I receive it graciously, because it is kindly meant, but I refuse to take it home and feed on it, because I have learned that feeding on the compliments is the very thing that grows the appetite for self-display. Instead I ask, in the quiet afterward, a different set of questions. Was the text honored? Did I get out of the way? Was anything in the sermon there for me rather than for them? Where did I reach for the effect instead of the truth? These questions are not pleasant, and they do not feed the ego the way the compliments do, but they keep me oriented toward the right measure, the measure of faithfulness rather than impression. And I have found that a man who consistently asks the faithfulness questions instead of feeding on the impression compliments slowly reorganizes his appetites, comes over years to care more about whether the text was honored than about whether he was admired, not because he achieved some heroic humility but because he kept asking the right questions until the right questions began to shape what he wanted. The flesh will always prefer the compliments. The discipline is to refuse them their power, to let them pass without lodging, and to interrogate yourself by a harder and truer standard, week after week, until the standard becomes second nature and the compliments lose their grip.

The verdict is unsparing, so let it be unsparing. The more the people see the preacher, the less they hear the Lord. There is a fixed economy here; attention spent on the man is attention withdrawn from the word. A preacher cannot magnify himself and Christ in the same breath, because magnification is a zero-sum thing and the eye goes to whatever is largest in the frame. The faithful preacher spends his whole working life making himself smaller in the frame, decreasing on purpose, removing his own fingerprints from the word so that the word can be heard as God's and not his. It is the most counterintuitive labor in ministry, and the culture of the church fights it at every turn, rewarding the very self-display the calling requires us to crucify.

There is a cost to decreasing that I should name honestly, because the chapter could make it sound easy and it is not. To get out of the way, to refuse the self-display the culture rewards, to preach in a manner that points past yourself, is to accept that you will be less impressive than you could be, less talked-about, less invited, less likely to build the platform that the self-displaying men are building. The discipline of decrease has a price, and the price is paid in the currency of recognition, and a man who decreases on purpose is choosing, deliberately, to be smaller in the eyes of the church than his gifts could make him, watching lesser men with louder self-promotion rise past him, and accepting it as the cost of faithfulness. This is genuinely hard, and I will not pretend I have paid it cheerfully. There is a part of me that watches the platform-builders and feels the pull, that wonders whether I am being faithful or merely timid, whether my refusal to promote myself is humility or just a failure of nerve dressed up as virtue. The line between the two is real but it is hard to see from the inside, and a man can talk himself into either reading. What I hold onto is the long view, the knowledge that the platform built on self-display collapses with the self, that the recognition I am foregoing is grass, that the choice to decrease is a choice to build on something that will outlast the recognition I am declining. But I will not pretend the choice is painless. It costs, in the only currency the ambitious heart cares about, and the man who tells you decreasing is easy has either never been gifted enough to face the temptation or is lying about how it feels.

I think often of John the Baptist, who is the patron saint of this whole struggle, and of the moment his own disciples came to him anxious because the crowds were leaving him for Jesus. Their teacher's ministry was shrinking. The numbers were moving to the new man. And John's response is the response every preacher should have tattooed on the inside of his eyelids. He must increase, but I must decrease (John 3:30). Not, he must increase and I must hold my position. Not, he must increase and I must maintain my brand. He must increase, and I must decrease, and the two are tied together, the decreasing of the herald serving the increasing of the Lord, so that John's shrinking is not his tragedy but his success, the very thing he existed for, the fulfillment of his calling rather than its failure. He had said it himself earlier, that he was the friend of the bridegroom, the best man at the wedding, and that the best man's joy is fulfilled precisely when he fades into the background and the bride goes to the groom. A best man who tried to keep the bride's attention on himself would be a monster. His whole joy is to disappear into the success of the marriage he helped bring about. That is the preacher. We are the friend of the bridegroom, and our joy is fulfilled not when the people love us but when the people go to Christ and forget us, and a preacher who has not learned to find his joy there has not understood his office at all and will spend his ministry competing with the very Lord he was ordained to introduce.

Get out of the way. They did not come to see you, whatever the applause suggests, and the day you forget that is the day you begin to starve the people who trusted you to feed them God.
chapters.verdict: The more the people see the preacher, the less they hear the Lord.
reflect: When people describe your preaching, do they describe you or what you said?
What gift of yours have you allowed to become the point rather than the instrument?
Could you preach a sermon designed to be forgotten so the text would be remembered?

chapters.title: The Whole Counsel and the Hard Texts
chapters.summary: A faithful pulpit must preach the difficult, the offensive, and the neglected portions of Scripture, not only the comfortable ones. Editing the canon is a failure of trust in the God who gave all of it.
chapters.body:
When Paul said goodbye to the Ephesian elders, knowing he would not see them again, he summarized his ministry among them in a single boast, and it is the only boast a preacher is permitted. He said he was pure from the blood of all men, for he had not shunned to declare unto them the whole counsel of God (Acts 20:26-27). The whole counsel. Not the popular fraction. Not the comfortable selection. The whole. And he tied his innocence of their blood to that completeness, which means that to preach only part of the counsel is, in Paul's accounting, to be in some sense responsible for what the unpreached part would have prevented. That is a terrifying thought, and we have largely stopped thinking it.

Every preacher edits the canon, and most of us do it without admitting we are doing it. We do not announce that we have decided to skip the doctrine of hell, or the texts on judgment, or the hard sayings of Jesus about money and family and the cost of discipleship, or the passages that offend the moral consensus of our particular moment. We simply, over time, do not get to them. The preaching calendar drifts, year after year, toward the texts that comfort and away from the texts that confront, and after a decade a congregation has heard the encouraging psalms many times and the imprecatory psalms never, has heard the love of God in a thousand forms and the wrath of God in none, has been told repeatedly that they are accepted and rarely that they must repent. The editing is invisible because it happens by omission, and omission leaves no fingerprints. But the people are shaped by it as surely as they would be shaped by open heresy, perhaps more surely, because they do not know it is happening.

Here is what I have come to believe about the skipped texts: they are preaching a sermon of their own, and it is a sermon about the preacher's actual theology, the one underneath the one he professes. A man who never preaches judgment is teaching his people that judgment does not much matter, whatever his stated doctrine. A man who never preaches the cost of following Christ is teaching that there is no cost, whatever he says about the cross. The canon he actually preaches is his real confession of faith, and it is often quite different from the confession he would sign. We learn what a preacher truly trusts by watching what he is willing to say, and even more by watching what he consistently refuses to say, because the refusals reveal the fears, and the fears reveal the gods.

I have noticed that the hard texts a particular preacher avoids are a kind of map of that preacher's own unsurrendered places, and the map is worth reading honestly. Show me the doctrines a man will not preach and I will show you, with fair accuracy, the idols he has not yet given up, because we do not avoid the texts that threaten other people's idols; we avoid the texts that threaten our own. A preacher who will not preach on money usually has a complicated relationship with money. A preacher who softens every text on sexual purity is often softening it for reasons closer to home than he would admit. A preacher who cannot bring himself to preach judgment frequently has a sentimental view of God that he is protecting in himself as much as in his people. The avoidance is not random; it traces the contour of the preacher's own resistance, and a man who wanted to know the truth about his own heart could do worse than to look at the list of texts he never quite gets around to. I have done this exercise on myself and it was not comfortable. The passages I had been quietly avoiding turned out to map, with embarrassing precision, onto the places where I had not yet fully surrendered, the loves I was protecting, the sins I was comfortable with, the corners of my life I had not handed over. The hard text I will not preach is the hard text I have not yet let win against me, and the avoidance in the pulpit traces a deeper avoidance in the soul, which means the discipline of preaching the whole counsel is not only a service to the people but a tool for the preacher's own searching, a mirror that shows him, by what he flinches from, where the work of his own sanctification still has the furthest to go.

The hard texts are hard for a reason, and the reason is usually that they cut against something we love. The texts on money are hard because we love money. The texts on sexual purity are hard because we love our autonomy. The texts on judgment are hard because we love a god who never finally says no. The texts on the exclusivity of Christ are hard because we love the approval of a pluralist culture. In every case the difficulty is located not in the text but in us, in our attachment to the very thing the text means to dislodge, and the preacher who avoids the hard text is protecting his people's idols, and his own, under the guise of pastoral sensitivity. He is not sparing them. He is colluding with the thing that is destroying them, because the idol the text would have named goes on unnamed and therefore unchallenged and therefore enthroned.

I want to distinguish two failures here, because they are different and they need different remedies. The first failure is cowardice, the deliberate avoidance of a text because you are afraid of the consequences. That one is straightforward sin, and the remedy is repentance and courage. But there is a second failure that is subtler and that traps the conscientious, and it is the failure of imbalance. A man may preach the hard texts when they come up, may never deliberately avoid one, and still produce a lopsided diet because his choices over the years have favored certain books and certain genres and certain themes. He preaches a great deal of Paul and very little of the prophets. He loves the Gospels and avoids Leviticus. He is comfortable in the epistles and lost in the apocalyptic. None of this is cowardice. It is just preference, the natural human drift toward what we find congenial, and over a long ministry it produces a congregation that has been fed a partial Bible by a man who never once decided to feed them a partial Bible. The remedy for the second failure is planning, the deliberate, prayerful mapping of a preaching diet over years that ensures the people get the whole counsel and not just the parts their pastor happens to relish.

Let me take the doctrine of hell as a case study, because it is the hard text most consistently dropped in our generation and the dropping illustrates everything. A pastor does not announce that he no longer believes in hell. He simply stops preaching it. The texts that teach it come up in the reading and he handles them quickly, abstractly, or skips to the surrounding verses, and over a decade his people hear about the love of God a thousand times and the judgment of God essentially never. And here is the result, which is worse than mere imbalance. The love of God, preached without the judgment it rescues us from, becomes sentiment, a vague divine niceness, because love only means something against the backdrop of the danger it saves you from. A father who pulls his child from in front of a truck has shown love; a father who hugs a child in no danger has shown affection, which is a smaller thing. Strip out the truck, strip out the real peril, and the rescue shrinks into a hug, and the cross, which was God's answer to a real and terrible judgment, becomes inexplicable, an extravagant gesture in response to no real threat. The people cannot understand why Christ had to die if there was nothing to be saved from, and so the cross drifts to the margins, becomes an example of love rather than an atonement for sin, and the whole gospel quietly collapses into a message about being nice, because the hard doctrine that gave the soft doctrine its weight was removed for the people's comfort. The dropped text did not merely leave a gap. It pulled down the structure around it, because the doctrines of Scripture are load-bearing and you cannot remove one without weakening the ones it held up. That is why the whole counsel is not a matter of completeness for its own sake. It is a matter of structural integrity, every doctrine supporting the others, the whole thing standing or falling together.

Bonhoeffer preached in a church that had made a catastrophic set of omissions, that had quietly stopped preaching the texts that would have armed its people against the ideology rising around them, and the cost of those omissions was a church that could not resist when resistance was the whole of faithfulness. The unpreached texts left the people defenseless. When the moment came that required them to stand on a hard word, they had never been given the hard word, and so they fell, in large numbers, with their pastors leading the fall. This is the long-range stakes of the whole counsel, and it is why Paul tied it to innocence of blood. The texts a preacher skips in the comfortable years are precisely the texts his people will need in the catastrophic ones, and the catastrophe always comes, and it always comes for the thing the comfortable preaching never prepared anyone to face.

I have skipped texts. I have looked at a passage coming up in a series and thought, not this month, the church is fragile right now, the timing is wrong, and sometimes the judgment was genuinely pastoral and sometimes it was cowardice wearing pastoral robes, and I have not always been able to tell the difference in the moment, which is exactly the problem. The flesh is endlessly inventive in supplying noble reasons for ignoble avoidances. The only defense I have found is structural, the same defense Calvin used: preach through the books, and let the hard texts arrive in their turn, not because I chose them but because they are simply next, so that my cowardice is denied the opportunity to do its quiet editing. When the hard text is next, I must either preach it or openly skip it, and the openness of the skip exposes it for what it is, where the invisible drift of selective preaching never has to face the light.

I should say something about how to preach the hard text, because deciding to preach it is only half the battle and a man can preach a hard text badly, in a way that does more harm than skipping it. The hard text must be preached with the same submission and the same love as any other, which means the preacher does not preach it triumphantly, as though he were glad to deliver the bad news, nor defensively, as though apologizing for God. He preaches it the way a faithful physician delivers a hard diagnosis, with clarity and with compassion, naming the thing fully because to soften it would be to lie, but naming it as a man who is himself under the same word, who is not standing above the text wielding it at others but standing under the text alongside the people, indicted with them, in need of the same grace. The hard text on greed must be preached by a man who feels the pull of greed. The hard text on pride must be preached by a man who knows his own pride better than he knows his congregation's. When the preacher is visibly inside the indictment, the hard text lands as truth and not as attack, and the people can receive it, because they can see it is not the preacher's weapon but God's surgery, and the preacher is on the table too.

Let me give the practical counsel I wish someone had given me, the discipline that has done more than anything else to keep my own preaching from drifting into a comfortable rut. Once a year, sit down and look back, not forward. Take the list of every text you preached in the last twelve months and lay it out and look at it honestly, as a diet, the way a doctor would look at a record of everything a patient ate in a year. What were they fed? Was it balanced, or was it the same few food groups over and over? How much Old Testament and how much New? How much of the hard and how much of the comfortable? When did you last preach on judgment, on hell, on money, on sexual sin, on the cost of discipleship, on the wrath of God, on the things that do not test well? When did you last spend a sustained season in a book you find difficult, a prophet, a section of the law, the harder reaches of the apocalyptic? The list does not lie, and it will tell you what you have actually been preaching, which is often quite different from what you imagine you have been preaching, because we all remember our courage and forget our avoidances. I have done this exercise and been ashamed by it, have discovered that a year I thought was balanced was in fact heavily weighted toward the texts I find congenial, that whole regions of Scripture had simply not appeared, not by decision but by drift. The annual look-back is the cheapest insurance there is against the slow editing of the canon, because it drags the drift into the light where you can see it and repent of it and plan against it for the year ahead.

There is a theological humility at stake here that I want to name precisely. When I edit the canon, I am claiming to know better than God what my people need. I am overruling his choice of what to include with my sense of what they can handle. But the canon is God's curriculum, assembled under his providence, every part of it given for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness, that the man of God may be perfect, thoroughly furnished unto all good works (2 Timothy 3:16-17). All scripture. The furnishing is incomplete without the whole, and the man of God is left half-equipped, missing exactly the tools the comfortable preaching declined to hand him. To trust God's choice of what to include over my sense of what to preach is an act of faith, and the refusal to trust it is, at bottom, the same unbelief that animates every other failure of the pulpit. It does not believe the hard word is for the people's good. It believes the hard word is a danger to be managed, and so it manages it, into silence.

I want to say a word about the genuine pastoral wisdom that the cowardly preacher counterfeits, because the counterfeit has discredited the real thing and we need the real thing badly. There is such a thing as timing, and Jesus practiced it. He told his disciples he had many things to say to them that they could not yet bear (John 16:12). He did not say them. He waited. The not-saying was not cowardice; it was love, the love that knows a soul can only receive so much at once, that there is a sequence to teaching, that some truths cannot land until other truths have prepared the ground. A faithful pastor knows this. He does not dump the whole counsel on a new believer in a week. He does not preach the hardest text to the most fragile congregation on its most fragile Sunday. He sequences, he prepares, he waits for the moment when the people can bear the word. The difference between this wisdom and the coward's excuse is that the wise pastor is always moving toward the hard word, building toward it, preparing the ground so that he can preach it when the people are ready, while the coward uses the language of timing to defer the hard word forever, always finding the present moment wrong, always discovering a fresh reason that this is not the season. The test is the trajectory. The wise man's delays are stops on a road that leads to the full counsel. The coward's delays are a road that leads nowhere, a permanent deferral dressed in the borrowed robes of patience. Ask yourself, of any text you are not preaching: am I waiting for the right time, or have I simply decided this is never the right time? The first is wisdom. The second is the canon being edited by fear, one reasonable-sounding postponement at a time.

The whole counsel includes the parts that will lose me people. It includes the doctrines that will draw the angry email, the rebukes that will cool a friendship, the claims that will mark me, in my cultural moment, as the wrong kind of person. Paul knew this. He told the Ephesians that grievous wolves would enter and that men would arise speaking perverse things, and his defense against that future was not strategy but completeness, the whole counsel declared in full so that the people would have everything they needed to stand. He did not curate. He delivered all of it, and then he could say his hands were clean. I want to be able to say that. I am not always able to say it, and the gap between Paul's confidence and my hesitation is the measure of the work I still have to do.

I keep returning to the phrase Paul used, pure from the blood of all men, because it is a strange and heavy way to talk and we have lost the seriousness of it. The image comes from the watchman in Ezekiel, the man set on the wall to warn the city of approaching danger, and the warning God gave that watchman is terrible. If the watchman sees the sword coming and does not blow the trumpet, and the people are not warned, and the sword comes and takes them, then their blood, God says, will be required at the watchman's hand (Ezekiel 33:6). The watchman who stays silent is held responsible for the deaths his silence failed to prevent. But if the watchman blows the trumpet and the people refuse to heed it, then their blood is on their own heads, and the watchman has delivered his soul. Paul is claiming the watchman's clean conscience. He blew the trumpet. He warned them of everything, the whole counsel, every danger the word names, and so whatever became of them, their blood was not on his hands. Now apply this to the preacher who edits the canon. He has seen the sword coming, the judgment, the sin, the danger the unpreached texts would have warned against, and he has not blown the trumpet, because the trumpet would have alarmed people and he preferred to keep them comfortable. And when the sword comes, as it always comes, their blood is in some measure on his hands, because he was the watchman and he chose silence over warning, comfort over faithfulness, his own standing over their safety. This is the stake the whole-counsel question actually carries, and we have softened it into a matter of preference and balance when Scripture frames it as a matter of blood. The texts you will not preach are the trumpet you will not blow, and the people are walking toward a sword you can see and they cannot, and your silence is not neutral. It has a cost, and the cost will be charged somewhere, and Scripture is unsettlingly clear about where.

The texts you skip are preaching a sermon of their own, and your people are hearing it, and it is teaching them that the parts of God you find inconvenient do not finally matter. That is the most dangerous sermon in any pulpit, and it is preached entirely in silence, by the man who thought his silence was kindness.

Declare the whole of it. The blood of the unprepared is on the hands of the preacher who decided, for their comfort, to give them only half.
chapters.verdict: The texts you skip are preaching a sermon of their own about what you really believe.
reflect: Which portions of Scripture have quietly disappeared from your preaching?
What hard doctrine have you not addressed because you feared the response?
Do you trust God's choice of what to include more than your own sense of what they can handle?

chapters.title: The Christ in Every Text
chapters.summary: All of Scripture testifies to Christ, and faithful exposition learns to preach him from every part of the canon without forcing the text or moralizing it into mere advice. The aim is not allegory but the gospel the text actually serves.
chapters.body:
On the road to Emmaus, two disciples walked with the risen Jesus and did not know him, and as they walked, grieving and confused, he did something that should govern how every preacher reads the Bible for the rest of his life. Beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself (Luke 24:27). All the scriptures. The things concerning himself. Jesus read the Old Testament, the only Bible those disciples had, as a book that was about him, from Moses forward, and he expounded it that way, and their hearts burned within them as he did (Luke 24:32). If the risen Christ read the Scriptures as a witness to himself, then a preacher who reads them as anything less is reading them more poorly than their Author intended.

This is the move that turns mere Bible teaching into Christian preaching, and it is the move that a great deal of otherwise faithful exposition never makes. A man can preach a text accurately, can establish its meaning and trace its structure and find its one idea, and can still produce a sermon that a faithful Jew or a thoughtful moralist could have preached, a sermon about being brave like David or patient like Job or pure like Joseph, a sermon that ends in advice about how to be a better person. And that sermon, however accurate, has stopped short of the destination the whole Bible is racing toward. It has handed the people a moral when it should have handed them a Savior. It has told them to imitate a hero when it should have shown them the one Hero in whom all the others find their meaning and their failure.

Let me be careful, because there is a way of preaching Christ from everywhere that is reckless and dishonest, and the cure for moralism is not allegory. There is a tradition of reading the Old Testament that finds Jesus in every detail by force, that turns the scarlet cord of Rahab into the blood of Christ and the wood of Noah's ark into the cross by sheer ingenuity rather than by any connection the text itself supports. That is not faithful. That is the topical performer's trick applied to typology, the preacher imposing a meaning rather than discovering one, and it trains people to read their Bibles as a code to be cracked rather than a story to be followed. The Christ in every text is not found by allegorizing the furniture. He is found by reading each text in its place in the one great story, the story that runs from creation through fall through the long history of Israel's failure and longing, to the cross and the empty tomb and the consummation, and asking how this particular passage serves that one story, what it contributes to the line that leads to Christ.

So how do you do it honestly? You ask where the text sits in the unfolding plan of redemption, and you let its place in that plan tell you how it points to Jesus. Sometimes the connection is by promise, the text holding out a hope that only Christ fulfills, the prophet longing for a king or a servant or a new covenant that arrives in him. Sometimes it is by pattern, the text showing a recurring shape, a deliverance, a sacrifice, a rescue, that finds its final and true form in Christ, so that the exodus is a real historical deliverance that also foreshadows the greater exodus Jesus accomplishes. Sometimes it is by contrast, the text showing a failure so deep that it cries out for the One who will not fail, the kings who all disappoint pointing forward by their disappointment to the King who will not. Sometimes it is by the human need the text exposes, the law's demand revealing a righteousness no one can produce, driving the honest reader to the only One who fulfilled it. None of these forces the text. All of them read the text in its own context and then in the larger context of the whole, and the larger context is Christ, because the Author wrote the whole thing with him in view.

Take David and Goliath, since it is the most abused story in this regard. The moralist preaches it as a lesson about facing your giants, and out comes a sermon about courage and your personal Goliaths, your debt and your diagnosis and your difficult boss, and the whole thing ends in a pep talk that has nothing to do with the gospel and everything to do with the self-confidence of the hearer. But read the text. David is not in that story as an example for you to imitate; you are not David in that story, you are the trembling army of Israel, cowering behind the lines, unable to face the enemy, paralyzed by a foe you cannot defeat. And into that helplessness comes an unlikely champion, the anointed one, the king God has chosen though the world overlooks him, and he goes out alone and fights the battle you could not fight and wins the victory you could not win, and his victory becomes yours, and you who could do nothing share in a triumph you did not earn. That is the gospel shape of the story, and it is in the text, not imposed on it, and it ends not in advice about your courage but in worship of the greater David who faced the greater enemy alone and won. The same story. A different destination.

Let me work another text, the binding of Isaac in Genesis 22, because it shows how the gospel road runs through a story most preachers either moralize or avoid. Moralize it, and the sermon becomes about Abraham's faith, his willingness to surrender what he loved most, and the application is about your own surrender, the Isaacs in your life God might ask you to give up, and out comes a sermon about sacrificial obedience that, while not false, leaves the people staring at Abraham and asking whether they could do what he did, which is the wrong question entirely. Read it in its place in the story, though, and something far greater opens. A father walks up a mountain with his only son, the son of promise, the son he loves, and the son carries the wood for his own sacrifice on his back up the hill, and the father intends to give him up, and at the last moment God provides a substitute, a ram caught in a thicket, and the son is spared because another dies in his place. And the mountain, Genesis tells us, is in the region of Moriah, the same region where the temple would later stand, the same area, by ancient tradition, near where another Father would one day walk another Son up a hill, a Son who also carried the wood of his own sacrifice on his back, except this time there would be no ram, no last-minute substitute, no voice from heaven to stay the hand, because this Son was the substitute, the Lamb God provided for himself, the one Isaac foreshadowed and pointed toward across two thousand years. Now the story is not finally about Abraham's faith at all. It is about a God who will one day do for us what he would not finally require of Abraham, who will give his own Son where he spared Abraham's, who provides the Lamb because no one else can. The people go home not staring at Abraham and measuring their own willingness to sacrifice but staring at the cross and undone by a love that did not spare its own Son. Same story. The road ran straight through it to Christ, and it was in the text, placed there by the Author who was telling one story all along.

Why does this matter so much that I would give it a whole chapter? Because moralistic preaching, even accurate moralistic preaching, finally crushes people, and it crushes them in the name of helping them. Tell people to be brave like David long enough and you will produce two kinds of Christians, the proud who think they have managed it and the despairing who know they have not, and both have been led away from the gospel into a religion of self-improvement that the gospel came to abolish. The good news was never that you should try harder to be like the heroes of the Bible. The good news is that there is one Hero, and that his record is given to those who could never produce it, and that the Christian life flows out of that gift rather than struggling toward it. A sermon that sends people home resolving to do better has, however unintentionally, preached the law as though it were the gospel, and the law cannot save, it can only condemn, and a steady diet of imperatives without the indicative of grace produces exhausted, guilty, self-focused people who eventually conclude that Christianity is just a harder version of the moralism they could get anywhere.

There is a way the New Testament itself authorizes this, and I want to ground it so that no one hears me commending a pious habit rather than an apostolic command. Jesus told the Pharisees, who knew their Scriptures better than any of us, that they searched the Scriptures because they thought that in them they had eternal life, and that these were they which testify of me (John 5:39). The whole point of the book, the testimony it exists to give, is to him. Peter says the prophets who wrote the Old Testament were searching their own writings to understand the sufferings of Christ and the glory that should follow, that they were serving us, a later generation, by writing of a Christ they only dimly saw (1 Peter 1:10-12). Paul says that all the promises of God are yes in him (2 Corinthians 1:20), that the whole sprawling system of promise finds its single affirmative answer in Jesus. This is not a clever interpretive trick the church invented. It is the way the apostles, taught by the risen Lord on roads like the one to Emmaus, actually read their Bibles, and they read them that way because Jesus had shown them how. To read the Old Testament and miss Christ is not to read it more soberly than the apostles did. It is to read it more poorly, to stop at the shadow and never look up to see what cast it, to study the signpost so carefully that you never travel to the place it points.

I want to address the fear that holds some good men back from this, the fear of reading Christ into texts where he is not, of becoming the kind of fanciful preacher who finds Jesus in every stray detail and embarrasses the cause. It is a legitimate fear, and I share it, and the discipline I have already described is the answer to it, reading each text in its place in the one redemptive story rather than mining its furniture for hidden symbols. But notice that the fear, left unchecked, produces its own error, the error of preaching the Old Testament as though Christ were not its subject at all, as though the responsible scholarly thing were to leave the text in its ancient setting and never connect it to the gospel. That is not responsible. That is, in fact, a failure to read the text the way its Author read it, the way Jesus read it on the Emmaus road, the way the apostles read it everywhere in the New Testament. The choice is not between reckless allegory and sober historical isolation. There is a third way, the way the New Testament itself models, which reads each text honestly in its own historical setting and then asks how that setting fits into the single story God was telling, the story that finds its center and meaning in Christ. The fear of fanciful preaching should make you careful, not silent. It should drive you to find the real, text-grounded, story-shaped road to Christ rather than the fanciful, detail-mining shortcut, but it should never let you off the hook of finding the road at all, because the road is there, the Author put it there, and a sober refusal to travel it is not scholarly caution but a failure to preach the text the way its Author intended it to be preached.

This is also, I have come to see, the answer to the relevance idol of an earlier chapter. The thing that makes any text relevant to any hearer in any century is precisely Christ, because Christ is the answer to the one need every human being in every age actually has, which is to be reconciled to God. A text about ancient sacrifices seems irrelevant until you see that it is about the problem of how a sinner can approach a holy God, which is the most relevant question there is, and that it points to the sacrifice that finally answers it. The gospel is what makes the whole Bible relevant, not by updating it but by revealing the Christ who was always its center and who meets the deepest need of the modern hearer exactly as he met the deepest need of the ancient one. Preach Christ from the text, and you will never have to manufacture relevance, because you will be handing people the one thing they were made for and cannot live without.

Spurgeon was famous for this. There is a story, perhaps polished in the retelling, of a young preacher who asked him for counsel, and Spurgeon's answer was that from every town in England there is a road that leads to London, and from every text in Scripture there is a road that leads to Christ, and the preacher's task is to find that road and take it. Whether he said it exactly that way I cannot prove, but he certainly preached that way, and his sermons, on any text, found their way to the cross, not by force but by the deep conviction that the cross was where every text was always headed. He would not let his people go home with a moral. He insisted on sending them home with a Savior. And that is why his preaching fed the poor and the desperate and the dying, the people for whom advice was useless and only grace would serve.

There is a diagnostic question that has sharpened my preaching more than almost any other, and I commend it to you because it cuts straight to whether a sermon has become Christian preaching or stopped at religious instruction. Ask of your finished sermon: could a Muslim, a Jew, a moral pagan, agree with everything I have said? If the answer is yes, if your sermon on honesty or generosity or courage or faithfulness contains nothing that a serious adherent of another religion or no religion could not affirm, then you have not yet preached a Christian sermon, however biblical your text. You have preached shared human morality with Scripture references, and shared human morality is real and good as far as it goes but it is not the gospel and it cannot save anyone, and a steady diet of it produces decent people who do not know Christ, which is precisely the most dangerous spiritual condition there is, the condition of the rich young ruler who kept all the commandments and walked away from the only One who could save him. The Christian sermon contains something the moralist cannot affirm, the scandal of grace, the cross, the impossibility of saving yourself, the gift given to those who could never earn it. If that scandal is missing, the sermon has stopped at the place all religions agree and never reached the place where Christianity stands alone. I run this test on my own sermons and I fail it more than I would like, catch myself having preached a fine piece of ethical instruction that any decent man would applaud and that left out the one thing that makes it Christian. The test is uncomfortable because the moral sermon is so respectable, so unobjectionable, so easy to applaud. But respectable and Christian are not the same, and the gospel was never respectable, and a sermon everyone can agree with has almost certainly left out the very thing that offends and saves.

I will confess that this is the discipline I find hardest, because moralism is the path of least resistance, and a text that contains a clear command practically begs to be preached as a command and nothing more. I preach a passage on forgiveness and the easy sermon is just, forgive, here is how, here are the steps. And that sermon is not wrong, exactly, but it is incomplete to the point of being a different religion, because it leaves out the only power by which anyone has ever actually forgiven a deep wound, which is the forgiveness they themselves have received at the cross. The faithful sermon on forgiveness must go through Calvary, must show the people the unpayable debt they have been forgiven before it asks them to forgive the smaller debts owed to them, must let the gospel be the engine of the obedience and not just tack the gospel on at the end as a formality. Every time I skip that, every time I preach the command without the cross that empowers it, I have handed my people a yoke without the grace that makes it bearable, and I have done it because the moralistic sermon is easier to build and lands more cleanly and lets everyone leave with a to-do list, which feels, falsely, like progress.

I want to guard one flank before I close, because zeal for this principle can produce its own kind of bad preaching, the sermon that races to the cross so fast it never actually preaches the text in front of it. There are men who have learned that they must preach Christ from every passage and have turned that into a formula, so that every sermon, on every text, becomes essentially the same sermon, a quick gesture at the passage followed by a long sprint to Calvary, the same gospel presentation tacked onto a different verse each week. That is not preaching Christ from the text; that is using the text as a launching pad to get to a gospel summary you would have preached anyway, which is the topical performer's error wearing a Reformed coat. The text deserves to be preached, fully, in its own particularity, with its own emphasis and its own demand, and then the road to Christ runs out of that particular text and not around it. The passage on the tabernacle should teach you what that passage actually teaches about God's dwelling with his people, in its detail and its strangeness, and then show how that longing is fulfilled in the Word made flesh who tabernacled among us. The passage is not skipped on the way to Christ. The passage is the road to Christ, and a sermon that does not honor the passage in its own right, that treats every text as interchangeable fuel for the same gospel engine, has not learned to preach Christ from the text at all. It has only learned a new way to avoid the labor of actually hearing what this text, this one, is saying.

I want to leave one practical encouragement, because this discipline can feel daunting to a man who was never trained in it and fears he will get it wrong. You do not have to find an elaborate or clever road to Christ from every text. You only have to find the true one, and the true one is usually simpler than the clever one. Ask of any passage the plainest questions: what does this show me about God, about my own heart, about my need, about the human condition that only Christ finally answers? A text that exposes human sin points to the Savior who deals with sin. A text that displays God's holiness points to the only One who could make sinners fit to stand before it. A text that holds out a promise points to the One in whom all the promises are yes. You are not hunting for hidden codes; you are reading honestly and following the plain line from the human need or the divine character the text reveals to the Christ who meets it. I have made this harder than it needed to be in seasons when I was trying to be impressive, straining for the ingenious connection when the plain one was sitting in front of me. The plain road is usually the right road. Read the text honestly, find what it shows about God and man, and follow that to the cross by the shortest true path, and you will preach Christ from everywhere without the strain, because he really is everywhere in the book, and finding him is less a feat of cleverness than an act of honest reading by a man who knows what the whole book is about.

A sermon that could have been preached in a synagogue, that names no Christ and needs no cross and ends in human effort, has not yet become Christian preaching, however true its individual statements may be. The dividing line is the gospel, and the gospel is a Person, and the whole Bible was written to bring you to him. Find the road from your text to Christ. It is there, because the One who wrote the text put it there, and the hearts of your people will burn within them, as those two disciples' hearts burned, not because you were clever but because they finally met, in the ancient words, the living Lord those words were always about.
chapters.verdict: A sermon that could have been preached in a synagogue has not yet become Christian preaching.
reflect: Did your sermon end in advice or in Christ?

When did you last preach Christ from a text that does not name him?

chapters.title: The Preacher Who Is Preached To
chapters.summary: The man who would preach the word must first be addressed by it; a sermon that has not first searched the preacher cannot search the people. Exposition begins with the preacher's own submission to the text.
chapters.body:
There is a question that exposes a preacher more completely than any other, and it is not about his theology or his technique. It is this: when was the last time the word you were preparing to preach to others first preached to you? Not informed you. Not supplied you. Preached to you, searched you, found you out, left you on your knees before you stood at the desk to build the outline. If the answer is that you cannot remember, then whatever you are doing on Sundays, you are not preaching in the full sense, because the word that has not first done its work on the herald cannot do its work through him.

The preacher is, before anything else, a hearer. This is the order Scripture insists on and the order the office most easily forgets. James warned that not many should become teachers, knowing that they would receive the greater judgment (James 3:1), and the greater judgment falls precisely here, on the man who handles the word professionally and ceases to be addressed by it personally. There is no more dangerous position in the church than the position of a man who has learned to study the Bible only for others, who opens it always with a sermon in mind and never with his own soul exposed, who has become a pipe through which the water flows without ever drinking. The pipe stays dry while everything passes through it. That is the occupational disease of the pulpit, and it is nearly invisible, because the man is constantly in the word and constantly speaking it, and who would suspect that the man most surrounded by Scripture might be the man least nourished by it?

I have lived in the dry pipe, and I want to describe how it happens, because it does not announce itself as backsliding. It happens through faithfulness, oddly enough. A man becomes so diligent in preparing the word for his people that he loses the habit of receiving it for himself. Every reading becomes professional. He cannot open the Psalms without scanning for a series; he cannot read the Gospels without filing illustrations; the text that should be addressing his own heart is intercepted, every time, by the working part of his mind that is already building Sunday. The very diligence that makes him a good craftsman makes him a starving man, because he has forgotten how to come to the word with empty hands, asking nothing for anyone else, only to be met by God himself. The cure is not less study. The cure is a separate hearing, a place where he comes to the word not as a preacher but as a sheep, and lets it feed him before he carries it to the rest of the flock.

There is a Puritan phrase for what the preacher must do that I have never improved on: he must preach to himself before he preaches to others, must be his own first congregation, must let the sermon find him in the pew of his own heart before he carries it to the pews of the church. They spoke of experimental religion, by which they did not mean experimental in our modern sense but experiential, the religion that has been tested in the experience of the man who holds it, proved on the pulse, known not merely in the head but in the life. A preacher of merely notional truth, truth he holds correctly but has never felt the weight of, preaches notionally, and his hearers receive notions, ideas correctly transmitted and never landing on the heart, because a notion in the preacher produces a notion in the hearer and an experienced truth in the preacher produces, by God's grace, an experienced truth in the hearer. This is why two men can preach the identical doctrine and one sermon is dead and the other is alive. The doctrine is the same. The difference is whether the man has been through the truth or merely past it, whether he is reporting a country he has visited or one he has only read about. The hearers can tell, always, eventually, because a man describing a place he has been speaks differently from a man describing a place he has only studied, with a particularity and a weight and a knowledge of the hard parts that cannot be faked. Be a man who has been through the truth you preach. Let it find you first. Then your reporting will have the ring of a witness and not the flatness of a guide reading from a brochure.

I made a practice some years ago, after a season where I felt myself going hollow, of keeping a portion of Scripture that I read only for myself, that I forbade myself to preach from, that existed in my life for no purpose except my own soul's feeding. It felt almost wasteful at first, like leaving good sermon material on the table. But it saved something in me. It restored a place where I was just a man before God and not a craftsman before a text, where the word could land on me without being immediately converted into a deliverable, where I could weep over a verse without wondering how to make a congregation weep over it. Every preacher needs that place. Without it he becomes a chef who never eats, a man surrounded by food who is quietly starving because he has forgotten that the food was meant for him too.
