I want to describe the particular danger of professional familiarity with holy things, because it is the occupational hazard that creeps up on the faithful rather than the lazy. A man who handles the word every day, who is constantly in it, around it, immersed in it, faces a danger the ordinary believer never faces, the danger of familiarity, of the word becoming so habitual that it ceases to strike him. The ordinary believer opens his Bible occasionally and the words still have the power to surprise him, to land, to wound and heal, because he comes to them fresh. The preacher comes to them constantly, and constant exposure dulls the edge, the way a man who works in a perfume factory stops smelling the perfume, the way a surgeon can grow casual about cutting human flesh that would horrify anyone else. The very intimacy with the word that the office requires is the thing most likely to deaden the preacher to it, and the deadening is gradual and unnoticed, so that a man can drift, over years, from trembling at the word to managing it, from being struck by it to being merely accurate about it, and never feel the moment the wonder left. This is why the preacher must fight, deliberately, to recover the freshness the ordinary believer has for free, must come to the word as a sinner and not only a scholar, must let the texts he has read a hundred times surprise him again, must refuse the casual professionalism that proximity breeds. The cure is not less exposure but a different posture within the exposure, a determined refusal to let familiarity become contempt, a daily seeking of the wonder that the work itself is constantly eroding. The man who keeps the wonder preaches with a freshness the people feel. The man who loses it preaches with the flat competence of a professional handling routine material, and routine handling of the word of the living God is a contradiction the people sense even when they cannot name it.

Bonhoeffer, who trained pastors in an illegal seminary at Finkenwalde while his country descended into evil in the 1930s, built that training around the daily, personal hearing of the word, the meditation on Scripture not for sermon material but for the soul, the discipline of letting the text address the man before the man ever addressed a congregation. He understood that a pastor formed only by his professional handling of Scripture would be hollow, and that hollow men cannot stand in the hour of testing. The personal hearing was the foundation. Everything public rested on it, and where it was missing, the public ministry was a shell waiting to crack. He proved the point with his life. The men who stood were the men the word had first searched in private; the men who fell were, so often, the men who had only ever used it in public.

The principle has a hard edge, and the edge cuts toward a kind of integrity that the people can feel even when they cannot name it. A preacher can only deliver a word with power to the degree that the word has had power over him. When I preach repentance from a heart that is itself repenting, the people feel the difference, even when they cannot name it. When I preach repentance as a topic I have mastered, having myself repented of nothing lately, the words are correct and the room is dead, and I go home wondering why the sermon did not land when the exegesis was sound. The exegesis was sound. The preacher was hollow. The word had not had its way with me, and so it could not have its way through me, because the Spirit who applies the word to the hearers is the same Spirit who must first apply it to the herald, and he will not be hurried past the herald to get to the flock.

Lloyd-Jones spoke of preaching as logic on fire, theology coming through a man who is aflame, and the fire is exactly this: the word having so gripped the preacher that it comes out of him hot, carrying the heat of its own work in his soul. A man cannot fake the fire. He can fake passion, can raise his voice and quicken his pace and manufacture the appearance of intensity, but the manufactured fire is cold underneath and the people feel the cold. The real fire is lit in the study and in the prayer closet, when the text catches the preacher himself, when the thing he is about to preach to others first burns through his own defenses and leaves him changed. That fire cannot be scheduled. It can only be sought, in the posture of a hearer, by a man humble enough to be preached to before he presumes to preach.

I want to say something here about the relationship between a preacher's private holiness and his public power, because we have separated them in ways that have wrecked men and churches. We have learned to evaluate preachers by their gifts, by their crowds, by their fruit measured in numbers, and we have largely stopped asking whether the man himself is being sanctified by the word he handles. But the New Testament will not let the two apart. Paul tells Timothy to take heed unto himself and unto the doctrine, in that order, self first, because a man who neglects himself while perfecting his doctrine is building a beautiful house on a crumbling foundation, and the collapse, when it comes, will be terrible and public and will take others down with it. We have watched it happen, in our own generation, more times than any of us can bear, gifted men whose private lives had quietly hollowed out beneath their public ministries until the gap between the two grew so wide that the whole structure fell. The word they handled had stopped having its way with them long before the world found out. The dry pipe became a broken one.

I have come to believe that the order of the words in Paul's charge to Timothy is not accidental and that it governs everything in this chapter. Take heed unto thyself, and unto the doctrine; continue in them: for in doing this thou shalt both save thyself, and them that hear thee (1 Timothy 4:16). Thyself first. The doctrine second. And the saving of the hearers tied to the man having first attended to his own soul. We have almost entirely inverted this. We evaluate preachers by their doctrine and their gifts and their results and we ask, far too late, whether the man himself was being kept by the word he handled. But Paul will not let the doctrine come first. He puts the man first, not because the man matters more than the truth but because a man who neglects himself while perfecting his doctrine is a leak in the very vessel that carries the truth, and the leak will eventually empty the vessel, however fine the truth it once held. I have watched this in my own life with a kind of fear. There are seasons when my doctrine was sharp and my soul was dull, when I could have passed any examination of my theology and failed every examination of my walk, and in those seasons the preaching had a quality I can only call brittle, correct and lifeless, a sound shell around a hollow center. The hollowing always started with the neglect of myself, the quiet decision that my own soul could wait while I served everyone else's, and the neglect always told, eventually, in the preaching, because you cannot pour out of a vessel you have stopped filling.

There is a deep mercy in this arrangement, and I want to end on it rather than on the warning. God will not let the preacher escape the word. He will not permit the herald to remain forever outside the message, dispensing a grace he has never received, naming sins he has never confessed, offering a Savior he has kept at professional distance. The very texts the preacher studies will, if he lets them, turn and search him, and the searching is a kindness, because it keeps him a Christian and not merely a clergyman. The man who is preached to as he prepares to preach is being pastored by the same word he is preparing to pastor others with, fed at the same table he is setting, and that double work of the word, on the herald and then through him, is one of the quiet graces of the office that makes the loneliness of the study bearable. He is not alone in there. He is being met.

I have come to think there is a particular sin we should name here, and it is the sin of preaching to others what you are not pursuing yourself, and Paul named it about himself with a bluntness that should frighten any of us. He said he disciplined his body and brought it into subjection, lest by any means, when he had preached to others, he himself should be a castaway (1 Corinthians 9:27). A castaway. Disqualified. Paul, the apostle, held open the genuine possibility that a man could preach the gospel faithfully and powerfully to others and himself be rejected at the last, could spend a life heralding a salvation he did not finally walk in, could point ten thousand people to a door he never went through. That possibility should keep every preacher awake. It means the work of preaching, however faithful, is no substitute for the work of being a Christian, that handling the word for others does not automatically secure the man who handles it, that a preacher can build a real ministry on a hollow soul and the hollowness will not show until the end, when it is too late. The defense against being a castaway is not better preaching. It is the daily, private pursuit of the very Christ you publicly proclaim, the keeping of your own soul, the refusal to let your public ministry become a substitute for your personal communion. Paul, who preached more powerfully than any of us, took heed to himself with fear, because he understood that the louder a man's public proclamation, the more catastrophic the private hollowness would be if it were ever allowed to set in. Take heed to yourself. The pulpit will not save you. Only the Christ you preach can do that, and you must come to him as a sinner in need of grace exactly like the people you preach to, or you will spend your life serving a feast you never sat down to eat.

Peterson resisted, his whole ministry long, the reduction of the pastor to a religious professional, a manager of spiritual goods, and insisted instead that the pastor must remain a person under the word, formed by it, addressed by it, kept small by it. He saw that the professionalizing of ministry was a way of escaping the word's authority while appearing to serve it, of handling the holy without being burned by it. The remedy was to stay a hearer, to refuse the distance that expertise offers, to come to the Bible always as one who needs it and not merely as one who dispenses it. That refusal is a daily discipline and a lifelong one, and the men who keep it are the men whose preaching stays alive into old age, while the men who lose it become, by degrees, eloquent corpses, technically proficient and spiritually dead, preaching a word that no longer touches them and therefore can no longer touch anyone.

There is an objection here that I should answer, because a thoughtful man will raise it. Are you saying, he asks, that a preacher's sermon is only as good as his current spiritual condition, that he cannot preach a truth he is not at that moment living, that the word is held hostage to the herald's mood? And no, that is not what I am saying, and the distinction matters. God can and does use the words of a hollow man; the wind blows where it will, and I have heard the gospel preached truly by men I later learned were frauds, and the gospel was still true and still saved, because the power was in the word and not in the preacher. So the people are not finally at the mercy of the man. But that is no comfort to the man, because the question for him is not whether God can use his words despite him; the question is what is happening to his own soul as he handles holy things while remaining cold to them, and the answer is that he is being hardened, calloused, made into a professional handler of a fire that no longer warms him. The danger is not primarily to the hearers, who have the Spirit and the word and other means of grace. The danger is to the preacher himself, who is daily near the fire and daily not warmed by it, and that proximity-without-warmth is a spiritual condition more perilous than open coldness, because it deceives the man into thinking that his familiarity with holy things is the same as communion with the Holy One. It is not. A man can know the Bible cold and not know God at all, and the pulpit is full of such men, and any of us could become one, and the only defense is the daily refusal to let our handling of the word replace our hearing of it.

You cannot hand the people a word that has never had its way with you. You can hand them the words, correctly arranged, accurately exegeted, beautifully delivered, and they will go home hungry, because words are not the word, and the word comes only through a man it has first laid hold of. Be laid hold of first. Be the preacher who is preached to, every week, before you climb the stairs. Then climb them, carrying not a lecture you have prepared but a fire you have caught, and let it spread.
chapters.verdict: You cannot hand the people a word that has never had its way with you.
reflect: Has the sermon you are preparing convicted you before it convicts them?
When did Scripture last change you rather than merely supply you?
Are you a herald of a word that owns you, or a vendor of words you have never obeyed?

chapters.title: The Knees Before the Pulpit
chapters.summary: Preaching without prayer is presumption; the preacher prepares on his knees as much as at his desk, and his private devotion is the hidden source of any public power. Prayer is not preparation for the work but is itself the work.
chapters.body:
There is a sentence in the book of Acts that the church has admired and ignored in roughly equal measure, and it deserves to be the constitution of every pastor's week. When the early church faced a crisis of administration, when the practical demands of caring for widows threatened to swallow the apostles' time, they did not respond by becoming more efficient administrators. They appointed others to the practical work and said of themselves, we will give ourselves continually to prayer, and to the ministry of the word (Acts 6:4). Prayer and the word. Named together, in that order, prayer first, as the two things the apostles refused to let anything crowd out. Not prayer as a warmup to the word. Prayer and the word as the twin labors that constituted the whole of their calling, the two things they would protect at any cost, the two things everything else had to be arranged around.

I am convinced that the great divide among preachers is not finally between the gifted and the ungifted, nor between the educated and the untrained, nor even between the orthodox and the heterodox, though all those divides are real. The great divide is between the men who pray and the men who only study. Both may handle the text well. Both may build the sermon competently. But the praying man is doing something the studying man has neglected, and over time the difference shows in a way that nothing else accounts for, a weight, a reality, a sense that this man has been somewhere the rest of us have not, that he comes from the presence of God and not merely from the presence of his commentaries. You cannot fake having been with God. You can fake having studied. The two are not the same, and the people can tell, even when they could never explain how.

Let me be honest about my own failure here, because it is the failure I am most ashamed of and least able to fix. It is easier to study than to pray. Study has a satisfying texture; you make visible progress, you fill pages, you feel the accumulation of understanding, and at the end of three hours you have something to show for it. Prayer has none of that. It is slow, it is often dry, it produces nothing you can hold up, and the part of me that wants to be productive resists it constantly, whispering that the time would be better spent on one more commentary, one more pass through the text, one more refinement of the outline. And so my study hours have always tended to crowd out my prayer hours, not by decision but by drift, because study feels like work and prayer feels like waiting, and a busy man chooses work over waiting almost every time. I have repented of this more times than I can count, and I keep needing to repent of it, which tells me something about how deep the disease runs.

I think the deepest reason we neglect prayer is that we do not really believe, in the operative part of us, that preaching is a supernatural act. We believe it intellectually. We would affirm it in a doctrinal statement. But the way we spend our time reveals a different and more practical belief, a belief that preaching is fundamentally a human transaction, the transfer of well-organized truth from a prepared man to a willing audience, an event whose success depends on the quality of the content and the skill of the delivery. And if that is what preaching is, then prayer is indeed a formality, a pious garnish on a fundamentally human act, and a busy man is right to cut it. But that is not what preaching is. Preaching is the occasion through which the living God addresses dead and dying souls and raises some of them to life, an event in which the decisive action is invisible and divine and entirely beyond the preacher's power to produce. If that is what preaching is, then prayer is not a garnish; it is the lifeline, the connection to the only One who can do the actual work, and to attempt preaching without it is like a man trying to conduct electricity through a wire he has refused to connect to the source. He can have a beautiful wire, well-insulated, expertly laid, and it will carry nothing, because the power was never in the wire. The neglect of prayer is, at bottom, a practical denial of the supernatural nature of the work, and the cure is not a new technique for praying more but a recovered conviction about what preaching actually is, because a man who truly believed he was the wire and not the source would never again dream of preaching unconnected to the power.

The old preachers understood what we have forgotten. There is a saying often attributed to Luther, that he had so much to do on a particular day that he could not get through it with less than three hours of prayer, and whether the words are exactly his or not, the spirit of them is the spirit of every preacher who has actually moved anything, that the busier the day, the more prayer it required, because the work was God's and could not be done in the flesh. We have inverted this. When our weeks get busy, prayer is the first thing we cut, which reveals that we secretly believe the work is ours and that prayer is a luxury we can afford only when there is slack in the schedule. There is never slack in the schedule. There is only the question of whether we believe the work is supernatural, and we answer that question not with our doctrine but with our datebook.

I have come to believe that the order in Acts 6, prayer first and then the word, is not arbitrary and that reversing it, as we functionally do, is part of what has gone wrong with us. We say the word and prayer, naming the word first, and the ordering reflects our practice, in which study comes first and prayer, if it happens, comes after, a blessing pronounced over work already done. But the apostles said prayer and the ministry of the word, prayer first, and I think the order matters, because prayer first means the whole enterprise begins in dependence rather than ending in it, means the man comes to the text already on his knees, already acknowledging that he cannot understand it without help, already a beggar before he is a scholar. The man who studies first and prays second approaches the text as a competent expert who will, as a pious courtesy, ask God to bless his findings. The man who prays first approaches the text as a dependent child who cannot see without the Father's light and asks for the light before he opens his eyes. These are different postures, and they produce different study, because the praying-first man studies in a spirit of dependence that keeps him humble and teachable, while the studying-first man too easily studies in a spirit of expertise that makes him the master of a text he was meant to sit under. Put the prayer first. Begin on your knees, before you open the commentary, before you trace the argument, before you do anything a competent man could do without God, and let the whole labor proceed from dependence rather than arriving at it as an afterthought.

What does it mean, practically, to pray over a text and not only study it? It means that before I ask what the passage means, I ask God to teach me, acknowledging that the natural man cannot understand the things of the Spirit and that I am, in my own resources, a natural man (1 Corinthians 2:14). It means that as the meaning comes clear, I pray it into my own heart, asking God to make it true in me before I ask him to make it true in the people. It means that as I build the sermon, I pray over the people who will hear it, the specific people, the ones I know are suffering and the ones I know are hardening, asking God to meet each of them in the word. And it means that when the sermon is done and the manuscript is finished, I do not then relax into confidence in my preparation, but fall to my knees and beg God to do what I cannot do, to take the dead words and make them living, because I know, in the place underneath my competence, that nothing I have built will save a single soul unless God himself shows up to inhabit it.

The prayer is not preparation for the work. The prayer is itself the work, the truest part of it, the part the apostles named first. We have a category problem here. We think of the sermon as the work and prayer as the spiritual hygiene that ought to surround the work, the way an athlete stretches before the game. But that is backwards. In the economy of preaching, the prayer is the game, or at least it is the half of the game that decides the outcome, because the sermon's effect was never in the sermon's quality but in the God who must carry it, and the way you engage that God is on your knees. The study makes the sermon faithful. The prayer makes it powerful. A faithful sermon without prayer is a loaded gun that no one fires. The prayer is the firing.

I want to be concrete about the kinds of prayer that surround a sermon, because "pray more" is a counsel so vague it changes nothing, and the vagueness is part of why we obey it so poorly. There is the prayer before the study, where you ask God to open the text, confessing that the natural mind cannot grasp spiritual things and that you need the Author of the book to teach you what the book means. There is the prayer during the study, where the text begins to do its work and you stop and pray it into yourself, asking God to make the truth real in you before you ask him to make it real in anyone else, letting the study become worship rather than mere labor. There is the prayer over the people, where you take the names and faces of the actual men and women who will sit under this word, the ones you know are in crisis and the ones you know are drifting, and you intercede for each of them by name, asking God to meet them in this particular passage on this particular Sunday. There is the prayer before you stand up, the last thing before the pulpit, where you let go of your dependence on your preparation and cast yourself wholly on God to do what no preparation can do. And there is the prayer after, the prayer that commits the preached word into God's hands and refuses to take responsibility for the harvest, asking him to carry the seed into soil you cannot see. Five kinds of prayer, threaded through the whole work, and the sermon that has been prayed over in all five ways is a different thing from the sermon that has merely been studied, even when the manuscripts are identical, because the one has been soaked in dependence and the other has only been built by skill.

Spurgeon, when people asked the secret of his ministry, would sometimes take them down beneath the platform of his great hall and show them the room where his people gathered to pray while he preached, and he would say, there is the secret, there is the powerhouse, there is the source of everything you see up top. He did not point to his sermons, which were extraordinary, nor to his voice, which could fill a hall of thousands, nor to his wit, which was legendary. He pointed to a room full of praying saints, and he meant it. He understood that his gifts were the visible thing and the prayer was the real thing, and that the visible thing was powered entirely by the real thing, and that a preacher who reversed the two, who trusted his gifts and neglected the prayer, was a fool building a furnace and never lighting the fire.

I want to say a word about the loneliness of this, because it is a hidden labor and hidden labors are heavy precisely because no one sees them. The prayer behind the pulpit happens where no one watches. The people see the sermon and assume the prayer, and their assumption is generous and, I am afraid, often wrong. They imagine their pastor on his knees and they would be horrified to know how often he was merely at his desk, that the time they credit to communion with God was in fact spent polishing phrases. The gap between the prayer the people imagine and the prayer the pastor actually offers is a gap I have lived inside, and it is a kind of low-grade fraud, an unspoken claim to an intimacy with God that the schedule does not support. The remedy is not to pretend better. The remedy is to actually pray, to close the gap, to become in private the man the people already believe you to be, so that when they assume their pastor has been with God, the assumption is true.

There is a connection here to everything else this book has argued, and I want to draw it out. The whole case for expository preaching rests on the conviction that the word is God's and that God himself addresses the people through it. But if that is true, then prayer is not optional decoration on the expository method; it is the method's necessary companion, because a man who truly believed that God speaks through the word would not dream of handling that word without speaking to the God whose word it is. Prayerless exposition is a contradiction. It claims to believe the word is God's living voice and then handles it as though it were a text to be processed by skill alone. The praying expositor is the only consistent expositor, the only man whose practice matches his doctrine, the only preacher who treats the supernatural word in a manner appropriate to its supernatural Author.

I want to address the dryness of prayer itself, because it is the reason many preachers quietly give up on it, and no one warns them. Prayer is often dry. It often feels like nothing, like talking to an empty room, like a discipline that produces no detectable result. And a man who measures prayer by how it feels will conclude, reasonably, that it is not working, and will drift away from it toward the study, which at least feels productive. But prayer is not measured by how it feels any more than preaching is, and the felt dryness of prayer is not evidence that it accomplishes nothing. The man praying in dryness, faithfully, without any sense of God's nearness, is doing something real and powerful in the unseen realm, exactly as the dry preacher's faithful sermon does real work he cannot detect. We have to stop measuring our spiritual disciplines by their emotional feedback, because the feedback is the least reliable instrument we own, and a great deal of the most important spiritual work happens precisely when the feedback says nothing is happening. I have prayed through long seasons where prayer felt useless, where I knelt out of sheer obedience with no sense of presence or progress, and I have learned, looking back, that those dry prayers were doing things I could not see at the time, sustaining a ministry that should have collapsed, holding a man together who was coming apart, accomplishing in the dark what the daylight disciplines could not. Pray when it is dry. Pray especially when it is dry, because the dry prayer is the prayer of pure faith, offered to a God you cannot feel because you believe he is there whether you feel him or not, and that prayer pleases him more than all the easy fervent prayers of the seasons when prayer is sweet.

There is a corporate dimension to this that the lonely preacher forgets, and recovering it changed my own ministry. I had carried the burden of prayer for my preaching almost entirely alone for years, as though it were a private discipline between me and God, and I was failing at it alone, and the failure compounded because no one shared the load. And then I began, slowly, to ask my people to pray for the preaching, not in a vague announcement but specifically, to recruit a handful of praying saints who would carry the sermon before God during the week and during the moment itself, the way Spurgeon's people prayed beneath his platform. It humbled me to ask, because asking admitted that my gifts were not enough, that I needed the prayers of plain church members more than I needed another commentary, that the power I lacked could come down through their intercession in a way it would not come down through my preparation alone. And it changed the preaching, not because I could measure it but because the whole enterprise was lifted out of my solitary effort and placed where it belonged, in the hands of a praying body asking God to do what no preacher and no congregation can do for themselves. Paul begged the churches to pray for his preaching constantly, asked the Ephesians to pray that utterance might be given him to open his mouth boldly (Ephesians 6:19), and if the apostle needed the prayers of ordinary believers to preach with boldness, the notion that you can carry your own pulpit on your own knees is a pride that will eventually break you. Recruit the prayers. You were never meant to do this alone.

I want to confess something that I think many preachers feel and few admit. There have been seasons when my public prayers were better than my private ones, when I could lead a congregation in prayer with a fluency and a feeling that my own closet had not seen in weeks, and the contrast was its own kind of indictment. It is possible to become good at praying in public while starving in private, to develop the gift of corporate prayer as a performance skill even as the personal discipline withers, and the gift can mask the starvation, can convince the man and the people that all is well because the public prayers sound so alive. But the public prayer, however fluent, cannot substitute for the private one, because the public prayer can be a performance and the private one cannot, there being no audience in the closet to perform for. The state of a man's private prayer is the true measure of his communion with God, the public prayer being too easily corrupted by the presence of listeners to be trusted as a gauge. And a man whose public prayers outrun his private ones is a man building a reputation for prayerfulness on a foundation of prayerlessness, which will not hold, because the power that the people sense in the public prayers, if it is real power and not mere fluency, comes from the private communion, and where the private communion has dried up, the public prayers become, over time, beautiful and empty, words about God offered in the presence of people to a God the man rarely meets alone. Close that gap too. Let your private prayer life be richer than your public one, not the reverse, so that the public prayers overflow from a real communion rather than performing a communion that has quietly ceased.

A prayerless preacher is a contradiction the people will eventually feel, even if they never name it, a man professing to bring them the word of a God he does not himself spend time with, a guide claiming to lead them to a country he rarely visits. Close the gap. Pray over the text as long as you study it, and longer in the hard seasons. Be the man on his knees before you are the man in the pulpit, because the kneeling is where the preaching is actually decided, and the standing is only where it becomes visible. Give yourself continually to prayer and to the ministry of the word, in that order, the order the apostles chose, the order that has always separated the men who merely spoke from the men through whom God spoke.
chapters.verdict: A prayerless preacher is a contradiction the people will eventually feel.
reflect: Do you pray over your text as long as you study it?
Is your prayer life behind the pulpit as real as the people imagine it to be?
What in your week proves that you believe preaching is a supernatural act?

chapters.title: When the Well Runs Dry
chapters.summary: Every preacher faces seasons of dryness, doubt, and exhaustion when the word feels dead and the preparation feels like a lie; faithfulness in those seasons means preaching the truth you cannot presently feel and trusting the word over your own emotional weather. The dry season is not disqualification but formation.
chapters.body:
No one tells you, when you start, about the Sundays you will preach with nothing in the tank. They show you the mountaintop sermons, the ones where the text caught fire and you caught fire and the room caught fire, and they let you assume that ministry is a series of those, strung together, getting better as you mature. They do not tell you about the long flat stretches, the weeks when you open the text and it says nothing, the seasons when your own faith feels thin and your prayers feel like talking to the ceiling and you have to stand up on Sunday and preach a certainty you cannot presently feel to people who are counting on you to have it. They do not tell you, so I will. The dry seasons are coming, if they have not come already, and how you preach in them will reveal and shape you more than the mountaintops ever could.

The blank page on a Tuesday morning when nothing comes is one of the loneliest experiences in ministry. You have the text. You have done this for years. And the text just lies there, inert, refusing to open, and the panic starts to rise because Sunday is coming whether you are ready or not, and there is no calling in sick from a sermon, no postponing the assembly because the preacher is empty. So you sit there, in the dryness, staring at words that have fed thousands of saints across thousands of years and that this morning feel like ashes in your mouth, and you wonder whether you ever had any business in this calling at all, whether the good Sundays were flukes, whether you are a fraud who has finally been found out. I have sat in that exact chair more times than I would like to admit, and I want to say some things to the man who is sitting in it now.

I want to say something about the shame that wraps around the dry season, because the shame is often worse than the dryness itself, and no one talks about it. A preacher in a dry season feels like a fraud. He stands up to proclaim a living God while feeling spiritually dead, to call people to joy he cannot find, to preach an intimacy with Christ he is not currently experiencing, and the gap between the public proclamation and the private experience produces a corrosive shame, a sense that he is deceiving people, that if they knew how dry he was they would never listen to him, that he has no business in the pulpit at all. And the shame isolates him, because he cannot tell anyone, cannot admit to his elders or his people that the man who feeds them is himself unfed this season, and so he carries the dryness alone, and the loneliness deepens the dryness, and the whole thing spirals. I have lived inside that spiral, and I want to say to the man in it now: the gap between your proclamation and your experience is not fraud. Fraud would be preaching what you do not believe. You believe it. You are simply not feeling it, and feeling and believing are not the same thing, and a man who proclaims what he believes while not feeling it is not a deceiver but a soldier, holding his post in the dark, doing his duty when the consolations have withdrawn. The shame is a lie. It tells you that the absence of feeling disqualifies you, when in fact the willingness to preach the truth without the support of feeling is one of the highest forms of faithfulness there is. Lay the shame down. You are not a fraud for preaching a joy you cannot presently feel. You are faithful, and the faithfulness in the dark is worth more than all the easy fervor of the light.

The first thing is this: the dryness is not necessarily a verdict on your faith, and it is almost never a verdict on the word. We are emotional creatures, and our sense of God's nearness rises and falls with a hundred things that have nothing to do with the truth, our sleep and our health and our griefs and the simple mysterious weather of the soul. The Psalms are full of men who felt abandoned by God while telling the truth about God, who cried out that the Lord had forgotten them in the same breath that they rehearsed his faithfulness. My soul is cast down within me, the psalmist says, and then in the same psalm, therefore will I remember thee (Psalm 42:5-6). He preaches to his own downcast soul. He commands it to hope when it does not feel like hoping. That is the model for the dry season. You do not wait until you feel the truth to preach it. You preach the truth, and sometimes, by preaching it, you come to feel it again, and sometimes you do not, and you preach it anyway, because it was never your feelings that made it true.

The second thing is that there is a kind of preaching that can only be learned in the dry seasons, and it is a better kind than the mountaintop kind, though it does not feel like it at the time. When the well is full, when you are overflowing with a sense of God, it is easy to preach, but it is also easy to mistake your overflow for power and your emotion for unction. The dry season strips that away. It forces you to preach the bare truth without the support of your feelings, to stand on the word alone, to discover whether you actually believe the thing you have been saying or whether you were only ever riding your own emotional momentum. And the discovery, when it comes, is precious, because a man who has preached the resurrection on a morning when he felt nothing but death, and meant it, and staked his soul on it, knows something about faith that the perpetually overflowing man has never had to learn. The dry season teaches you to live by faith and not by sight, which is the whole of the Christian life, and a preacher who has never preached in the dark has never fully learned it.

I want to be careful here, because there is a dryness that is a warning and not merely weather, and the two must be distinguished. Sometimes the well runs dry because of unconfessed sin, because the preacher has grieved the Spirit and the dryness is the natural consequence, and in that case the dryness is a mercy, a summons to repentance, and the answer is not to preach through it but to deal with the sin that caused it. Sometimes the dryness comes from sheer exhaustion, from a man who has given and given without ever receiving, who has run himself into the ground in the name of faithfulness and is now reaping the body's refusal to continue, and in that case the answer is not more willpower but rest, sabbath, the recovery of the receiving that the giving had crowded out. And sometimes the dryness is simply the ordinary weather of a long obedience, no sin behind it and no exhaustion, just the mysterious withdrawal of felt grace that God uses to wean us off our dependence on feelings and onto dependence on himself. Wisdom in the dry season begins with discerning which kind you are facing, and the discernment requires the honesty to ask hard questions of yourself before you blame the weather.

I want to offer a word of practical counsel for the dry Tuesday, because the man sitting in that chair needs something to do and not only something to believe. When the text will not open and the panic rises, go back to the most basic acts of study, the ones that do not depend on inspiration. Read the passage again, slowly, aloud. Write out, by hand, what it plainly says, sentence by sentence, demanding nothing clever, only the plain sense. Look up the words. Trace the connections, the therefores and the becauses. Do the mechanical work, the work that a man can do whether or not he feels anything, and very often, though not always, the mechanical work primes the pump, and somewhere in the plodding the text begins to open after all, not because you summoned inspiration but because you did the humble work and God met you in it. Inspiration is not a precondition for study; it is more often a byproduct of it, and the man who waits to feel inspired before he opens the text will wait forever, while the man who opens the text and does the work in the absence of feeling frequently finds the feeling arriving in the middle of the labor, drawn out by the labor itself. And on the Tuesdays when even the mechanical work yields nothing, when you have plodded faithfully and the text is still closed, you preach the plain sense you found by plodding, trusting that the plain faithful sense, even without the fireworks, is the word of God and carries the power of the word of God, fireworks or not. The dry Tuesday does not excuse you from the work. It calls you to the most basic, humble, mechanical form of the work, the form that does not need your feelings, and it is astonishing how often God honors that plodding with exactly the opening the panic was sure would never come.

There is a danger in the dry season that I have watched destroy men, and it is the temptation to fake what you no longer have. A man in a long dryness, terrified that his emptiness will be discovered, learns to perform the fullness he has lost. He raises his voice to compensate for the fire he does not feel. He borrows other men's passion, plays the emotional notes he knows produce a response, becomes an actor playing the part of the anointed preacher he used to be. And this is the road to ruin, because the gap between the performed fullness and the actual emptiness widens until the man is living a lie in the most sacred space in his life, and a man who lies in the pulpit will eventually lie everywhere, and the rot spreads. The faithful response to dryness is not to fake fullness but to preach honestly from your emptiness, to say, in effect, even from the dryness, this is true, I am preaching it because it is true and not because I presently feel it, and God can use that honesty more than he can ever use the performance. Honest dryness preaches better than dishonest fire.

I want to be honest about the exhaustion that produces some of these dry seasons, because the most common cause of ministerial dryness in the men I know is not exotic spiritual desertion but plain depletion, the slow grinding-down of a man who has given without receiving until there is nothing left in the tank. Ministry is a giving profession, and a particular kind of giving, the giving out of yourself, your attention and your compassion and your energy and your soul, to people in need, day after day, and a man can do this for a long time on momentum before he notices that he has stopped refilling, that the input dried up while the output continued, that he is running on reserves he is not replenishing. And eventually the reserves run out, and the dryness that follows is not a sign that God has withdrawn but a sign that the man has neglected the ordinary means by which God sustains him, rest and sabbath and sleep and friendship and the receiving of the word for himself rather than only for others. We have romanticized the burnt-out pastor, treated his collapse as evidence of his devotion, as though running yourself into the ground for the sheep were a kind of holiness. It is not holiness. It is often pride, the pride that thinks the work depends on me, that I cannot rest because there is no one else, that the church will fall if I stop, which is unbelief dressed as dedication, because the church is Christ's and he does not need my exhaustion to keep it standing. The dry season produced by depletion is healed not by gritting your teeth and preaching through it forever but by the humbling discipline of rest, of admitting you are a creature with limits, of receiving before you give, of trusting the work to the God who never sleeps so that you, who must sleep, can. Jesus, who had infinitely more reason than you to feel indispensable, withdrew to lonely places and slept in boats and refused to let the endless need set his pace. If the Son of God rested, your refusal to rest is not devotion. It is a quiet claim to be stronger than he was, and the dry season is the bill coming due for the claim.

What do you actually do on the Tuesday when nothing comes? You do the labor anyway, is the short answer, the unglamorous answer, the answer that the romantic view of preaching as inspiration cannot accommodate. You do the exegesis even when it does not thrill you. You trace the structure even when your heart is not in it. You build the sermon by craft when you cannot build it by passion, trusting that the craft is a gift God gave you precisely for the seasons when the passion fails, and that a sermon built faithfully by a dry man can still be carried by the Spirit to people the dry man cannot see and cannot help. I have preached sermons I built entirely out of obedience, with no felt sense of God in them at all, and learned afterward that God had used them mightily in someone's life, and the lesson was humbling and freeing at once: the power was never in my feelings, so the absence of my feelings does not cancel the power. God can blow his wind through a dry man's faithful work as easily as through a wet man's overflow, and sometimes more easily, because the dry man is less tempted to take the credit.

I want to speak directly to the doubt that sometimes hides inside the dryness, because for some preachers the dry season is not only a withdrawal of feeling but a genuine crisis of belief, a season when the things they preach every Sunday no longer feel certain, when the questions they thought they had settled rise up again with teeth. I know this country. I came to faith out of atheism, and the old doubts did not vanish at my conversion; they went quiet, and they have come back, more than once, in the night, asking whether the whole edifice I have built my life and my family and my ministry on is true. And a preacher in that season faces a peculiar agony, because he cannot simply withdraw to sort out his doubts in private; Sunday comes, and he must stand up and proclaim with confidence a thing he is, this week, struggling to believe. What do you do? You do not fake certainty you do not have, but neither do you spill your unprocessed doubt onto people who are leaning on you for stability. You preach the truth, honestly, as a man who has staked his life on it and is staking it again this Sunday in the teeth of his own questions, which is not hypocrisy but faith, the very definition of faith, believing and proclaiming what you cannot at the moment feel or fully see. And you take the doubts to God and to a few trusted brothers, privately, refusing both to hide them and to broadcast them. The doubts, handled this way, do not disqualify you; they deepen you, because a man who has preached through his own dark nights preaches to other people's dark nights with a credibility the never-troubled man can never have. My doubts have made me a better preacher to doubters, because I am not pretending from the far shore that the crossing was easy. I am out in the water with them, telling them I have found the ground holds, even when I cannot see it, even when I am afraid.

The masters of the soul understood this. The old writers spoke of spiritual desertion, the felt absence of God, as a normal and even necessary part of mature faith, a thing every serious Christian eventually passes through, not a sign of failure but often a sign of growth, God removing the felt comforts so that the soul learns to cling to him for himself and not for the feelings he gives. If that is true for every believer, it is doubly true for the believer whose job is to handle holy things daily, who is in particular danger of loving the comforts of God more than the God who comforts. The dry season is God's way of purifying the preacher's love, of teaching him to preach for God's sake and not for the sake of the emotional reward preaching can give, of weaning him off the drug of his own felt fervor so that he can preach from a deeper and steadier place that the weather cannot reach.

There is a question that haunts the dry preacher and deserves a straight answer: should I be preaching at all in a season like this, or is the very fact of my dryness a sign that I should step down, that I am a fraud for standing up empty? And the answer, in the great majority of cases, is no, the dryness is not a call to quit, it is a call to endure. Elijah, fresh off the greatest victory of his ministry, collapsed under a tree and asked God to let him die, certain he was finished, the only faithful man left and too exhausted to go on (1 Kings 19:4). And God did not agree with his self-assessment. God did not tell him he was right to quit. God fed him, let him sleep, fed him again, and then gently corrected his theology and sent him back to work, because Elijah's exhaustion had distorted his judgment and a man in that state should not be trusted to decide whether his ministry is over. The dry season lies to you. It tells you that you are finished, that you were never any good, that the honest thing would be to walk away. Do not believe it, and do not make permanent decisions in a temporary darkness. Eat. Sleep. Let God correct the theology your exhaustion has bent. And then, restored, go back to the work, because the well that has run dry has run dry before in better men than you and filled again, and the God who emptied it for his own purposes will fill it again in his own time, and your job in the meantime is not to quit but to endure, faithfully, in the dark, until the morning comes.

So preach the word you believe, especially on the mornings you cannot feel it. The feeling was never the foundation. The word is the foundation, true on the mornings it thrills you and equally true on the mornings it leaves you cold, and your calling is to deliver it faithfully in all weather, in season and out of season, which surely includes the inner seasons of your own dry and doubting heart. The dry season is not your disqualification. It is your formation, the workshop in which God is making you into a preacher who can be trusted, a man who will preach the resurrection at a graveside even when his own faith is hanging by a thread, because he has learned, in a hundred dry Tuesdays, that the word does not depend on his feelings and never did. Stand up. Preach it anyway. The well will fill again, in God's time and not yours, and meanwhile the obedience of the dry season is worth more than all the easy fervor of the full one.
chapters.verdict: Preach the word you believe, especially on the mornings you cannot feel it.
reflect: Have you confused your spiritual dryness with the word's failure?
What do you do on the weeks when the text says nothing to you?
Are you preaching from the overflow only, or also from sheer obedience when the overflow is gone?

chapters.title: The People Who Must Hear
chapters.summary: Preaching is not complete in the speaking but in the hearing; the congregation has a calling too, and the preacher must labor to form hearers, not merely to deliver sermons. A church that cannot hear will starve under the best preaching.
chapters.body:
We have spent eleven chapters on the preacher, and that is right, because this is a book for preachers, but it would be a lie to end without turning to the other half of the transaction, because preaching is not finished in the mouth. It is finished in the ear, and then in the will, and a sermon perfectly preached to people who cannot or will not hear is like seed scattered on a road, sown with care and eaten by birds. Jesus told a parable about exactly this, and we usually preach it as a warning to the preacher about his methods, when in fact it is mostly a warning about the soils, about the hearers, about the radically different fates of the same seed depending on the ground it falls into (Luke 8:4-15). The same word. Four kinds of hearing. One harvest. The preacher is responsible for the seed. But the soil has a calling too.

I have come, late and reluctantly, to believe that one of the preacher's central tasks is the formation of hearers, and that we have almost entirely neglected it. We labor over the sermon and assume the hearing, as though our only job were to deliver and theirs were automatically to receive. But hearing is a skill, a discipline, even a spiritual gift to be cultivated, and a congregation can be taught to hear well or left to hear badly, and the difference over years is the difference between a church that thrives under ordinary preaching and a church that starves under excellent preaching. Jesus said it constantly: he that hath ears to hear, let him hear. The phrase assumes that hearing is something one does, actively, with effort, not something that happens to a passive recipient. There is a way of sitting under the word that receives it and a way that lets it run off, and most of our people have never been taught the difference.

I want to name a hearing problem we rarely diagnose because it wears the costume of devotion, and that is the hearer who loves the preaching and changes nothing. He is at every service. He takes notes. He tells the pastor how much the sermon meant to him. He can discuss the finer points of the morning's text over lunch. And his life does not move, year after year, the same besetting sins, the same shallow obedience, the same unchanged heart underneath a great enthusiasm for the word. James named this man with surgical precision: he is like a man who beholds his natural face in a mirror, and goes his way, and straightway forgets what manner of man he was (James 1:23-24). The mirror showed him the truth about himself. He saw it. And he walked away and forgot it, because seeing was never going to be enough, because the word James says must be received is the word that is done, not merely heard, and a man who hears without doing has deceived himself, James says, deceived himself, convinced himself he is in a good place because he loves the preaching, when the love of the preaching has become a substitute for the doing of the word rather than a path to it. This man is harder to reach than the open skeptic, because the skeptic knows he is resisting and this man does not, this man thinks his enthusiasm is obedience, mistakes his appreciation of the sermon for the transformation the sermon was meant to produce. The preacher must love this man enough to disturb him, to tell him that hearing is not doing, that the test of whether the word has been received is not how it made you feel but how it changed your week, that a lifetime of moving sermons that moved you to nothing is a lifetime of looking in the mirror and forgetting your own face.

What does bad hearing look like? It looks like the consumer in the pew who has come to evaluate the performance, who sits with arms folded asking whether the preacher is good enough to hold his interest, who treats the sermon as a product offered for his approval and himself as the critic whose job is to render a verdict. That posture cannot receive the word, because the word does not come to be evaluated; it comes to evaluate. The consumer has the relationship exactly backwards. He thinks he is judging the sermon when in fact the word in the sermon is judging him, and his folded arms and raised eyebrow are not the posture of a discerning Christian but the posture of a man who has made himself the lord of a word that came to make him a servant. We have produced congregations of sermon-tasters, connoisseurs who can tell you whether the preaching was good the way they could tell you whether a meal was good, and who have no idea that this very connoisseurship is starving them, because the word cannot feed a man who is busy critiquing the plating.

What does good hearing look like? It looks like the Bereans, who received the word with all readiness of mind and searched the Scriptures daily to see whether those things were so (Acts 17:11). Notice the combination, because it is exact and it is rare. Readiness of mind, an eager, open, expectant posture, leaning in to receive rather than sitting back to judge. And searching the Scriptures, a discernment, a checking of the preaching against the text, a refusal to swallow whatever they were told. The Bereans were not gullible and they were not cynical. They were hungry and they were careful, both at once, and that combination is what a well-formed hearer looks like. They wanted the word and they tested the word, and the testing served the wanting, and Luke calls them more noble than the Thessalonians for exactly this. We need to produce Bereans, and we will not produce them by accident.

There is a structure to the church that either helps or hinders the formation of hearers, and we rarely think about it as a discipleship question, but it is one. A church where the entire spiritual life happens in the Sunday gathering, where people arrive, receive, and leave, with no other engagement with the word all week, will produce passive hearers almost by default, because the sermon is the only spiritual input they get and they receive it the way they receive every other piece of media, as content delivered to a consumer. But a church where the word is engaged all week, in small groups that discuss the preaching, in families that talk about it around the table, in individuals who carry the text into their own reading, produces a different kind of hearer, one who comes to Sunday already engaged, who hears the sermon as one moment in an ongoing engagement with Scripture rather than as a standalone performance to be rated. The preacher who wants to form hearers should think hard about the whole structure of his church's engagement with the word, not just the sermon, because the sermon does not form hearers by itself; it forms them in concert with everything else the church does or fails to do with the word. A great sermon preached into a passive structure is mostly wasted, eaten by the birds of distraction and consumerism, while an ordinary sermon preached into a church that engages the word all week bears thirty and sixty and a hundredfold, because the soil was prepared by everything that surrounded the sowing. Build the structure that forms hearers. The sermon is the seed, but the soil is built by a thousand other things, and a wise preacher tends the soil as carefully as he prepares the seed.

How does a preacher form hearers? Partly by teaching them explicitly, by preaching now and then on how to receive a sermon, on what their calling as hearers is, on the parable of the soils as a word to them and not only to him. I have done this, and it changes things, because most people have simply never thought about it, have never been told that they have a job on Sunday morning beyond attendance, have assumed that hearing was passive and the preacher did all the work. When you tell them otherwise, when you call them to active, prayerful, expectant, discerning hearing, many of them rise to it, relieved almost, glad to have a part to play, glad to be told that the word is not a performance for them to rate but a feast for them to eat. The preacher forms hearers also by his own example as a hearer, by being visibly under the word himself, so that they see that this is how a Christian relates to Scripture, with hunger and submission, and they learn the posture by watching it modeled in the man up front.

I want to name the four soils precisely, because they are not random and they map onto people every pastor knows. The seed by the wayside, snatched away before it can take root, is the hardened hearer, the one whose heart is packed down like a path by long traffic, who hears and nothing penetrates because nothing has been allowed to penetrate in years. The seed on the rock, springing up fast and withering for lack of root, is the enthusiastic hearer, the one who responds with great emotion to every sermon and changes nothing, whose faith is all surface and no depth, who weeps on Sunday and is unchanged by Wednesday because the word never went down past the feelings into the will. The seed among thorns, choked by the cares and riches and pleasures of this life, is the divided hearer, the one who genuinely receives the word but lets it be crowded out by a hundred competing loves, the busy and prosperous and distracted, whose lives are simply too full of other things for the word to bear fruit. And the seed on good ground, which Jesus says are they who, having heard the word, keep it and bring forth fruit with patience, is the hearer who receives and retains and obeys over the long haul. Notice the words attached to good hearing: an honest and good heart, keeping the word, patience. Good hearing is not a single dramatic response; it is a settled, patient, retaining, obeying posture sustained over years. The preacher cannot manufacture an honest and good heart in his hearers, but he can teach them what the four soils are, can hold the mirror up so that each hearer asks which ground he is, can warn the enthusiast that emotion is not faith and the busy man that his fullness is choking him, and that warning, received, is itself a means by which God breaks up the packed paths and clears the thorns.

But the deepest formation of hearers happens through the steady diet itself, through the long, patient, week-after-week feeding of the whole counsel, which slowly produces a congregation that knows its Bible and can therefore hear well. A congregation that has been fed thin gruel for years cannot suddenly hear a substantial sermon; their capacity has atrophied, their palate has been ruined, they have been trained to expect the spiritual equivalent of fast food and they find real food strange and heavy and hard to digest. But a congregation that has been fed well for years develops a capacity for the word, an appetite for substance, an ability to follow an argument and sit under a hard text and receive correction, and this capacity is itself a creation of the preaching, built up slowly, sermon by sermon, until you have a body of people who can hear things that would have been wasted on them a decade earlier. The preaching forms the hearers who can then receive the preaching. It is a long, slow, mutual thing, and it does not happen in a year.

I want to say a word to discourage a misuse of this chapter, because a preacher in a hard church will be tempted to use it as an excuse. There are pastors with genuinely difficult congregations, hard soil, resistant hearers, people who will not receive the word however faithfully it is preached, and such a pastor might read this chapter and feel justified, might conclude that his fruitlessness is entirely the soil's fault and none of his own. Resist that. Yes, the soil matters, and yes, some hearing is bad through no fault of the preacher, and Jesus himself preached to soil that mostly rejected the seed. But the preacher's first response to hard soil is never to blame it; it is to examine his own seed and his own sowing, to make sure that what he is scattering is actually the word and not his own opinions, to make sure he has sown faithfully and prayed earnestly before he concludes that the failure is theirs. The parable of the soils is a comfort to the faithful preacher whose good seed falls on bad ground, but it is not a hiding place for the lazy preacher who wants to blame his people for the consequences of his own thin sowing. Sow well first. Then, if the soil still rejects it, you may grieve like Jesus grieved, but not before.

There is a practical counsel I give to congregations, and it has done more good than any sermon I have preached on the subject, because it is small and concrete and people can actually do it. Come to church having prayed. Not having prayed elaborately, just having asked God, before you walk in, to speak to you through the preaching, to give you ears to hear, to show you the one thing he wants you to see and do. A congregation that prays its way into the service is a different congregation from one that stumbles in cold, distracted, half-present, treating the gathering as one more item on a busy weekend. And come expecting. Expectation is most of hearing. The person who comes expecting God to speak hears God speak, because he is listening for it, leaning in, ready; the person who comes expecting a presentation to evaluate hears a presentation to evaluate, because that is what he came for and that is what his posture will receive. The same sermon falls on both, and the first goes home fed and the second goes home with a verdict on the preacher, and the difference was not the sermon but the coming, the posture, the expectation, the prayer that preceded the listening. And then, after the service, do one thing with what you heard. Not ten things. One. Take the single clearest thing the word pressed on you and obey it that week, and you will find that a lifetime of single obediences, week after week, builds a Christian, where a lifetime of admiring sermons and obeying none of them builds only a connoisseur. I tell my people this constantly, because it puts their growth back in their own hands where half of it belongs, and it frees them from the passive consumer's posture that was slowly starving them.

I want to say a word about the children, because they are hearers too, and most preaching ignores them entirely or condescends to them, and both are mistakes. A child sitting in the service, even a young one, is absorbing more than we think, learning, by watching the adults around him and by the atmosphere of the gathering, what the word of God is and how it is to be received. He may not follow the argument, but he is learning whether his parents take this seriously, whether the book is treated as holy, whether the gathering is a place where God is expected to speak, and those lessons, absorbed young, shape him more deeply than any sermon he will later understand. I have five sons, and I have watched them learn the posture toward Scripture long before they could grasp its content, learn it from how their mother and I handled the Bible, from whether we came to church hungry or distracted, from whether the word was central in our home or a Sunday formality. The preacher cannot reach the children directly with much of his content, but he shapes the atmosphere they are absorbing, and a church where the word is genuinely revered raises children who revere it, while a church where the word is treated casually raises children who treat it casually, whatever the words of the sermons say. Form the children by forming the reverence of the room, by treating the word as the holy thing it is, by your own visible hunger for it, because the children are watching the adults far more than they are listening to the preacher, and they are learning, in those formative years, the posture that will determine whether the word ever has a chance with them when they are old enough to receive its content.

There is a beautiful thing that happens in a church where hearers have been well formed, and I have been privileged to see it, and it is the closest thing to a reward the patient preacher gets this side of glory. You stand up to preach and you can feel the room leaning in, not to evaluate you but to receive God, a body of people who have learned to come hungry and expectant, who have their Bibles open and their hearts open, who are doing the work of hearing as hard as you are doing the work of preaching, so that the sermon becomes a genuine collaboration, the preacher sowing and the people receiving and the Spirit moving between them. That kind of congregation makes a mediocre preacher effective and an effective preacher dangerous, in the best sense, because the word lands in soil prepared to bear it, and the harvest is thirty and sixty and a hundredfold. I would rather preach to a hundred well-formed hearers than to a thousand sermon-tasters, because the hundred will receive the word and bear fruit and pass it to their children, while the thousand will applaud and forget and go home unchanged.

There is a responsibility laid on the hearer that we have almost stopped preaching, and the writer of Hebrews states it without flinching. Take heed, he warns, lest the word preached fail to profit, because it was not mixed with faith in them that heard it (Hebrews 4:2). The word can be preached faithfully and still fail to profit, and the failure is located in the hearing, in the absence of the faith that must be mixed with the word for the word to do its work. This is sobering for the hearer and freeing for the preacher both. Sobering for the hearer, because it means he cannot sit passively and blame the preacher when nothing changes; the word came, and whether it profits depends in part on whether he received it in faith or let it run off. Freeing for the preacher, because it means the failure of a sermon to profit a particular hearer is not automatically the preacher's fault; he sowed the word, and the hearer did not mix it with faith, and that mixing was the hearer's responsibility and not the sower's. We have created congregations that believe the entire weight of Sunday rests on the preacher, that their only job is to attend and evaluate, and Hebrews demolishes that assumption. The hearer is a participant, not an audience. The word must be mixed with his faith or it will not profit him, however faithfully it was preached, and a preacher who never tells his people this has left them ignorant of half their own calling and has quietly taught them that the responsibility for their growth lies entirely outside themselves, which is a lie that keeps people spiritual infants for decades.

A sermon is finished not when it is preached but when it is heard and obeyed, when the seed has gone down into good ground and brought forth fruit with patience. The preacher cannot make the soil good; that is the Spirit's work, the same wind we cannot command. But the preacher can sow faithfully, and he can labor to form hearers, and he can call his people to their own calling, which is not to rate the preaching but to receive the word, not to judge the sermon but to be judged and fed and changed by it. Form your hearers. Teach them to come hungry, to listen actively, to test what they hear and then to obey what they have tested. And then preach, and trust the word and the wind to do, in the soil you cannot control, what no amount of preaching skill could ever accomplish on its own.
chapters.verdict: A sermon is finished not when it is preached but when it is heard and obeyed.
reflect: Are you forming hearers, or only producing sermons?
What have you taught your people about how to receive the word?
Do you preach to a passive audience or to fellow servants under the same word?

chapters.title: A Word That Outlasts the Voice
chapters.summary: The preacher's labor is to deliver something that will hold after he is gone; the grass withers and the flower fades, but the word of God endures forever. Faithful exposition builds on the only foundation that survives.
chapters.body:
Every preacher is building something that will outlast him, or failing to, and the question of which one is decided not at the end but in the daily choice of what to put at the center of the sermon. A ministry built on a man ends when the man ends. A ministry built on the word endures, because the word endures, and the only way to build on the word is to preach it, week after week, in submission, refusing every easier foundation that the sand of personality and relevance and applause is constantly offering. This is the final argument for expository preaching, and it is an argument about time, about what survives, about what a preacher leaves behind when the voice that thrilled the room has fallen silent forever.

Isaiah saw it. The grass withereth, the flower fadeth, because the spirit of the LORD bloweth upon it; surely the people is grass. The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever (Isaiah 40:6-8). The preacher is grass. His gifts are grass. His charisma, his reputation, his ability to fill a room, all of it is grass, and the wind of God is already blowing on it, and it is already fading, though he cannot feel the fading in the years of his strength. The word alone stands. And the only ministry that stands is the ministry that bound itself to the word, that made the standing thing its foundation rather than the fading thing, that built its house on the rock of what God said rather than the sand of who the preacher was. Peter quotes this very passage and then adds the line that turns it toward us: this is the word which by the gospel is preached unto you (1 Peter 1:25). The enduring word is the preached word. The thing that lasts forever is the very thing the preacher holds in his hands on Sunday morning.

There is a question worth asking about every sermon, and it reframes the whole enterprise: am I building something that will hold when this person is dying? Because that is the real test, the one that strips away every lesser measure. The sermon may be clever, may be relevant, may be moving, may draw a crowd, but the only question that finally matters is whether the thing I am depositing in this person will be there, standing, holding, on the day the diagnosis comes back terminal, on the night the marriage finally ends, at the graveside of the child, in the hour when every comfortable thing has been stripped away and the soul is left with only what was built into it deeply enough to survive the stripping. Most of what we preach for, the response in the room, the growth in the numbers, the affirmation at the door, none of it will be there in that hour. The crowd will not be there. The preacher's charm will not be there. The relevance, so carefully tuned to a moment, will be revealed as belonging to a moment that has passed. Only the word will be there, if the word was built in, only the truth deposited deeply enough over years of ordinary Sundays to rise up when it is needed and hold. So I have learned to ask, of the sermon I am building, not will this work but will this hold, not will they like it but will it be there for them in the dark. And that question, asked honestly, changes what I preach, drives me toward the deep and enduring and away from the clever and immediate, because I have stood at enough gravesides to know which one a person actually needs, and it was never the clever thing, never once.

I have buried members of my congregation, and I have learned at gravesides what I could not learn in the comfort of the study. At a graveside the preacher's eloquence is worth exactly nothing. The grieving do not need a clever man; they need a word from outside the grave, a word that the grave cannot touch, and the only such word is the word of God. I have stood at the edge of holes in the ground and watched people reach back for whatever they had been given over the years, and I have seen the difference, stark and unmistakable, between those who had been fed the word and those who had been fed the preacher. The ones who had only the preacher had nothing at the graveside, because the preacher's charm does not reach into a casket. The ones who had the word had something to stand on, because the word of God reaches places no human voice can follow, into the ground and past it. That is the moment the whole argument of this book comes due. That is when you learn what you actually built.

I think of a woman in my church, years ago now, who lost a child, the worst grief there is, the grief that has no natural floor. And I sat with her in the days after, helpless, with nothing to offer that would not have been an insult, and what held her was not anything I said in those days. What held her was the word that had been deposited in her over years of ordinary Sundays, the passages she had heard a hundred times and half-forgotten she knew, rising up in her in the worst hour to do exactly what they were given to do. She quoted Scripture to me, in her grief, the very texts she had received under preaching she probably could not have told you the content of a week after she heard it. The sermons were gone. The word remained. And it stood under her when the ground had given way, and I understood, watching her, what I am actually for, what all the study and the labor and the dry Tuesdays are actually building toward. Not memorable sermons. A deposited word, available in the dark, when nothing else will serve.

Bonhoeffer was hanged at Flossenburg in April 1945, days before the camp was liberated, and the witnesses said he went to the gallows composed, having just led a final service. What held him in that hour was not his theology as an achievement but the word as a possession, the Scripture he had heard and obeyed and let search him for years, returning to him at the end as the only thing strong enough to face the rope. The word he had preached to others held him when nothing else could, because he had not merely studied it but submitted to it, had let it become the foundation rather than the material. His books endure, yes, but what endured in the moment of his death was the word itself, the thing he had bound his life to, standing for him when everything else had been stripped away. That is the test no preacher can dodge forever, and it is the test the comfortable seasons of ministry are quietly preparing us either to pass or to fail.

I think about the long history of the church here, because it is the most powerful evidence for everything this book has argued. Consider how the gospel actually reached us. It did not reach us primarily through the famous preachers whose names survive in the books. It reached us through ten thousand forgotten men in forgotten places, ordinary pastors in ordinary towns who opened the book and preached it, week after week, and were buried and forgotten, their sermons lost, their names erased, and yet the word they preached went down into people who passed it to their children who passed it to theirs, across centuries, until it reached you and me. The chain that brought the gospel to us is almost entirely a chain of forgotten heralds, men whose only monument is the faith of people they never met in a century they could not imagine. Calvin's name survives, and Spurgeon's, and a handful of others, but they are the rare exceptions, and even they will fade in time. The vast machinery by which the word has traveled through history is a machinery of forgotten faithfulness, plain men preaching the enduring word and then vanishing, their work surviving not in their reputations but in the word itself, standing in lives long after the men who deposited it had turned to dust. You are a link in that chain. You will be forgotten like almost all the links before you.
