And the word you preach, if you preach the word and not yourself, will go on past you exactly as it came to you, carried by people you will never know toward a future you will never see, which is the only immortality the pulpit offers and the only one worth wanting.

What we are doing, in the unglamorous labor of expository preaching, is depositing the enduring word into people who will need it at the hour when nothing else will serve. We are building, in them, a foundation we will not be present to defend, equipping them for catastrophes we will not witness, putting into their hands a word that will speak after our own voices have fallen silent. This is the long obedience of the pulpit, and it does not look like much in any given week. A man stands up, opens a text, gives its sense, sits down. The room half-listens. Nothing visibly changes. But over the years, sermon by sermon, the word is being deposited, and the deposit is the thing that lasts, and one day, in a hospital room or a graveside or a midnight of the soul, the deposit will be drawn upon by a person the preacher may have long forgotten, and the word will be there, standing, when the preacher himself is dust.

There is a passage that has become, for me, the quiet motto of a long ministry, and it is Paul's word to Timothy about succession. The things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also (2 Timothy 2:2). Count the generations in that one sentence. Paul to Timothy. Timothy to faithful men. Faithful men to others also. Four generations of the word being handed down, and Paul is in a cell, about to die, thinking not about his own legacy but about the chain that will carry the word past him, into people he will never meet, taught by people he is now teaching. This is the long vision the pulpit requires, the vision that sees past the present Sunday to the unborn generations who will receive the word through the people you are depositing it in now. You are not preaching only to the people in front of you. You are preaching to their children, and their children's children, depositing a word that will be handed down a chain you cannot see the end of, and your faithfulness this Sunday is a link in a chain that may run for centuries past your death. That changes how a man preaches. It makes him patient, willing to build slowly, content to deposit the word in people who will carry it forward long after he is gone, freed from the tyranny of the immediate result because he is building for a harvest he will not live to see. Paul died not knowing what would become of the word he committed to Timothy. We are what became of it. And the word you commit to faithful men this year will become, in time, a future you cannot imagine, which is reason enough to commit it faithfully and then, like Paul, to let go and trust the chain.

So the final discipline is the discipline of building for a time you will not see. It is the willingness to make the sermon about the enduring thing rather than the impressive thing, even when the impressive thing would serve you better in the short term, because the short term is grass and the word is not. It is the choice, repeated across a ministry, to decrease so that the word might increase, to get out of the way so that what survives the preacher might be deposited cleanly, unmixed with the preacher's own fading glory. The man who preaches himself builds a monument that the first strong wind will scatter. The man who preaches the word builds on the rock, and though the building looks plainer and draws smaller crowds and earns less applause, it stands, and it goes on standing after the builder is forgotten, which is exactly as it should be, because the building was never about the builder.

There is a kind of monument-building that goes on in ministry, and it is so respectable we rarely call it what it is. A man builds a large church, or a network, or a reputation, or a body of books and recordings, and he tells himself, and we all tell him, that he is building the kingdom, when a good deal of what he is building is a monument to himself, a structure dependent on his presence, his energy, his personality, a thing that will not outlast him because it was never built on the only foundation that outlasts a man. The test of whether you have built a monument or a foundation is brutally simple: what happens when you leave? The monument-builder's work collapses when he goes, because he was holding it up, because the people had gathered around him and there was nothing underneath when he was removed. The foundation-builder's work continues without him, perhaps grows, because he had pointed the people past himself to the word and to Christ, had deposited something in them that did not depend on his presence, had built on the rock rather than being the rock. I have watched both. I have watched a famous ministry evaporate within a few years of its founder's departure, the crowds scattering, the structure folding, because the structure had been a man, and men do not last. And I have watched an obscure faithful pastor die and his work go on, his people standing strong decades later, his deposit still bearing fruit in lives he never knew, because he had built on the word and not on himself. The first man got the bigger funeral. The second man got the longer harvest. And only one of those is worth a life.

I have five sons, and I will tell you what I want them to remember of me when I am gone, because it sharpens this for me more than any abstraction. I do not particularly want them to remember that their father was a good preacher. I want them to remember the word their father preached, to have it deposited in them so deep that it rises up in their own dark hours long after I am unavailable to say it to them, to find them at gravesides and in midnights I will not be alive to share. If they remember me and forget the word, I have failed at the one thing that mattered. If they forget the particulars of me and carry the word, I have succeeded, even though my own memory fades, because the word will be doing in them what I most wanted to do and could not, standing under them when their father is dust. That is the strange ambition I want to commend to you, the ambition to be the forgotten conduit of an unforgettable word.

I will be forgotten. This is not false humility; it is arithmetic. Within a generation or two of my death, no one will remember my sermons, my turns of phrase, the way I held a room on a good Sunday. The grass withers. But if I have preached the word, then something will remain that is not me, deposited in people and passed to their children, the enduring word standing in lives I will never know about, doing its work long after my own work has ended. That is the only success the pulpit offers that is worth wanting, and it requires the preacher to want his own forgetting, to labor for an outcome in which he disappears and the word remains. It is the strangest ambition in the world, the ambition to be forgotten so that God might be remembered, and it is the only ambition the office permits.

I find a strange freedom in this that I did not expect when I was younger, and I want to offer it to the preacher who is still striving, still anxious about his impact, still measuring himself against the men whose names are large. The freedom is this: you do not have to be remembered. The whole crushing weight of building a legacy, of mattering, of leaving a mark, of being one of the names that survives, lifts off the moment you accept that you are grass and that your forgetting is not a tragedy but the natural and appointed end of a creature, and that the only thing meant to survive you was never you but the word you carried. The men who are destroyed by ministry are so often the men who could not accept their own forgetting, who needed to matter, who built monuments because they could not bear the thought of vanishing, and the need to be remembered drove them into the very self-display that hollowed out their preaching. But the man who has made peace with being forgotten is free, free to decrease, free to point past himself, free to deposit the word in people who will never remember his name, free to spend his one life on a thing that will outlast him precisely because it was never about him. I am going to be forgotten, and I have stopped fighting it, and the stopping has been one of the great releases of my ministry, because the energy I once spent trying to matter is now available to spend on the word, which is the only thing that will matter when I am gone. Make peace with your forgetting. It is the doorway to the only freedom the pulpit offers, the freedom of a man who has nothing left to protect because he has surrendered the one thing he was clutching, his own enduring significance, and received in its place the joy of serving something that will endure when he does not.

They will forget your sermons. They will forget your name, eventually, and your face, and the particular gifts you were so tempted to display. The wind is already blowing on the grass, and you are the grass. Make sure, then, that what you hand them is not the grass but the word, the thing that does not wither, the thing that will stand at their gravesides and yours and at the great appearing Paul invoked when he first laid the charge. Preach the word. Build on the only foundation that survives the builder. And then, having built it, be willing to vanish into it, content to be the forgotten herald of a word that will never, world without end, be forgotten.

The grass withers. The word stands. Spend your one life on the thing that lasts.
